Enthusiasmo; Dum è contrario Protestantes tàm Enthusiasmum, quàm Verbum non-Scriptum, Scripturae adversa, explodunt penitus; Rationem verò, utcunque illuminatam, non Principium probandi, sed nudum apprehendendi instrumentum arbitrantur. (2.) Elementorum Christianae Religionis in omnibus particulis suis ingenua infucatâque receptione ac professione, Symboli Scilicet Apostolici, Decalogi, Precationis Dominicae, & duorum duntaxat Sacramentorum, Signata sua non significantium tantùm, sed & exhibentium & obsignantium.
english: §. III. That Protestants agree fundamentally among themselves has already been shown a priori; the same can be confirmed a posteriori by running through the general necessary heads of Christian doctrine.

(1.) They agree on the first and only adequate principle for knowing all Christian dogmas — at least all the necessary ones — namely Holy Scripture: held by Protestants with one voice as a rule and norm, both sufficient and perfect and clear enough, for everything Christians must believe and must do.

Other so-called Christians (synonymously or only equivocally) differ here: they either set something beside Scripture as co-principle — Traditions, the unwritten word — or put Scripture under something else, native light (reason) or fictitious light (enthusiasm).

Protestants, by contrast, explode enthusiasm and the unwritten word as hostile to Scripture; and they treat reason, however illuminated, not as a principle of proof but as a bare instrument of apprehension.

(2.) They agree in an honest, unvarnished reception and profession of the elements of Christian religion in all their parts: the Apostles' Creed, the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer, and only two sacraments — which not only signify their significates but also exhibit and seal them.

source_text: [3.] Augustanae Confessioni, eidemque Invariatae, facta sincera adstipulatione, etiam quod ad X. ejusdem Articulum attinet, Germanicè hic, vel Latinè legatur, dummodò Species panis & vini, in Germanica editione memoratae, non sensu Pontificio, pro accidentibus eorum, sed sensu Lutherano, pro Symbolis Corporis & Sanguinis Christi, accipiantur. Unde Reformati Collocutores Lipsienses testati sunt, se nunquam non ad subsignandum Invariatae Confessioni paratos fore, totôque illi pectore adhaesuros, uti jam tum diximus Annotat. I., infrà verba ipsorum adducturi. Denique (4.) ipsius Formulae Concordiae strictè sic dictae, i. e. tùm Epitomes Articulorum quorundam controversorum, tùm solidae Declarationis ac Repetitionis eorundem, tàm quoad Substantiam, quam quoad Modos, admissione, exceptis duntaxat Modis duobus, alterô ad Articulum de Coena S., ad articulum de Persona Christi alterô pertinente, quorum tamen Modorum binorum diversitatem Fundamentum Fidei Christianae ne è longinquo quidem attingere, locis suis demonstrabimus. Vide interim Tractatulum nostrum German. de Consensu Protestantium fundamentali à §. 10. ad 24.
english: (3.) They agree in sincere adhesion to the Augsburg Confession — and to it as Invariata — even on Article X, whether the German or the Latin is read here, provided the "species" of bread and wine in the German edition are taken not in the Roman sense (as accidents) but in the Lutheran sense (as symbols of Christ's body and blood).

Hence the Reformed colloquists at Leipzig testified they would always be ready to subscribe the Invariata Confession and cling to it with their whole heart — as we already said in Annotation I, and will quote their words below.

(4.) They agree in admitting the Formula of Concord strictly so called — both the Epitome of certain disputed articles and the Solid Declaration and Repetition of the same — as to substance and as to modes, except only two modes: one on the Holy Supper, the other on the Person of Christ.

Even that twofold modal diversity, we shall show in due place, does not touch the foundation of the Christian faith even from afar. See meanwhile our German tract on the Protestants' fundamental consensus, §§. 10–24.

source_text:
§. IV.
Itaque omnis Dissensus Protestantium, inter se, Praeter-Fundamentalis meritò audit, cujus & Ortus & Progressus & ἀκμὴ seu Fastigium, hoc loco per compendium recensenda. Initium dicti dissensûs ponendum in Controversia de Interpretatione verborum Coenae, quam aliam aliamque primi Reformatores tres, Carolostadius, Lutherus, & Zwinglius, Pontificiis abusibus opponendam, meditati fuerant non per omnia aequè commodam. Calixt. Jud. Controv. §. 47. Et Lutherus quidem, à Praeceptore quondam suo Petro de Aliaco, Cardinali Cammeracensi, haustam, & Pontificiis paucioribus melioribusque adhuc receptam, retinebat, quâ ita Corpus Christi de pane praedicari innuebat, ut cum pane manente Corpus Christi in usu Coenae conjungeretur. Tom. II. Wittenb. Lat. fol. 70. B. eóq; praedicaretur de pane ceu in pane contentum, per propositionem inusitatam quidem, interim propriam, ac Tropô Rhetoricô quocunque cassam. Carolostadius Pontificiis adversaturus magis, Propositionem Identicam comminiscebatur, Corpus Christi, (haud secus ac Pontificia communior Sententia,) Panem Coena Domini exturbaturus, quasi Christus acceptum, benedictum fractumque panem eumque solum discipulis suis dedisset, inter dandum verò, digito in corpus suum directo, de hoc, non autem de Pane, dixisset: Hoc est corpus meum. Zwinglius denique, medius inter duos, & Panem, & Corpus Christi in Coena, sed istum Corporali, hoc Spirituali modo retenturus, Corpus Christi de Pane impropriè praedicari docebat improprietate omnibus Propositionibus Sacramentalibus communi, quâ per Metonymiam, Signatum de Signo dicitur, quod per signum significatur, modoque spirituali exhibetur.
english: §. IV. So every dissent among Protestants is rightly called praeter-fundamental. Its origin, progress, and peak (akme) may be sketched here in brief.

That dissent begins in the controversy over interpreting the words of the Supper — which the three first Reformers, Carlstadt, Luther, and Zwingli, each framed differently as a counter to Roman abuses, and not equally handy in every respect (Calixtus, Judgment of Controversies §. 47).

Luther kept the line drawn from his former teacher Peter d'Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, and still held by the fewer and better Romanists: that Christ's body is predicated of the bread so that, the bread remaining, Christ's body is joined with the bread in the Supper's use (Wittenberg Latin Tom. II, fol. 70 B) — predicated of the bread as contained in the bread, by a proposition unusual yet proper, and empty of any rhetorical trope.

Carlstadt, pressing the Romans harder, invented an identical proposition: driving the bread of the Lord's Supper out by Christ's body (much as the more common Roman view), as if Christ had given his disciples only the received, blessed, broken bread, and while giving, pointing to his own body, had said of that — not of the bread — "This is my body."

Zwingli, midway between them, meant to keep both bread and Christ's body in the Supper — the bread corporally, the body spiritually — and taught that Christ's body is improperly predicated of the bread by the impropriety common to all sacramental propositions: by metonymy the significate is said of the sign, which signifies it and exhibits it spiritually.

source_text: Media seu Carolostadii interpretatio, ceu Fabulosa & Historiolam quandam, extra Scripturam confictam, haud absimilem Fabulae socinianae, verbis Joh. 1. v. 3. Et verbum erat apud Deum, assuta (quâ Deitati Christi infesti imminent Sociniani) in medium adducens, adstipulatores invenit paucissimos, & paulò post evanuit, residuis duabus, alterâ in superiori Germania, in Inferiori alterâ, tantò majori cum animi contentione edoctis, quantò sibi initiò videbantur invicem obnitentes magis. Illa Corporalem Localemve in pane Corporis Christi praesentiam; Haec verò nullam omnino, & ne Spiritualem quidem praesentiam admittere primô intuitu visa. Illa in subsidium corporis Christi Ubiquitatem, praeteritis inauditam Seculis; Haec ejusdem Corporis ad dextram Dei in coelis Sessionem, in qua ascenderat, assumens.
english: Carlstadt's middle reading — fabulous, and dragging in a little story forged outside Scripture, not unlike the Socinian fable stitched onto [[John 1:3 >> Bible:John 1:3]] "And the word was with God" (by which Socinians hostile to Christ's deity press their case) — found very few backers and soon vanished.
The other two remained, taught with all the more heat — one in upper Germany, the other in Lower — the more they first seemed to clash.
The one: a corporeal or local presence of Christ's body in the bread. The other: at first glance seeming to admit no presence at all, not even a spiritual one.
The former called in aid the ubiquity of Christ's body, unheard of in past ages; the latter, that body's session at God's right hand in the heavens into which it had ascended.

source_text:
§. V.
Quô ipsô Dissensus Protestantium, in interpretatione Verborum Coenae & in Praesentiae Corporis Christi modo, in usu Sacrae Coenae, exorsus, Incrementa cepit, per Controversiam de Ubiquitate Corporis Christi, à Luthero quidem in aestu disputationis semel atque iterum, duobus potissimum Confessionis suae majoris locis, Calixto allegatis, loc. cit. num. 41. 42.
english: §. V. That same Protestant split — begun over how the Supper words are read and over the mode of Christ's bodily presence in the Holy Supper's use — then grew through the controversy on the ubiquity of Christ's body.
Luther himself, once and again in the heat of debate, had drawn it in, chiefly from two places in his Greater Confession — the ones Calixtus cites at loc. cit. nos. 41–42.

source_text: eam in rem adductam, ut corporalem in Coena S. Corporis Christi praesentiam tantò faciliùs defendere valeret, sed posteà neglectam,
english: He brought ubiquity in so he could defend a corporeal presence of Christ's body in the Holy Supper more easily — then later let it drop.

source_text: à Brentio verò & Jacobo Andrea (uti annot. precedenti §. 14. diximus) contradicente tamen ejusdem licèt sententiae de Coena participe Tillemanno Heshusio (videatur Hospin. Hist. Sacr. pag. 40.) reassumtam
english: Brentius and Jacob Andreae took it up again (as we noted in the preceding Annotation, §.14) — even though Tillemann Heshusius, who shared their Supper view, contradicted them (see Hospinian, Historia Sacramentaria, p. 40).

source_text: & à Marbachio Sen. aliis etiam propositionibus similibus & absurdioribus confirmatam defensamque, quibus Humanam Christi Naturam vel DEum ipsum rectè dici posse, ausus est affirmare, id quod ipse Celeberr. Fechtius refert, in Supplem. Historiae Eccl. pag. 30. Conf. Hospin. Concord. discord. cap. 55.;
english: Marbach the Elder then confirmed and defended it with further like — and even more absurd — propositions, daring to say Christ's human nature can rightly be called God Himself.
So Fechtius reports in his Supplement to Ecclesiastical History, p. 30 (cf. Hospinian, Concordia discordans, ch. 55).

source_text: à Torgensibus in priori Conventu, anno 1574. habito, Articulô 4. rejectam rursus,
english: The Torgau assembly of 1574 rejected it again in Article 4.

source_text: in posteriori, anni 1576. (in quo, Corpore Doctrinae Philippicô abrogatô, in ejus locum Novum hodieq; Formulâ Concordiae comprehensum Doctrinae Lutheranae Corpus successit) tacitam, tandemque à Patribus Bergensibus de Potentiali explicatam, in solid. Explicat. & Declarat. Artic. Controv. pag. mihi p. 754. Edit. in 4to. Anno 1580.
english: In the later Torgau meeting of 1576 it went silent — the year the Philippist Corpus Doctrinae was set aside and today's Formula of Concord body of Lutheran doctrine took its place.
At last the Bergen Fathers explained it as potential, in the Solid Declaration and Explanation of the Controverted Articles (my copy p. 754; 4to ed. 1580).

source_text:
§. VI.
Dissensus ad Fastigium pervenit quando, paulò post Formulam Concordiae in lucem publicam editam, cujus Historia satis superque nota, Sententiam de Praedestinatione inde ab Augustini temporibus Occidentali Ecclesiae tantùm non Universa, etiam Reformatoribus ejus primis utriusque Protestantium partis, Luthero Zwinglio, utpote Augustini & Thomae Aquinatis Discipulis, receptam, Ægidius Hunnius oppugnavit,
english: §. VI. Not long after the Formula of Concord came into print — a story already more than familiar — the Dissensus hit its peak.

Aegidius Hunnius struck at the Predestination teaching that, from Augustine onward, had been all but the rule of the Western Church, and that the first Reformers on both Protestant sides had taken over: Luther and Zwingli, as pupils of Augustine and of Thomas Aquinas.

source_text: & Patrum Augustino antiquiorum opinionem amplectendam suasit.
english: He pressed for taking up the view held by the Fathers who came before Augustine.

source_text: Enimverò ab hoc tempore, Hunnium plerique Lutheranorum sequuti sunt, Reformatis utplurimùm Augustinianae Doctrinae constanter insistentibus.
english: From then on the greater part of the Lutherans went with Hunnius, while most of the Reformed held fast to Augustinian teaching on this point.

source_text: Nostri (inquit saepius laudatus Calixtus) è quibus olim multi itidem Absolutum Decretum approbarunt, paulatim ad Sententiam primorum Quatuor Seculorum (nempe Decretum juxta praescientiam factum) sese receperunt, qua in re multùm & egregiè laboravit Ægidius Hunnius:
english: As the often-praised Calixtus puts it: many of our own once approved the Absolute Decree as well, then by degrees fell back to the teaching of the first four centuries — a decree framed according to foreknowledge — and Aegidius Hunnius did a great and distinguished work in that change:

source_text: Difficile autem est, Sententiam hanc ita proponere, ne quid Pelagianismo affine habere videatur, quemadmodum sanè Pelagianismi Hunnium accusant, tum Daniel Tossanus Calvinista, tùm Adamus Tannerus Jesuita. cit. loc, num. 22. Confer ejusdem Calixti Considerat. Doct. Reform, juxta Confess. Thoruniens. de Gratia p. 62.
english: Still, it is hard to set out that teaching without seeming to shade toward Pelagianism — and Daniel Tossanus the Calvinist and Adam Tanner the Jesuit both charge Hunnius with Pelagianism (cited place, no. 22).
See also the same Calixtus, Consideration of Reformed Doctrine according to the Thorun Confession, on Grace, p. 62.

source_text: interim nec hunc, nec antecedentium Dissensuum quemquam, Fundamentalem arbitrati, Tractatuló priori à num. 23. ad 35. num. 45. & à num. 76. ad 82, inclusivè.
english: And they still did not count this split — or any of the earlier ones — as Fundamental: see the earlier Tractate, nos. 23–35, no. 45, and nos. 76–82 inclusive.

source_text:
ANNOTATIO III.
De Moliminibus pro Consociatione susceptis, ad pag. 334. ad 341.
§. I.
Simulac Dissensus initium subortum fuisset, in ipsa herba suffocare illud annisus est nullis satis laudibus evehendus Landgravius Hassiae Philippus,
english: ANNOTATIO III. On the Attempts Made toward Consociation (pages 334–341).
§. I. The moment the Dissensus first broke out, Landgrave Philip of Hesse — a prince hard to praise enough — tried to choke it off in the bud.

source_text: pluribus eam in rem ad Lutherum, Melanchtonem & Brentium datis literis, Concordiam, tàm ante Augustana Comitia, quàm in ipsis celebratis, & fraternitatem cum Zvinglianis ineundam servandamq; seriò suadentibus, quae exstant apud Chytraeum in Actis cum Zwinglianis, indignantibus quoq;, dictos Theologos, Consensum fidei fundamentalem Zwinglianorum secum, haud agnoscere velle.
english: He wrote again and again to Luther, Melanchthon, and Brentius, pressing hard for Concord — both before the Augsburg Diet and while it sat — and for fraternity with the Zwinglians that would actually be kept.

Those letters are still in Chytraeus’s Acts with the Zwinglians; and the named theologians, for their part, were angry and would not admit that the Zwinglians shared with them a fundamental consensus of faith.

source_text: Sic enim Illustrissimus Princeps pro Zwinglianis in quadam Epistola disputat: Itaque mihi videtur, cùm in aliis Articulis vobiscum consentiant Zwingliani & Christum eâdem ratione, quâ vos, confiteantur, concedant etiam Christum in Coena per fidem manducari, quae Manducatio ad Salutem necessaria est, nec Omnipotentiae laudem Deo adimant, sed juxta Analogiam fidei Secundum Scripturam, sic intelligenda esse verba sentiant, ut ipsi intelligunt: Cùmq;, Christus, quia clarificatum Corpus habet, quô venter cibari nequit, vix aliter manducari possit, quàm à credentibus & per fidem; hac, inquam, cum ita se habeant, mihi videtur Sententia & Responsio vestra durior & non necessaria esse, spero etiam, Deo dante, vos diligentiùs cogitaturos & veriorem Sententiam secuturos esse, Chytraeus. Hist. August. Confess. p. 652. Responsorias Lutheri vide in Supplemento Buddeano nupero, Epistola 122. pag. 1024. 102.
english: So the Most Illustrious Prince argues for the Zwinglians in one letter (Chytraeus, History of the Augsburg Confession, p. 652): since they agree with you in the other articles, confess Christ as you do, grant that Christ is eaten in the Supper by faith — and that eating is needed for salvation — and do not strip God of omnipotence, but read the words by the analogy of faith according to Scripture as they take them; and since Christ’s glorified body cannot feed a stomach, so He can scarcely be eaten except by believers and through faith — your sentence and reply look harder than they need to be, and I hope God will bring you to a truer view.
For Luther’s answering letters, see the recent Buddeus Supplement, Epistle 122, pages 1024 and 102.

source_text: Quibus omnibus Landgravius tandem effecit, ut Marpurgum ad se excurrerent Theologi utriusque partis, seque praesente, anno 1529. Consensum Universalem, uno excepto de Coena Domini Articulo, inirent.
english: By all of this the Landgrave at last got the theologians of both sides to come out to him at Marburg, and there in 1529, with him present, they entered a Universal Consensus — one article excepted: the Lord’s Supper.

source_text: Qua de re ita Chytraeus: Zwinglius & Oecolampadius libenter, in caeteris omnibus, Lutheri Sententiam secuti sunt, de Sacramento tantùm sequi noluerunt p. 643. Etsi autem, an verum Corpus & Sanguis Christi Corporaliter in Pane & Vino Coenae Domini praesens sit, hoc tempore non concordavimus, tamen una pars alteri Christianam dilectionem, quantum cujusq; Conscientia feret, declarabit, & utraque pars Deum Omnipotentem diligenter orabit, ut nos Spiritu suo in vera Sententia confirmet, pag. 646. Addit Clariss. Buddeus, Prof. Hallensis celeberrimus, in Supplemento, Epistolam Lutheri 98. Joh. Agricolae inscriptam suasoriam quò omnia aspera verba & Scripta cessarent in posterum pag. 71. 72. Ipse praetereà Chytraeus contestatur initio Hist. suae de Actis cum Zwingl. secum omnibus piis optare, quò dissidiorum odiorumq; acerbitas leniatur & mitigetur. pag. 636.
english: On that outcome Chytraeus writes: Zwingli and Oecolampadius gladly followed Luther’s teaching in everything else; only on the Sacrament they would not follow (p. 643).

Though they had not yet agreed whether Christ’s true body and blood are corporally present in the bread and wine of the Lord’s Supper, each side would still show the other Christian love as far as conscience allowed, and both would pray God to confirm them by His Spirit in the true teaching (p. 646).
Buddeus, the noted Halle professor, adds in his Supplement Luther’s Epistle 98 to Johann Agricola, urging that harsh words and writings stop from then on (pp. 71–72).
Chytraeus himself, opening his History of the Acts with the Zwinglians, says he and all the pious wish the bitterness of these splits and hatreds softened and eased (p. 636).

source_text: MARPURGENSE hoc, Primum perfectiorum Consociationis moliminum dixerim, etsi Gradûs infimi: Perfectiorum, quia Consensus fuit ratione omnium dogmatum, exceptô unô; At Infimi Gradus, quia dextram Fraternitatis Lutherus dare noluit Chyt. pag. 647.
english: I would call this Marburg attempt the first of the more complete Consociation efforts — though still of the lowest grade.
More complete, because they agreed on every dogma but one; lowest grade, because Luther would not give the right hand of fraternity (Chytraeus, p. 647).

source_text: Quin Haereticos Zwinglianos appellavit, in Epistola 103. Buddei Supplementi pag. 105. scribens Jacobo Probstio Theologiae Licentiato, his inter cetera, verbis: Indignissimè affecti sunt Zwingliani, quod Fratrum nomen non potuerunt obtinere, sed pro haereticis discedere cogerentur, tamen sic, ut pacem interim haberemus mutuis scriptis, si fortè Deus illis aperuerit Cor. Hôc pacto Schismatis Protestantici primus Autor, Lutherus; tantò intempestivè magis, quantò studiosius altera pars concordiam quaesivit, ipso fatente Luthero, Epist. 98. & 123. apud Buddeum, quando scribit: Zwinglium palam lacrymantem coram Landgravio & Ordinibus rogasse inque haec verba erupisse: Es seynd keine Leut auff Erden / mit denen ich lieber wolte Eines seyn / dann mit den Wittenbergern pag. 105. Iterumque: Zwinglianos promisisse, se velle cum Lutheranis dicere, Christi Corpus veraciter esse in Coena praesens, sed spiritualiter tantum, ut eos fratres dignaremur appellare. Ibidem.
english: Worse: Luther called the Zwinglians heretics — Epistle 103 in Buddeus’s Supplement, p. 105, to Jakob Probst, Licentiate of Theology: they were treated most unfairly in being denied the name of brothers and forced to leave as heretics, yet so that peace might hold for a time by mutual writings, if God should open their heart.

On that footing Luther became the first author of the Protestant schism — and the more out of season, the more carefully the other side had sought Concord, as Luther himself admits in Epistles 98 and 123 in Buddeus.
He records that Zwingli, weeping openly before the Landgrave and the Estates, begged and cried out: there are no people on earth with whom I would rather be one than with the Wittenbergers (p. 105).
And again: the Zwinglians had promised they would say with the Lutherans that Christ’s body is truly present in the Supper, but only spiritually — if only they might be called brothers. Same place.

source_text:
§. II.
Sequitur perfectius Consociationis Molimen, Martino Bucero, vel cum placidissimo Melanchthone de palma moderationis modestiaeque Theologicae certaturo, debitum, hisce Chytraei verbis praecedenti Molimini attextum: Cùm autem, inquit, Landgravius Intercessione obtinere non potuisset, ut Zwingliani in Fratrum numerum à Saxonibus recepti admitterentur, tamen post exhibitam quoque à Nostris Confessionem, Bucerus non destitit, ineundae Conciliationis & Concordiae rationes omni curâ & studio urgere, pag. 658. Et pag. 679.
english: §. II. Next comes a more complete Consociation attempt — one owed to Martin Bucer, who could even vie with the gentlest Melanchthon for the palm of theological moderation and modesty.

Chytraeus tacks it onto the Marburg effort in these words: when the Landgrave’s intercession could not get the Saxons to receive the Zwinglians as brothers, Bucer still did not quit — even after our Confession had been shown — but kept pressing every path to conciliation and Concord (pp. 658 and 679).

source_text: Nihilominus Bucerus pautò post, ante Comitiorum exitum, praesciente Electore Saxoniae & suo Magistratu, ad Lutherum, Coburgam profectus est, ut de piis rationibus & mediis componendae hujus Controversiae, cum eo transigeret; eâdem de causa aliquanto post ad Oecolampadium & Zwinglium se contulit. Sed variis subinde intervenientibus remoris, actionis illius conclusio in sextum usque annum dilata & Wittenbergae tandem Concordia constituta est.
english: Still, a little later — before the diets closed, and with the Elector of Saxony and Bucer’s own magistrates knowing — Bucer went to Luther at Coburg to work out godly ways of settling the controversy.
For the same cause he soon went on to Oecolampadius and Zwingli.
One delay after another pushed the close of that business out to the sixth year; Concord was finally constituted at Wittenberg.

source_text: Perfectius eo nomine reputandum duco Molimen hoc Consociationis Secundum, WITTENBERGENSE, ob Formulam Concordiae Wittenbergensem, etiam Consensum in Dogmate de Coena explicantem, ab undecim Reformatae, & sex Lutheranae partis Theologis subscriptam, legendamque apud Chytraeum pag. 680. 681.; Utut Interimisticum quasi dicendum, quòd Concordiam illam (sunt verba Chytraei) non concludere omninò voluerint dicti Theologi, priusquam ad caeteros etiam Theologos & Magistratus, eam, ceu ab his quoque approbandam, retulissent.
english: On that account I rank this second Consociation attempt higher — the Wittenberg one — because of the Wittenberg Formula of Concord, which even spells out agreement on the doctrine of the Supper.
Eleven Reformed and six Lutheran theologians subscribed it; read it in Chytraeus, pp. 680–681.

Call it almost Interim-like if you like: those theologians (Chytraeus’s words) would not finish the Concord until they had also referred it to the other theologians and magistrates for their approval.

source_text: Accedit ad Perfectionem Concordiae Wittenbergensis à parte LUTHERANORUM, Bucerum ad hanc Concordiam quaerendam, à Luthero ipso incitatum fuisse, Literis ad Argentinenses datis, Anno 1535. apud Buddeum Epist. 120. pag. 248.; Post Formulam Concordiae constitutam, approbationem Argentinensium Anno 1536. Lutherum ursisse, Epistola 223. pag. 257. etiam Helvetiorum Anno 1537. 1. Decembr. Epist. 231 & Anno 1538. Epist. 232.
english: From the Lutheran side, another mark of the Wittenberg Concord’s completeness is this: Luther himself spurred Bucer to seek it — letters to the Strasburgers, 1535 (Buddeus, Epistle 120, p. 248).
After the Formula was set, Luther pressed Strasbourg’s approval in 1536 (Epistle 223, p. 257), and the Swiss as well — 1 December 1537 (Epistle 231) and 1538 (Epistle 232).

source_text: A PARTE REFORMATORUM Formulam Concordiae Wittenbergensem nunquam fuisse revocatam, sed declaratam duntaxat vid. Crocium, Comment. August. Confess. pag. 162. sigillatim ab Helvetiis approbatam, Croc. pag. 100. & 107. cujus approbationis, quippe à nonnullis in dubium vocatae, non possumus non testes Helvetiorum advocare responsorias paulò licèt seriùs Tiguro, ad Lutherum datas; non tamen Annô demum 1539. cui anno, fortè per errorem typographicum, assignatas eas invenio in parte Concionis Werenfelsianae, hôc ipsô, quô haec scribo, annô, Berolini typis exscripta, sed exaratas Anno 1538, die 4. Maji, adeoque dimidio circiter post anno à reddita sibi Lutheri Epistola, uti memorant Historiae Augustanae Confess. Scriptores tres Lutheranorum celebratissimi, Selneccerus, Kirchnerus & Chemnitius, dictas literas verbis sequentibus recensentes:
english: From the Reformed side: the Wittenberg Formula of Concord was never revoked — only declared (Crocius on the Augsburg Confession, p. 162).
The Swiss approved it point by point (Crocius, pp. 100 and 107).

Because some have doubted that approval, we must call the Helvetians’ own reply letters from Zurich to Luther as witnesses — written a little later, yet not as late as 1539 (the year a Berlin printing of Werenfels’s sermon assigns them, perhaps by typographical error, in this very year of my writing).

They were drawn up on 4 May 1538 — about half a year after Luther’s letter reached them — as Selneccer, Kirchner, and Chemnitz, the three most celebrated Lutheran historians of the Augsburg Confession, recount when they cite the letters in these words:

source_text: Ehrwürdiger Hochgelahrter in Christo / w. sonders geliebter Herr und Freund / wir haben euere freundliche und gutherzige Antwort / die ihr uns auf das Schreiben / welches wir euch gen Schmalkalden gethan / verschienen Tagen zugesandt / mit höchster Freud und Frolocken zu GOtt unserm himlischen Vater / empfangen / ... Und dieweil wir den nicht allein aus eurem Schreiben / sondern auch der hochgelehrten unserer insonders geliebten Herrn / Freunde und Brüdern / D. Capitonis und Buceri ... nicht anders verstehen können / denn das ihr den Handel dieser heiligen Einigkeit wol und gut meinet / ... desgleichen auch unser zu Basel gestellete Confeßion / zu sampt der darauff gefolgten Declaration ... zu gutem gefallen annemet / ... Dieweil wir auch der Artickel halben vom eufferlichen Wort und Tauffe / sehen / das E.E. keinen Misverstand findet / ... und daneben bey dem Artickel des heiligen Sacraments des Leibs und Bluts Christi verstanden / das ihr noch nie gelehret habt / auch noch nicht lehret / daß Christus vom Himmel / von der rechten Hand Gottes seines Vaters hernieder und auffahre ... und also keine Gegenwärtigkeit / oder Niessung des Leibes und Bluts Christi im heiligen Abendmahl setzet / aus der etwas folgete / das der wahren Menschwerdung und Himmelfahrt Christi ... wiedrig ... wir auch dagegen nicht wollen / das im Abendmahl allein blosse oder leere zeichen / sondern auch der Leib und das Blut des HErrn empfangen und genossen werde / also / das dis an ihm selbst allein durch das gläubige Gemuth warlich begriffen und empfangen werde / ... so können wir numehr nicht anders sehen noch befinden / denn das wir / (Gott hab Lob) im Verstande und rechter substanz mit einander einig / und zu gutem Frieden / auch kein Streit mehr zwischen uns sey ... Pag. integra Hh / Hucusque verba Tigurinorum,
english: The Zurich letter opens: Honorable, highly learned friend in Christ — we received with highest joy your kind answer to the writing we sent you toward Schmalkalden, thanking our heavenly Father.

From your letter and from Capito and Bucer’s faithful report while they were with us, we can only take it that you mean this holy unity well, and that you gladly accept our Basel Confession with the Declaration that followed.

On the outward Word and Baptism you find no misunderstanding; on the holy Sacrament of Christ’s body and blood we gather you have never taught — and do not teach — a descent or ascent from the Father’s right hand that would set a presence or eating in the Supper contrary to the true incarnation and ascension.

We for our part refuse bare empty signs in the Supper: the Lord’s body and blood are received, yet truly grasped only by the believing mind, as our Confession and Declaration sent to Schmalkalden still hold.
So we now see nothing else than that — God be praised — we are one in understanding and right substance, at peace, with no dispute left between us. (Full page Hh.) Thus far the Zurichers’ words.

source_text:
quibus B. Werenfelsius, Theologiae Professor quondam Primarius Basiliensis, permotus videtur, in dicta Concione, Votô sequenti defungi, subjectâ praeterea Epistola Lutheri, quae paulò antè recensitas Tigurinorum responsorias elicuerunt: Ware wol zu wünschen / daß diß in acht genommen / und die / bald nach der Reformation Anno 1536. / zwischen den Evangelischen Theologis beyder Theilen / gemachte / aber leyder nicht mehr als 3. Jahr warende Concordi oder Einigkeit / wieder erneuert würde / von deren Doctor Luther an die Evangelischen Eidgenossen also geschrieben: Bitte demühtig / wollet euch zu mir versehen / als zu einem / der es ja auch von Herzen meinet / und was zur Förderung der Concordi dienet / so viel nur immer möglich / an mir nichts mangeln soll ... Der Brieff ist datirt den 1. Decembr. Anno 1537. Operum Lutheri Tom. 6. Jenensi f. 507.
Voto Werenfelsiano & nostrum jungimus, tantò ferventiùs, quantò, proh dolor certius est, ob causas mere carnales, B. Calixto Seniori Jud. Controv. Num. 72. & 75. memoratas, Concordiam Wittenbergensem à Luthero priori ruptam fuisse, quin Lutherum (quod tamen saltem citra intentionem scientiamque ejus evenisse speramus) Schismati immortuum videri posse per Epistolam suam ad Jacobum Praepositum mense, antequàm è vivis die 18. Februarii Concordiae sacrô, excessisset, hisce verbis conceptam: ... Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio Sacramentariorum, nec stetit in via Zwinglianorum, nec sedet in cathedra Tigurinorum. Habes quid sentiam. ... 17. Jan. 1546. Clariss. Buddeus Supplem. Epistol. Lutheri, Epist. 255. pag. 287. 288.
english: Those Zurich words seem to move Werenfels — once chief theology professor at Basel — to end his sermon with this wish, adding the Luther letter that had drawn the Zurich replies: would that the Concord made in 1536 between the evangelical theologians of both sides — alas lasting no more than three years — were renewed.

Of that Concord Luther wrote to the evangelical Swiss on 1 December 1537 (Jena Works, Tom. 6, f. 507): take me for one who means it from the heart; so far as I can, nothing that furthers Concord shall be lacking in me.

We join Werenfels’s wish — the more warmly because, alas, it is surer still that for merely carnal causes (Calixtus the Elder, Jud. Controv. nos. 72 and 75) the earlier Luther broke the Wittenberg Concord.

Worse: by his letter to Jakob Praepositus in the month before he died — 18 February, the holy day of Concord — Luther can seem to have died into the schism (we hope at least beside his intention and knowledge): Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the Sacramentarians, nor stood in the way of the Zwinglians, nor sits in the chair of the Zurichers. You have what I think. (17 January 1546; Buddeus, Supplement, Epistle 255, pp. 287–288.)
Stop before §. III — the third, Frankfurt attempt after Luther’s death.

source_text:
§. III.
Tertium, hujus, i. e. Reformationis Seculi, Molimen, FRANCOFURTANUM est, post fata Lutheri, Melanchthone tamen adhuc superstite, annis 1557. & 1558., ab ipsis Imperii Statibus & horum Antefignano, Ottone Henrico Palatino, susceptum, evocatis Francofurtum, 25. Theologis, hosque inter Joh. Pistorio, Andrea Hypperio, & Nicolao Rhodingo, Professoribus Marpurgensibus, rigidis vulgò habitis Calvinistis.
english: §. III. The third Consociation attempt of this Reformation century is the Frankfurt one.
It came after Luther’s death, while Melanchthon was still alive — in 1557 and 1558 — undertaken by the Imperial Estates and their leader, Otto Henry the Palatine.
Twenty-five theologians were called to Frankfurt; among them Johann Pistorius, Andreas Hyperius, and Nicolaus Rhodingus, Marburg professors commonly counted as rigid Calvinists.

source_text: ANNO PRIORI, Papistis, cum quibus erat colloquendum, dicunt Theologi congregati: Non esse inter se, qui erroneas foveant Opiniones, à Confessione alienas, Consensumque esse in fundamento.
english: In the prior year, the assembled theologians tell the Papists with whom they were to confer: none among them fosters erroneous opinions alien to the Confession, and they stand in consensus on the foundation.

source_text: POSTERIORI ANNO, collatis rationibus, in hanc de Sacra Coena quoque Formulam (cujus summarium Autor quoque noster pagina 335. recitat) consentiunt: De hoc Articulo, inquiunt, in Ecclesiis nostris doceri debet juxta Augustanam Confessionem, nempe quod in hac Domini nostri Jesu Christi Ordinatione Sacrae Coenae, vere, vivificè & Substantialiter Christus praesens sit, & cum pane & vino sic ab ipso ordinatis, Corpus & Sanguinem suum manducandum & bibendum nobis Christianis exhibeat, atque testetur, quod ipsius membra simus, & quòd se ipsum una cum promissione Gratiae nobis donet, & quod in nobis sit efficax & operetur, quemadmodum Hilarius inquit: Haec sumta & hausta, faciunt, ut Christus sit in nobis & nos in ipso.
english: In the later year, after comparing reasons, they also agree on a Formula for the Sacred Supper (our author summarizes it at p. 335).
On this article, they say, our churches must teach according to the Augsburg Confession: in the Lord’s ordinance of the Sacred Supper, Christ is truly, vivifically, and substantially present.

With the bread and wine he has so ordained, he exhibits his body and blood for Christians to eat and drink, testifies that we are his members, gives himself with the promise of grace, and works efficaciously in us — as Hilary says: what is taken and drunk makes Christ to be in us and us in him.

source_text: Verba clarè loquuntur de actione seu usu: sicut & Paulus expressè de usu seu Actione inquit: Panis quem frangimus, est Communio Corporis Christi. Id enim de Pane extra usum intelligi non potest, sed hôc modo accipiendum est; hic Panis est res illa, quâ nobis Communio Corporis Christi exhibetur, & sic loquuntur veteres scriptores & Patres praecipui in Ecclesia.
english: The words clearly speak of action or use — as Paul says expressly of use or action: the bread we break is the communion of the body of Christ.

That cannot mean bread outside the use; take it this way: this bread is the thing by which communion of Christ’s body is exhibited to us — and so speak the older writers and chief Fathers in the Church.

source_text: Irenaeus inquit: Eucharistia constat duabus rebus, Terrena & Coelesti, & Epiphanius ac Theodoretus clarè dicunt, quod natura & substantia maneat, & quod tamen cum Pane dona nobis dentur, videlicet Corpus & sanguis Christi. Postea nova locutiones introductae sunt: Panem mutari, sicut Baculus Mosis mutabatur in Serpentem. Crocius Comment. in August. Confess. pag. 204.
english: Irenaeus says the Eucharist consists of two things, earthly and heavenly; Epiphanius and Theodoret clearly say the nature and substance remain, yet with the bread gifts are given — namely Christ’s body and blood.
Later new phrases came in: that the bread is changed, as Moses’ staff was changed into a serpent (Crocius on the Augsburg Confession, p. 204).
Stop before §. IV.

source_text:
§. IV.
Francofurtano Molimini, ob annorum Connexionem, adnectere liceat HEIDELBERGENSE, Ottone Henrico & Friderico III. Electoribus Palatinis Autoribus, in Palatinatu, Anno 1559., summo studio Protestantium Concordiam molientibus, & turbulento admodum (Judice Schmidlino apud Hospinianum Concord. Discord. cap. 46. haud procul a fine, Nov. Edit. Genev. p. m. 409) Heshusio sese opponentibus, ex consilio verò Philippi Melanchthonis, modos de Sacra Coena loquendi veterum, reducentibus. Consilium Melanchthonis, Annô ante obitum praeterpropter dimidio, datum, exstat Parte posteriori Consiliorum & Judiciorum ejus Theologicorum, Friderico III. Electori suppeditatum pag. 378. & seqq.
english: §. IV. To the Frankfurt attempt, by the link of years, one may join the Heidelberg one.

Its authors were Electors Palatine Otto Henry and Frederick III, in the Palatinate in 1559 — pressing hard for Protestant Concord, and opposing the very turbulent Heshusius (so Schmidlin in Hospinian, Concordia Discordans ch. 46 near the end, new Geneva ed. p. ~409).

From Philip Melanchthon’s counsel they restore the Fathers’ ways of speaking about the Sacred Supper. That counsel, given about half a year before Melanchthon’s death, stands in the later part of his Theological Counsels and Judgments supplied to Elector Frederick III (p. 378ff).

source_text: Verba quaedam memorari juvat: Probo (scribit Melanchthon ad Electorem) Consilium Illustrissimi Electoris, quod rixantibus utrinque mandavit silentium, ne distractio fiat in tenera Ecclesia & infirmi turbentur in illo loco & vicinia, & optarem rixatores in utraque parte abesse. Secundò, remotis contentiosis, prodest reliquos de una Forma verborum convenire & in hac controversia optimum est retinere verba Pauli: Panis quem frangimus κοινωνία ἐστὶ τοῦ σώματος, & copiosè de fructu caenae dicendum est, ut incitentur Homines ad amorem hujus pignoris & crebrum usum; & vocabulum κοινωνία declarandum est. Paucisque interfertis: Adest, inquit Melanchthon, Filius Dei in Ministerio Evangelii & ibi certè efficax est in credentibus, ac adest, non propter Panem, sed propter Hominem, sicut inquit: Manete in me, & ego in vobis. Item: Ego sum in Patre meo, & vos in me & Ego in vobis. Et his veris Consolationibus facit nos sibi membra & testatur se corpora nostra vivificaturum esse.
english: Some of Melanchthon’s words to the Elector are worth keeping: he approves the Elector’s counsel that both sides’ quarrelers be silenced, lest the tender church split and the weak nearby be troubled — and he wishes such quarrelers gone from either party.

Second, once the contentious are removed, the rest should agree on one Forma of words; best here is to keep Paul’s: the bread we break is the κοινωνία of the body — and to speak richly of the Supper’s fruit so people love this pledge and use it often, declaring what κοινωνία means.

Melanchthon inserts: the Son of God is present in the ministry of the Gospel and efficacious in believers — present not for the bread but for the man ("Abide in me…"; "I am in my Father, and you in me…"). By these consolations he makes us his members and promises to vivify our bodies.

source_text: Sed hanc veram & simplicem Doctrinam de fructu nominant quidam Cothurnos, & postulant dici, an sit Corpus in Pane, aut Speciebus panis, quasi verò Sacramentum propter Panem & istam Papisticam Adorationem institutum sit. Postea fingunt, quomodo includant Pani; Alii Conversionem, alii Transsubstantiationem, alii Ubiquitatem excogitarunt. Haec portentoze omnia ignota sunt eruditae Vetustati.
english: Yet some brand this true, simple fruit-doctrine as Cothurnos (inflated tragic boots) and demand a yes/no: is the body in the bread, or in the species of bread — as if the sacrament were instituted for the bread and that papistic adoration.
Then they invent how to shut it into the bread; some invent Conversion, others Transubstantiation, others Ubiquity.
All these portentous inventions are unknown to learned antiquity.

source_text: Negat Heshusius, se assentiri Origini, qui nominat Panem & Vinum σύμβολα σώματος καὶ αἵματος; rejicit calumniosè Clementem Alexandrinum; pronunciabit eodem modo de Augustino, Ambrosio, Prospero, Dionysio, Tertulliano, Beda, Basilio, Nazianzeno, qui nominat ἀντίτυπον σῶμα; Theodoreto, qui ait de Pane φύσιν & μεταβαλών pag. 379. & 380.
english: Heshusius refuses assent to Origen, who calls bread and wine σύμβολα of body and blood; he calumniously rejects Clement of Alexandria.

The same verdict would fall on Augustine, Ambrose, Prosper, Dionysius, Tertullian, Bede, Basil, and Nazianzen (who speaks of an ἀντίτυπον body), and on Theodoret, who says of the bread φύσιν and μεταβαλών (pp. 379–380).

source_text: Memoratu quoque digna Pericopa ex Testamento Sereniss. Electoris Friderici III. ad Filios Celsissimos, ex Joh. Jac. Grynaeo excerpta, & pia Commonefactioni ejus de Officio piorum Hominum, qui necesse habent versari ad Catadupa Anathematismorum adversus sanam doctrinam de Eucharistia à pag. 47. ad pag. 49. subjuncta, his verbis: Tertiò ac praecipuè moneo ac hortor charissimos filios meos, ut sibi quam diligentissimè à turbulentis tam Ecclesiarum quam Scholarum ministris caveant, qui nunc in Religionis & fidei negotiis omnis generis contentiones, logomachias & exitiales condemnationes in pias Ecclesias & Scholas, quae tamen in fundamento, & praecipuis Christianae Religionis capitibus consentiunt, & salutem suam unà nobiscum in unicum nostrum Servatorem Jesum Christum collocant, ex vera ambitione & perverso zelo, ac praetextu ministerii sui, per quod Sanctum Spiritum mundum arguere volunt, idque indictâ causa, nec sine scandalo introducere, & non minùs, quàm in execrando Papatu factum est, tam in Magistratuum, quam in subditorum conscientias dominari, & sibi novum quendam primatum passim erigere ac constituere conantur.
english: Also worth remembering is a passage from Elector Frederick III’s Testament to his sons, taken from Johann Jacob Grynaeus and joined to his pious admonition on the duty of godly men who must live beside the cataract of anathemas against sound eucharistic teaching (pp. 47–49).

Third and above all, he warns his dearest sons to watch most carefully against turbulent ministers of churches and schools who, in religion and faith, spawn every kind of contention, word-fight, and deadly condemnation against pious churches and schools that still agree on the foundation and the chief heads of Christian religion and place their salvation with us in Christ alone.

From ambition and crooked zeal, under pretext of a ministry by which they claim the Spirit should convict the world, they introduce this without declared cause and not without scandal — trying, no less than in the cursed Papacy, to dominate magistrates’ and subjects’ consciences and raise a new primacy for themselves everywhere.

source_text: Ex qua re sanè non tantùm in Politica, & in Ecclesiastica gubernatione distractiones & exulcerationes animorum, utriusque illius gubernationis perturbatio & interitus sequitur: verùm etiam Papa & ejus satellitio praebetur occasio, veram nostram Christianamque Religionem ferro, flammâ, exiliis, aliisque innumeris suppliciis persequendi, suamque tyrannidem hoc modo stabiliendi: quae res quantas & quàm miserandas pepererit distractiones, miserias & calamitates, etiam nostrâ hac aetate nimis proh dolor multa in Electorum aliorumque Germaniae Principum provinciis, nec non apud exteras & vicinas gentes extant exempla. Ex quibus meritò omnes Christiani Principes, Ecclesiae & Scholae, exemplum sibi quod ex usu sit, capere, ideoque summoperè à turbulentis istis hominibus, & pacis ac tranquillitatis publicae inimicis sibi cavere, nec permittere, ut ab illis occupentur, & vel inter sese, vel contra alios exacerbentur, aut à se invicem divellantur, ac distrahantur, sed potiùs ejusmodi homines vitare & fugere, & si nulla in eis emendationis spes appareat, prorsus à se removere debebunt: sicuti hac de re inter me aliosque Electores & Principes non semel ex jam dictis aliisque pluribus piis & gravibus causis convenit. Sic tamen, ut hac ratione nihil piis Ecclesiarum ministris, quod attinet ad debitam eorum, quae quotidie offeruntur, vitiorum reprehensionem & correctionem, & errorum, Christiana adhibitâ moderatione & aequitate, ex verbo Dei desumtam refutationem, quae non ad destructionem, sed ad aedificationem, dirigenda & instituenda est, derogaretur.
english: From such turbulence follow not only political and church distraction and ulcerated minds — disturbance and ruin of both governments — but also an opening for the Pope and his retinue to persecute our true Christian religion with iron, flame, exile, and countless other punishments, and so to fix their tyranny.
How great and miserable the resulting divisions and calamities are, even our own age shows too many examples in Electors’ and other German princes’ lands, and among neighboring peoples.

Christian princes, churches, and schools should therefore take the lesson: guard hard against these turbulent enemies of public peace; do not let them seize posts, inflame parties, or tear people apart; avoid and flee them; and if no hope of amendment appears, remove them outright — as Frederick says he and other Electors and princes have more than once agreed for these and other pious, weighty reasons.

Yet nothing in that counsel should strip godly church ministers of due daily reproof and correction of vices, or of error-refutation drawn from God’s word with Christian moderation and equity — aimed at building up, not tearing down.
Stop before §. V.

source_text:
§. V.
Postremum Seculi ejusdem Reformationis primi molimen Concordiae Protestanticae, non in Germania quidem, sed in Polonia An. 1570. susceptum omnium perfectissimum SENDOMIRIENSE est, Consensus Sendomiriensis cognomine celebratum.
english: §. V. The last Consociation attempt at Protestant Concord in that first Reformation century was not in Germany but in Poland in 1570.
It is the most perfect of all — the Sendomir attempt, celebrated under the name Consensus Sendomiriensis.

source_text: Hujus verò, cùm non tantùm editionem novam Latino-Germanicam nunc paraverimus, sed & Perfectionem ejus, quâ Consensus Protestanticos ad unum omnes, multis post se parasangis relinquit, in peculiari praemissa Prefatione, novem evidentissimis argumentis adstruxerimus, solutis etiam, quae hic opponi vulgò solent, exceptionibus cunctis, non est, cur vel causae ejus dicendae, vel excellentiae commendandae immoremur amplius.
english: Of this Consensus we have not only prepared a new Latino-German edition, but in a special Prefatio set out nine clearest arguments for the perfection by which it leaves every other Protestant consensus many parasangs behind — and we have answered all the usual objections.
So there is no need to linger further either stating its cause or praising its excellence.

source_text: imitationem potiùs tàm salutaris, cordati ac Christiani prorsus facti atque exempli, Protestantibus in Germania nostra, aliisque vicinis regnis septentrionalibus, quin in orbe Europaeo integro, ubicunque tandem Protestantes utriusque partis inveniuntur, totô pectore apprecati,
english: Better to pray with whole heart that Protestants in our Germany, in the neighboring northern kingdoms, and throughout Europe — wherever either party’s Protestants are found — imitate so wholesome, clear-headed, and thoroughly Christian a deed and example.

source_text: acquiesuri de cetero in Judicio B. Hornbeckii de hoc Consensu, quod semper & nostrum faciemus, quando: Nulla, inquit, hâc melior vel augustior & perfectior Confessio facta unquam fuit, quae Politice & Ecclesiasticè approbata, & quam jucundâ & illustri admodum Sacrorum Communione invicem confirmarunt.
english: For the rest we rest in blessed Hornbeck’s judgment on this Consensus — and we will always make it ours — when he says: no better, more august, or more perfect Confession than this was ever made.
It was approved politically and ecclesiastically, and they confirmed it mutually by a most joyful and illustrious communion of the sacraments.

source_text: Ab utraque parte haud semel Confessiones & Ecclesias mutuo agnoscunt pro veris: Convenimus, ut quemadmodum illi (August. Conf. Socii) nos, nostrasque Ecclesias & Confessionem nostram in hac Synodo publicatam & Fratrum, Orthodoxas testantur [ita Bohemicae Confessionis Socii de se & Helveticae Confessionis sociis loquuntur] sic etiam nos illorum Ecclesias [puta Augustanae Confessionis Sociorum] eodem Christiano amore prosequamur & Orthodoxas fateamur, Miscel. Sacr. Part. 1. p. 703.
english: From both sides they more than once acknowledge each other’s Confessions and churches as true.

We have agreed: just as the Augsburg Confession’s associates testify that we, our churches, and our Confession published in this synod of the Brethren are Orthodox — so the Bohemian Confession’s associates speak of themselves and of the Helvetic Confession’s associates — so also we will pursue their churches (the Augsburg associates’) with the same Christian love and confess them Orthodox (Hornbeck, Miscel. Sacr. Part 1, p. 703).
Stop before §. VI.

source_text:
§. VI.
Seculi Reformationem insecuti, Duo famosissima, Protestantes inter se conciliandi, numerantur Molimina, LIPSIACUM unum, Theologis Saxonicis, Brandenburgicis & Hassiaciis An. 1631; alterum CASSELLANUM, ab Hassiaciis solis, Marpurgensibus scilicet & Rintelenfibus, A. 1661, Collocutoribus, celebrata. PRIUS triplici nomine perquam insigne.
english: §. VI. After the Reformation century come two most famous Consociation attempts at reconciling Protestants with one another.
One is the Leipzig attempt — Saxon, Brandenburg, and Hessian theologians, 1631; the other the Cassel attempt — Hessian collocutors alone (Marburg and Rinteln), 1661.
The prior (Leipzig) is marked out in three ways.

source_text: (1) Quòd sub ipsum initium Reformati Theologi, Confessioni Augustanae Invariatae sese addicere nulli dubitarunt, paratissimi etiam subscribere eidem, quandocunque istud altera pars desideraret, non rejectâ interim aut repudiata Variata, seu Philippicâ, defensâ verò eô modô, quô Status Imperii in Conventu Nauenburgico An. 1561. hanc quoque ipsam admittendam duxerant. Cum hujus Reformatorum Lipsiensium facti jam aliquoties meminerimus, juvabit hôc locô verba eorum huc facientia in medium adducere, ex Relatione de Colloquio Lipsiaco, germanica.
english: (1) Right at the start the Reformed theologians did not hesitate to bind themselves to the Unaltered Augsburg Confession, and were fully ready to subscribe it whenever the other side asked — without rejecting or repudiating the Variata (Philippica), which they defended as the Imperial Estates had admitted it at the Nauenburg Convention in 1561.
Since this Leipzig Reformed act has been remembered before, it helps to bring in their own words from the German Relation of the Leipzig Colloquy.

There the Brandenburg and Hessian theologians voluntarily confessed with mouth and heart the 1530 Confession delivered to Charles V at Augsburg, and said they would subscribe it — even the Saxon Elector’s exemplar in the Augapfel — whenever and wherever asked, because they and their lords already bound themselves to it in church and school.

source_text: (2.) Quòd in fine Colloquii, utraque pars, eum in finem Colloquium inter se habitum innuit, quò innotesceret, tum quousque in Articulis Aug. Confess. consentirent, tum quae spes superesset, unionis arctioris in posterum ineundae, ad ampliandam veram Christi Ecclesiam & extinguendam Pontificiorum Fiduciam, ex Dissidio Protestantium istis subnatam, dum intereà Christianum amorem sibi invicem stipulati essent.
english: (2.) At the colloquy’s end both sides signal why they met: to see how far they agree in the Augsburg Confession’s articles, and what hope remains of a closer union later — to enlarge Christ’s true church and quench the papists’ confidence drawn from Protestant division — while stipulating Christian love to one another in the meantime.

Their Relation words put it thus: the colloquy was meant first to learn, in summary, whether and how far both parties are one in the twenty-eight Augsburg articles, and whether further conferences of peace-loving theologians, with Christian high authority, might raise a nearer holding-together; and both sides’ theologians would show each other Christian love going forward, faithfully and without deceit.

source_text: Denique (3.) quòd Status Imperii, tertio post anno, Francofurti ad Moenum congregati, non tantum Colloqv. Lipf. aprobarunt, sed Spe Theologorum Lipsiensium se haud frustratum iri arbitrati, Decreto peculiari sanciverunt, Electores Serenissimos, Saxonicum & Brandenburgicum, publico suo nomine rogandos esse, quò Pacis Protestanticae Negotium, Lipsiae inchoatum, plurium Theologorum moderatiorum operâ, continuandum, & ad felicem exitum perducendum curarent. Decretum Statuum, cùm ad paucorum notitiam pervenerit, exhibemus hic Lectori nostro, iis verbis, quibus illud in Joh. Durai Prodromo Irenicorum descriptum legimus, pag. 1.
english: (3.) Finally, in the third year afterward the Imperial Estates gathered at Frankfurt am Main not only approved the Leipzig Colloquy, but — judging they would not be cheated of the Leipzig theologians’ hope — sanctioned by a special decree that Electors Saxony and Brandenburg be asked in the Estates’ public name to keep the Protestant peace business begun at Leipzig going through more moderate theologians’ work, and to bring it to a happy end.
Because few know that decree, we set it out here in the words printed in John Dury’s Prodromus Irenicorum, p. 1.

source_text:
DECRETUM ORDINUM EVANGELICORUM Francofurti factum.
Posteaquam in praesenti Evangelicorum, qui ex Imperii Circulis adsunt, Ordinum & Eorum, qui absunt, Legatorum & Deputatorum conventu, Johannes Duraeus, Evangelicus Theologus, Unionis fraternaeque Reconciliationis inter Evangelicos, tàm intra, quàm extra Imperium Ecclesias in Capitibus Christiana Evangelicaque Religionis nostra fundamentalibus stabiliendae negotium, aliquoties antehac propositum & considerationi objectum, iterum proposuisset, & in spectabili Deputatorum consessu, ab omnibus confæderatis Statibus auditus fuisset, ac multorum utriusque partis tàm in Germania, quàm Gallia, Anglia & Transylvania, praestantissimorum Theologorum & Academiarum protulisset sententias de viis, quibus Christianus iste atque in se laudabilis unitatis scopus obtineatur; cumque unanimi planè consensu Sex Imperii praenominati Circuli prolatas praedictorum Theologorum sententias perpendentes, hoc equidem opus Domino Deo, ut pacis Deo, gratum, laudabile, summeque necessarium & Evangelicis Ecclesiis omni modo utile & commodum judicassent, simul tamen estimassent, illud esse magni ponderis atque momenti negotium, de quo multi Legatorum ac Deputatorum, qui hac vice aderant, nullas haberent Instructiones: Ideo praesentes Statuum Legati atque Deputati receperunt, se rem recto Instituto propositam, & sententias Theologorum unà communicatas, fideliter relaturos.
english: Decree of the Evangelical Estates made at Frankfurt.

John Dury again laid before the Evangelical Estates’ convention (Circles present, and absent princes’ legates) the business of union and fraternal reconciliation among Evangelicals inside and outside the Empire on the fundamental heads of Christian evangelical religion — a matter floated before — and in a notable deputies’ sitting he was heard by all confederated Estates, citing many leading theologians and academies of either party in Germany, France, England, and Transylvania on how that Christian unity-aim might be reached.

The six Circles unanimously judged the work grateful to the God of peace, praiseworthy, most necessary, and useful to evangelical churches — yet also a heavy business for which many deputies present had no instructions. So the present legates and deputies undertook to report home faithfully the proposal and the theologians’ opinions shared with them.

source_text: Adhaec quaedam optimo animo a Legatis quibusdam proposita fuere: nempe, quòd ab una parte consultum judicabant, ut praedictam Declarationem (quae de modo procedendi, quem praenominatus Duraeus proposuit, deque via, pacificorum quorundam Theologorum colloquium, in quo unanimis fidei de fundamentalibus salutis nostrae capitibus confessio institui possit, ad exemplum amicae illius collationis, quae ante triennium Lipziae inter Theologos Electorales Saxonicos, Brandenburgicos & Hassiacos-Cassellanos inita fuit) primo quoque tempore superiores Imperii Circuli mittant; atque ut ab hisce Electoribus invitentur scriptis Literis Invitoriis tam exteri Principes & Reges: Ab alia autem parte Alii hanc quoque proponebant utilem rationem, ut salvis cujusque Electoris, Principis & Status praetensionibus & juribus, rogarentur Serenissimi Electores Saxonicus atque Brandenburgicus, dignentur inceptam Lipziae ante tres annos amicam collationem continuare, atque hunc in finem conventum indicere, cui etiam alii utriusque partis evocati pacifici Theologi intersint; atque in eo conventu buc praesertim fore respiciendum, ut consensus, quoad fieri potest, modestè ineatur in Christiana atque unanimi Confessione, quae contineat omnia & singula, quae salutis fundamentum concernunt, Religionis capita: in reliquis autem capitibus disputationem atque contentionem Scholasticam esse seponendam. Praeter haec etiam & in hoc aliqui amicam consensionem suam apertè declararunt; quòd intereà temporis omnis ab utraque parte tàm in docendo, quàm scribendo Christiana moderatio & lenitas usurpanda sit; atque hoc fine, in utriusque partis templis, publicas preces esse concipiendas, quibus negotium Deo O. M. commendetur. In cujus rei testimonium hic recessus hac de re factus est. Actum Francofurti ad Moenum 14. Sept. Anno 1634.
english: Some legates also offered friendly proposals: that the Circles forward at once a declaration on Dury’s proposed procedure and on a peaceable theologians’ colloquy — modeled on the Leipzig collation three years earlier among Saxon, Brandenburg, and Hessian-Cassel electoral theologians — and that the Electors invite foreign princes and kings by letters.

Others usefully proposed that, saving each Elector’s, prince’s, and Estate’s rights, Electors Saxony and Brandenburg be asked to continue that Leipzig-friendly collation and call a convention where other peaceable theologians of either party can sit or send judgments — aiming at a modest Christian consensus-confession on every salvation-foundation head, while parking scholastic fights on the rest.

Several also agreed that meanwhile both sides should use Christian moderation and mildness in teaching and writing, and that public prayers for the work be framed in both parties’ churches, committing the business to God Most High.
This recess was made in witness of that. Done at Frankfurt am Main, 14 September 1634.
Stop before §. VII (Cassellanum).

source_text:
§. VII.
POSTERIUS hujus Seculi Molimen Pacis Protestanticae, CASSELLANUM puta, tria alia sibi peculiaria vindicat:
english: §. VII. This century’s later Protestant-peace Consociation attempt — the Cassel one — claims three peculiarities of its own:

source_text: (1.) Quòd specialium Dogmatum controversorum momenta accuratè expenderit, Consensum Dissensumque ubique, citra fucum, annotaverit, & tum demum de Consensûs Dissensûsque Pondere magis, quàm Veritate, modestum judicium, illaesis utrinque Conscienciis, tulerit.
english: (1.) It carefully weighed the force of the special disputed doctrines, marked consensus and dissent everywhere without varnish,
and only then gave a modest judgment on the weight of that consensus and dissent more than on bare truth — leaving both sides’ consciences unhurt.

source_text: (2.) Quòd omnibus ritè examinatis, ingenuè cordatéque statuerit, convenire Evangelicis de Fundamento Fidei & Salutis: Quaestiones Controversas fundamentum istud minus attingere, minus multò tollere aut evertere;
english: (2.) After everything was duly examined, it candidly and heartily judged that Evangelicals agree on the Foundation of Faith and Salvation:
the disputed questions touch that foundation less — and still less tear it up or overturn it;

source_text: & ne pars altera deinceps propter dissensum aliqualem, alteram, vel convitiis proscinderet, vel damnaret, consultum putaverit conveneritque, Controversias, quae adhuc superessent, aut non tractandas fore in Ecclesiis pro Concione, aut certè summâ cum modestia, si Necessitas planè exigeret, Dissentientium nulla mentione, nulla Verborum asperitate, nullis Consequentis affictis, sola veritatis ex Scriptura declaratione; In Scholis verò & Academiis magna pariter cum moderatione citra insectationem, citra Personalia, aut nominum indicia, quicquid reliqvum esset controversorum Capitum, tractaretur. Autor p. 330.
english: and lest either side next tear or damn the other for some leftover dissent, they judged it wise and agreed:

remaining controversies should not be handled from church pulpits — or if necessity plainly forced it, only with utmost modesty, naming no dissenters, using no harsh words, forging no consequences, declaring truth from Scripture alone;
and in schools and academies likewise with great moderation, without persecution, personal attacks, or name-pointing (Autor p. 330).

source_text: (3.) Quòd utraque Colloquentium pars colloquium suum Charitativum contra obtrectatores Pacisque Protestanticae osores quoscunque, impigre doctéque defenderit, & exterorum Protestantium propemodum omnium amplissimum applausum meruerit; Rintelensium etiam Epistola Apologetica, sublimis Judicii ac multijugae Eruditionis Theologorum biga, Petro Museo & Joh. Hennichio Auctoribus debita, in alias linguas translata sit. Confer Defension. Colloq. Cassel. Maresii, Hornbeckii, Heideggeri &c.
english: (3.) Both colloquy sides vigorously and learnedly defended their charitable colloquy against detractors and every hater of Protestant peace, and won near-universal applause from foreign Protestants.
Even the Rinteln Epistola Apologetica — by that pair of high-judgment, many-sided theologians Peter Musaeus and John Hennichius — was translated into other languages.
Compare the Cassel Colloquy defenses of Maresius, Hornbeck, Heidegger, and others.
Stop before §. VIII (fruits of Lipsiacum and Cassellanum into the present age).

source_text:
§. VIII.
Utriusque, dicti Moliminis, Lipsiaci & Cassellani fructus haud exiguus fuit, qui se non ad suum tantùm, in quo suscepta sunt, paucisque abhinc annis finitum, sed modernum etiam non ita diu coeptum Seculum extendit.
english: §. VIII. The fruit of both those Consociation attempts — Leipzig and Cassel — was not small.
It reaches not only the age in which they were begun and finished a few years back, but even our present century, itself not long under way.

source_text: Nam praeterquàm quòd meliores utriusque Partis Theologi, mitius dehinc benigniusque de se mutuo Sectisque suis, sentire assuevêre, auditoresque suos ad idem faciendum, exemplis suis induxêre; ita Magistratus suos amore ac desiderio Pacis Ecclesiasticae conciliandae magis magisque implevêre.
english: For besides this: the better theologians on both sides grew used to thinking more mildly and kindly of one another and of their own parties, and by example led their hearers to do the same;
so they filled their magistrates more and more with love and desire for reconciling church peace.

source_text: Post Lipsiacum enim Colloquium, Carolus Ludovicus Palatinus pacificum Institutum prae manibus habuit, Autori nostro celebratum, licèt per virulenta Danhaueri Scripta tùm temporis interversum, uti refert Autor p. 335.
english: After the Leipzig Colloquy, Charles Louis of the Palatinate had a pacific project in hand — one our Author celebrates —
though Dannhauer’s virulent writings then overturned it (Autor p. 335).

source_text: Post Cassellanum verò, Mavortis istius Germaniae, Libertatisque juxtà ac Religionis Statoris, optimô suô meritô, Autori nostro p. 341. dicti, FRIDERICI WILHELMI MAGNI Electoris Brandenburgici, pacifica conamina quam plurima, vel in vulgus nota sunt, similiter tamen à Theologis aliis, in vicinia Marchiae, Danhaueri istius vel Discipulis, vel Symmystis, pro exitiali, quô adversus Reformatos odio perciti erant, & Deum tantùm non blasphemè precabantur, quò se magis magisque odio Calvinianorum impleret, (nescientes profectò quid peterent,) praepedita.
english: After Cassel, the many peace attempts of Frederick William the Great, Elector of Brandenburg — whom our Author (p. 341) rightly calls Germany’s Mars and upholder of liberty and religion — are even publicly known;
yet other theologians near the March, Dannhauer’s disciples or fellow-initiates, blocked them out of deadly hatred of the Reformed,
and all but blasphemously prayed God to fill them ever more with hatred of Calvinists — not knowing what they asked.

source_text: Quô pactô immortalis Gloriae Principi, Pietatis non minus in Deum & Sinceritatis Cordis sui, quàm Fortitudinis bellicae famâ, maximè inclyto, strenuo utrobique S. Davidis aemulatori, idem videtur accidisse, quod isti Hebraeo: Quemadmodum enim hic, maximo licèt Jehovae Templum aedificandi lapideum desiderio flagrans, ab instituto tamen, certis ex causis, prohibebatur, aedificandi negotio in filium Salomonem devolutô, cui etiam à Deo destinatum idem fuerat; ita simili prorsus modô Gloriosissimus Marchicorum Achilles, incredibili Pacis Evangelicae (à Suasore Autoreque Lipsiae olim quaesitae) indies magis magisque promovendae, zelo accensus, cum vel lacrymis, nobis, Differtatiunculam nostram de Pace Ecclesiastica, (speciali ejus jussu in vernaculam paulò post transferendam, Serenissimaeque ejus, tantô Heröe dignissimae Conjugi DOROTHEAE inscribendam) humillimè offerentibus testatus est, varia etiam de hac Pace, meditata sua tum temporis, uti aliàs pluries, aperturus clementissimè, pacisque studium perpetuum nobis, quantâ poterat vi virtuteque quâ pollebat maximâ, inculcaturus, Deo sic disponente, & ob causas soli sapientissimo notas, à Sacrario Pacis Protestanticae exstruendo abstractus est, supellectili tamen ad Sacrarium istud perficiendum, copiosiori à se collectâ, unà cum desiderio Pacis suo, in Filium suum, SALOMONEM NOSTRUM, undequaque pacificum, Regioque nunc Diademate à Deo exornatum, per haereditatem transmissâ.
english: So the same seems to have befallen that prince of immortal glory — famed no less for piety toward God and sincerity of heart than for warlike fortitude, a strenuous emulator of St. David on both sides — as befell that Hebrew:
David burned to build Jehovah a stone temple, yet was barred from the work for set causes, and the building passed to his son Solomon, for whom God had also destined it;
likewise the most glorious Achilles of the Marchers, kindled with zeal to advance day by day the Evangelical peace once sought at Leipzig with him as persuader and author,

even with tears attested as much to us when we humbly offered our little Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Peace (which by his special order was soon to be put into the vernacular and dedicated to his most serene consort Dorothea, worthy of so great a hero),
and was about, as often before, most kindly to open his then thoughts on that peace and press perpetual peace-zeal upon us with all his force —
yet God so disposing, for reasons known to the All-wise alone, he was drawn off from raising the sanctuary of Protestant peace,

and transmitted by inheritance to his son — our Solomon, everywhere pacific, now crowned by God with the royal diadem — both richer furniture collected for finishing that sanctuary and his own desire for peace.

source_text: Hic REX NOSTER PIENTISSIMUS, ut aedificium Pacis Sacrae, (cujus Fundamentum praeteritô annô denuò jacere molitus est, exilique opellâ nostrâ, ad id quam clementissimè usus) benedicente Pacis DEO O. M. quàm felicissimè provehat, adque ipsum Fastigium, succurrentibus etiam aliis Regibus Principibusque, Almae Pacis Ecclesiasticae Promotoribus indefessis, in DEI Gloriam & Evangelicorum omnium Solatium Gaudiumque perducat, est, quod animitus vovemus precamurque. Rescriptum in hoc Negotio Regium, ad Episcopum suum primum, Reverendissimum Dominum BENJAMIN URSINUM, datum, & ex Germanico in Latinum versum, Lectori nostro hôc locô communicandum ducimus, quò de sincerissima AUGUSTI REGIS NOSTRI Intentione, deque Ejus studio, Pacem Ecclesiasticam promovendi fervidissimo, judicare cuivis integrum sit.
english: This is what we vow and pray from the heart for our Most Pious King:

that, with the Most High God of Peace blessing him, he may carry the building of Sacred Peace as happily as possible to its very summit — last year he again strove to lay its foundation, most kindly using our slight labor —
other kings and princes also helping as tireless promoters of kindly church peace, for God’s glory and the comfort and joy of all Evangelicals.
We judge the Royal Rescript in this business — given to his first bishop, the Most Reverend Lord Benjamin Ursinus, and turned from German into Latin — should be set before our reader here,
so anyone may judge the most sincere intention of our August King and his most fervent zeal to promote ecclesiastical peace.
Stop before the Rescript body (Nos Dei Gratia Fridericus Rex Borussiae…).

source_text:
Ita verò habet:
Nos Dei Gratia FRIDERICUS REX BORUSSIAE &c. &c.
Salutem & Clementiam nostram!
Admodum Reverende Episcope, Dilecte & Fidelis.
english: It runs thus:
We, by God’s grace, Frederick King of Prussia, etc.
Our greeting and clemency!
Most Reverend Bishop, beloved and faithful.

source_text: Perspectum Tibi est, quò pacto, Nostri praesertim regiminis tempore, pacis inter Evangelicos promovendae summa Nobis cura fuerit, qua etiam, adjuvante Divina Gratia, tantùm profecimus, ut in Regno caeterisque Imperio Nostro subjectis Provinciis publicae illae acerbitates, haeresium imputationes ac mutua Protestantium condemnationes vix ampliùs pro concione audiantur. Unde certa nobis spes affulget, pacifica Nostra consilia, benedicente Deo, felicem fortitura exitum.
english: You know how, especially under Our reign, promoting peace among Evangelicals has been Our highest care —

and with God’s grace helping we have come so far that in the Kingdom and Our other subject provinces those public bitternesses, charges of heresy, and Protestants’ mutual condemnations are scarcely heard any longer from the pulpit.
So a sure hope shines on us that Our peace-counsels, God blessing them, will reach a happy end.

source_text: Cùm verò hinc inde varia, ab utriusque partis Evangelicis, de modo arctioris unionis, vel saltem mutuae majorisque tolerantiae ineundae, consilia typis mandata fuerint, Nosque, tùm publicis ejusmodi scriptis, tùm unanimi omnium desiderio, prae reliquis Principibus, ad manus salutifero huic instaurandae pacis negotio admovendas animati & expergefacti sumus; Collegium Theologorum, ut pacis, ita salutaris intentionis Nostrae, amantium, ad majorem Dei Gloriam Regnique Christi incrementa promovenda, in ipsa Metropoli nostra, erigere clementissimè statuimus; Teque Episcopum Nostrum, Praesidem ejus praesentibus hisce designamus,
english: But since Evangelicals of both sides have here and there put into print various counsels on closer union — or at least on mutual and greater tolerance —
and We, moved by such public writings and by everyone’s unanimous desire ahead of other princes, have been stirred to set hand to this salutary work of restoring peace,
We have most clemently resolved to erect in Our very capital a College of Theologians who love both peace and Our salutary intent, for God’s greater glory and the increase of Christ’s kingdom.
By these presents We name You Our Bishop its President.

source_text: sequentes Tibi in praesentiarum Assessores adjungentes; nominatim Viros nobis à Concionibus sacris & SS. Theologiae in Academia Nostra Francofurtana Professorem Ordinarium, Samuelem Strimesium, & Danielem Jablonski; nec non Consistorii Nostri Consiliarium & Praepositum Coloniensem, Franciscum Julium Lütkens, nec non Basilicae Magdeburgicae Archidiaconum Winklerum.
english: joining to You for now these Assessors:
Samuel Strimesius, Our man for sacred sermons and Ordinary Professor of Sacred Theology in Our Frankfurt Academy, and Daniel Jablonski;
also Francis Julius Lütkens, councillor of Our Consistory and Provost of Cölln; and Winkler, Archdeacon of the Magdeburg Basilica.

source_text: Tuum itaque, ceu Episcopi, totiusque hujus Consessus Praesidis, erit, nominatos Viros Assessores tuos de clementissima voluntate Nostra, Rescripto hoc declarata, certiores facere, cum iisdem, intra privatos primùm parietes, sine strepitu, convenire ac colloqui, idque agere, ut tùm per colloquia, tùm literas, ad extraneos Theologos dandas, valida media inveniantur, quibus Pax Ecclesiastica, omnibus Protestantium Evangelicorum votis exoptata, si non alibi, in Nostro saltem Regno, Electoratu exterisque terris, procuretur & stabiliatur.
english: Yours, then, as Bishop and President of this whole assembly, will be to make those Assessors sure of Our most clement will declared in this Rescript.
Meet and confer with them first inside private walls, without noise.

See that — by colloquies and by letters to foreign theologians — solid means are found by which the church peace all Evangelical Protestants long for may be procured and settled, if not elsewhere, at least in Our Kingdom, Electorate, and other lands.

source_text: Quòd si Tibi Assessoribusque Tuis opus esse videbitur, exteros etiam Theologos Collegio huic vestro ac Conventui adhiberi, eos, praevia tamen clementissima approbatione Nostra, ea, qua par est, humanitate invitabitis, deque omnibus, quae inter vos acta sunt, ad Nos, ore scriptoque referetis. Quò verò in Collegio vel Conventu hoc Charitativo ordinatiùs cuncta consignetur, Secretarium Nostrum Intimum ac Bibliothecarium Fridericum Henricum Ursinum, Proto-Notarium vobis adjungimus, eumque ab ordinario officii nexu quô Bibliotheca Nostra tenetur, durante hoc negotio, clementissimè dispensamus atque absolvimus. Et quemadmodùm nulli dubitamus negotium hocce Irenicum Deo gratissimum fore & Regiam hanc Christianamque intentionem nostram Divina benedictione beatum iri, ita quoque clementissimè confidimus, Vos omnes & singulos, ex vero sinceroque veritatis & pacis studio, curam hanc ac laborem lubentes suscepturos, & omnes nervos intensuros, quò ardentissimi voti Nostri, quod pro pace inter Evangelicos, diu & anxie expetita, stabilienda concepimus, compotes reddamur.
english: If You and Your Assessors judge foreign theologians should also be brought into this College and convention, invite them with fitting courtesy — yet only after Our prior most clement approval — and report to Us by word and writing all that is done among you.

And so that everything in this charitable College or convention may be recorded in better order, We join to you Our intimate secretary and librarian Frederick Henry Ursinus as Proto-Notary, and for this business most clemently free him from the ordinary library duty that binds him.

As we do not doubt this irenical work will please God and that Our royal Christian intent will share divine blessing, so we most clemently trust you all, from true zeal for truth and peace, will gladly take up this care and strain every nerve.
Then we may obtain Our most ardent vow — the long, anxiously desired peace among Evangelicals made firm.

source_text:
Caeterùm clementia nostra Regia securum Te esse jubemus. Dabantur Coloniae ad Spream d. 25. Martii 1703.
FRIDERICUS REX.
COMES de WARTENBERG, ad Dn. Episcopum Ursinum.
Admodum Reverendo Episcopo nostro Primo, Dilecto & Fideli, Benjamino Ursino.
english: As for the rest, take security from Our royal clemency.
Issued at Cölln on the Spree, 25 March 1703.
Frederick, King.
The Count of Wartenberg addresses Lord Bishop Ursinus.
Directed to Benjamin Ursinus, our Most Reverend First Bishop, beloved and faithful.
Stop before Annotatio IV (Obices Consociationis Ecclesiasticae).

source_text:
ANNOTATIO IV.
De Obicibus Consociationis Ecclesiasticae ad pag. 341. 343.
english: ANNOTATION IV.
On the Obstacles to Ecclesiastical Consociation (Autor pp. 341–343).

source_text:
§. I.
Post tot Pacis Ecclesiasticae componendae molimina frustrata, non immeritò in OBICES, Conatibus tam piis oppositos, inquirit Autor P. 341. & seq. ad speciales tamen digitum solùmmodò intendens, generalioribus, ex quibus isti derivantur, silentio praetervectis, quos intereà & ipsos summarium saltem memorâsse è re fuerit, eum potissimum in finem, quò studiosius caveantur.
english: §. I. After so many frustrated attempts to compose church peace, the Author not without cause turns to the OBSTACLES set against such pious efforts (p. 341ff.).
He points only at the special ones, passing the more general sources in silence — yet it is worth at least summarizing those generals too, mainly so they may be more carefully guarded against.

source_text: Herciscimus a. eos in Externos, seu extra hominem positos, & in Internos, seu homini domesticos.
english: We divide them, first, into Externals — placed outside the person — and Internals — at home in the person.

source_text: Priores variis Diaboli, mendaciorum, rixarum ac calumniarum parentis primi instinctibus, technis artibusque nefariis comprehenduntur, uti neutiquam cum vulgo, omnia propemodum malefacta sua horumque culpam in Diabolum transferre solito, supramodum exaggerandis, ita neque cum fascinati Mundi Autore vel rerum vel actionum humanarum Communitate eximendis:
english: The external sort fall under the Devil’s varied instincts, tricks, and wicked arts — he being the first parent of lies, quarrels, and slanders.
We must neither exaggerate with the crowd that dumps nearly every misdeed on the Devil, nor, with the author of this fascinated world, exempt him from the community of human things and deeds.
