source_text: Quandoquidem ab ipso Spiritu S. dissidiorum non minus ac calumniarum, quam homicidiorum ex istis pullulantium, Pater, Diabolus nuncupatur Joh. 8. 44. non hominibus duntaxat inhians, Leonis rugientis ad instar 1. Pet. 5. adque opera sua incitans, Jacob. 4. quin permittente ex justo judicio Deô, operationem etiam suam in filiis infidelitatis perque eos peragens, Eph. 2, 2. collat. cum 5, 6. inque Judam etiam aliquem, Proditorem Christi, illapsus, Joh. 13; sed rixas insuper in specie excitans, alens, promovensque; ob id, respectu primae earum scaturiginis, denominandas Diabolicas. Jac. 3, 15. hincque tritico Veritatis ac Pacis, Mendaciorum ac Dissidiorum Zizania interferens.
english: For the Holy Spirit Himself names the Devil father of dissensions no less than of slanders and of the murders that sprout from them (John 8:44).

He does not only gape after people like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5) and spur them to his works (James 4); God permitting by just judgment, he also works in the sons of unbelief and through them (Ephesians 2:2 with 5:6), and even entered a Judas, betrayer of Christ (John 13).

Moreover he stirs up, feeds, and pushes quarrels of that kind — so, from their first spring, they are rightly called diabolical (James 3:15) — sowing tares of lies and dissension in the wheat of truth and peace.

source_text: Ut Proinde quaesituro: Quis molimina Pacis supra recensita demolitus sit, haud ineptè verbis Christi respondeas: πονηρὸν Inimicumque communem id perpetrâsse, Matth. 13, 28.
english: So to anyone who asks who wrecked the peace attempts recounted above, you may aptly answer with Christ’s words:
the wicked one — our common enemy — did it (Matthew 13:28).
Stop before §. II (internal fountains: pravity of will and error of intellect).

source_text:
§. II.
Posteriores, Fontes dixeris alios, ex primis Actionum humanarum Principiis, Intellectui & Voluntati inhaerentibus vitiis communibus duobus, Pravitate & Errore exoriturus; alios Rivulos, ex fontibus memoratis scaturientes, eosque numero plures.
english: §. II. The later obstacles you may call other fountains — arising from two common vices in the first principles of human action, intellect and will: pravity and error.
From those fountains spring still more rivulets, greater in number.

source_text: Fontium binorum Priorem, Pravitatem Voluntatis facio-liberam, non minus sub Foedere Gratiae, quam Operum, errorem Intellectûs praevertentem: cum vel ipsius Foederis divini cujuscunque cum homine initi natura, tantum Luminis in intellectu humano supponat, quantum sufficit Pravitati voluntatis malitiosae vel cohibendae, vel repellendae, ut sic ad rixas sacras & dissidia Ecclesiastica praeter necessitatem, etiamsi instigante Diabolo, progressus, sciat, se non invitum, vel per errorem intellectûs, vel per Diaboli persuasionem, sed per liberam potius electionem suam ac προαίρεσιν, ad eandem provolâsse, promoventibus dissidiorum negotium rivulis majoribus tribus ex pravitate Voluntatis emanantibus & Johanni Apostolo probè notatis, hôc locô, inverso ordine recensendis:
english: Of the two fountains, the first is the free-acting pravity of the will — which, under the covenant of grace no less than of works, runs ahead of intellect’s error.
For any divine covenant with man presupposes enough light in the mind to restrain or repel malicious will-pravity.

So whoever has gone on to needless sacred quarrels and church splits — even with the Devil prodding — should know he rushed in not unwillingly, nor merely by intellect’s mistake or the Devil’s talk, but by his own free choice and προαίρεσις.
Three larger rivulets from will-pravity, well marked by the Apostle John, promote that work of dissension; we list them here in reverse order:

source_text:
Scilicet (1.) Fastu vitae, seu ambitione, sacro etiam ordini ut plurimùm adhaerente (uti constat in Pharisaeis Matth. 23, 5, 6, 7.) Veritati ac Paci perquam infesto Joh. 5, 44. & 7, 18. rixarum verò feracissimo 2. Tim. 3, 1, 2, 3. Ut vel ex vulgato isto, in Arrium rixatorem dicto, patet:
Quaeritur Haereticus (Schismaticus,) quare sit factus Arius,
In promptu Causa est, ambitiosus erat.
english: (1.) Pride of life — or ambition — which usually clings even to the sacred order (as in the Pharisees, Matt. 23:5–7).
It is most hostile to truth and peace (John 5:44; 7:18) and most fertile of quarrels (2 Tim. 3:1–3).
That common couplet on quarrelsome Arius makes the same point: ask why the heretic (schismatic) Arius became what he was — the ready answer is, he was ambitious.

source_text: (2.) Cupiditate oculorum, intellige Spiritualium, seu animae, verbô unô, Curiositate in Sacris nimiâ, ex ambitione ortâ, contra istud Apostoli ad Rom. 12, 3. μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ’ ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν (nam inflatus languet circa quaestiones. 1. Tim. 6, 3. 4. 5. Episcopo fugiendas, 2. Tim. 2, 23. 24. Tit. III. 9.), duo admodum mala, Paci Ecclesiasticae quam maximè infensa, progeneratura, dogmatum scil. Theologicorum multiplicationem eximiam; & noviter inventorum malesanam deperitionem.
english: (2.) Lust of the eyes — meaning spiritual lusts of the soul; in a word, excessive curiosity in sacred things, born of ambition — against Romans 12:3: do not think beyond what you ought, but think unto sobriety.
For the puffed-up man languishes among questions (1 Tim. 6:3–5) that a bishop must flee (2 Tim. 2:23–24; Titus 3:9).
This breeds two evils most hostile to church peace: an extraordinary multiplication of theological dogmas, and an unhealthy doting on novelties.

source_text: (3.) Cupiditate Carnis i. e. rerum Carnalium & mundanarum, unâ φιλαργυρίας vitiositate ab Apostolo redargutâ, quam Pharisaeis falsisque Doctoribus propriam Luc. 16. v. 14., & cum φιλαυτίᾳ cohaerentem. 2. Timoth. 3, 2, à Christianis Doctoribus alienam cupit Petrus 1. Pet. 5, 2.
english: (3.) Lust of the flesh — craving carnal and worldly goods — plus the love-of-money the Apostle rebukes as the mark of Pharisees and false teachers (Luke 16:14).
It sticks close to self-love (φιλαυτία, 2 Tim. 3:2), which Peter insists Christian teachers must keep far from (1 Pet. 5:2).

source_text: Posterior Fons, Error Intellectus est, quem pronus incurrit, quisquis voluntatis pravitati habenas laxat, sicuti vice versa, malitiam detestatus, veritati propior imminet. PS. 25. v. 14. Matt. 5. v. 8. Joh. 7. v. 17. Subnascitur autem error proximè ex praejudiciis, affectuum praedominio etiam educatione & informatione perversis, lectione librorum calumniosorum, hisque similibus;
english: The second fountain is error of intellect — which anyone who loosens the reins to will-pravity is apt to fall into; conversely, whoever hates malice draws nearer the truth (Ps. 25:14; Matt. 5:8; John 7:17).
Error is born nearby from prejudices, passions in the saddle, warped schooling and teaching, the reading of slanderous books, and the like.

source_text: Perficitur vel malè & aegrè apprehendendo res Theologicas, adque amussim rerum terrestrium dijudicando, cum Nicodemo Joh. 3, 12. & Capernaitis Joh. 6. vel perversè componendo & apparenter contradictoria, extra Scripturam, conciliando. e. g. effata Christi duo Matt. 26. v. 11. & 28. v. 20. confictione duplicis Corporis Christi, visibilis & invisibilis, concilianda a. quàm facillimè distinctione Biblica inter duplicem Christi naturam, tàm Paulo Rom. 1. v. 3. 4. & Cap. 9. 5. quàm Petro 1. C. 3. v. 18. & Cap. 4. 1. recepta. Vel Confundendo diversa nec satis distinguendo, e. g. inter Veritates Theologicas quascunque, & inter Fundamentales magisque necessarias; vel Colligendo ineptè, e. g. negari omnipotentiam Divinam, dum de Dei voluntate & Revelatione in Dogmatibus quibusdam ambigitur; item, dissentientem omnia pro veris certisque habere, quae vel rectè, vel malè, ex Sententia ejus colliguntur. &c.
english: It is finished either by grasping theological things badly and weakly and measuring them by earthly standards — with Nicodemus (John 3:12) and the Capernaites (John 6) —

or by twisting apparent contradictions into harmony outside Scripture: for example Christ’s two sayings in Matt. 26:11 and 28:20, reconciled by inventing a double body of Christ, visible and invisible, though the biblical distinction of Christ’s two natures (Paul, Rom. 1:3–4; 9:5; Peter, 1 Pet. 3:18; 4:1) does it far more easily.
Or by confusing what differs and not distinguishing enough — e.g. any theological truths whatever versus the fundamental and more necessary ones;

or by inferring clumsily — e.g. that God’s omnipotence is denied when his will and revelation in some dogmas are debated; or that a dissenter holds as sure everything rightly or wrongly drawn from his opinion; and so on.
Stop before §. III (further rivulets from either fountain, noted by our Author).

source_text:
§. III.
Ex utroque Obicum Fonte alii aliique Rivuli, consimilem aquam trahentes, deducuntur, Autori nostro notati.
english: §. III. From either fountain of these obstacles still other rivulets run down, drawing the same kind of water — ones our Author notes.

source_text: Ex Priori (1.) Errorem quemvis, in haeresin pro libidine vertere, vel dissensum minoris momenti, in fundamentalem; In fundamentalem, inquam, quando vel omnino fictus est dissensus eoque nullus, vel Verbalis tantùm, vel ad summum, Modum rei concernens.
english: From the first fountain: (1.) Stretch any error into heresy at will, or turn a lesser dissent into a fundamental one.
“Fundamental,” I mean, when the dissent is wholly feigned and so none at all, or only verbal, or at most about the mode of the thing.

source_text: (2.) Haeresi practica laborare, i. e. Charitatis judicio nullum locum relinquere, omniaque à dissentientibus dicta in pessinam quamque partem interpretari.
english: (2.) Labor under practical heresy — leave no room for charity’s judgment, and take everything dissenters say in the worst possible sense.

source_text: Ex posteriori [1.] Sensu suô abundare, novitates suas bonâ fide aliis instillare, in Ecclesiae Pacisque Ecclesiasticae praejudicium.
english: From the second fountain: [1.] Swell with your own sense, and in good faith drip your novelties into others — to the hurt of the church and of church peace.

source_text: (2.) Adiaphoris Ecclesiasticis, ob inolitam consuetudinem, pertinaciter, etiam ubi periculum peccandi est, itemque cum apertissima adversus Magistratum Superiorem inobedientia, per Zelum, ignorantiae debitum, inhaerere.
english: (2.) Cling stubbornly to church adiaphora from long habit, even where sin is a real risk,
and even with open disobedience to the higher magistrate, under a zeal that is really owed to ignorance.

source_text: Plura collige ex Ramo Olivae Septentrionalis Joh. Matthaei Stregensis Episcopi, Bacca quartâ, Sexta, Septima & Octava.
english: Gather more from the Northern Olive-branch of Johannes Matthiae, Bishop of Strängnäs — berries four, six, seven, and eight.
Stop before Annotatio V (Limites Consociationis Ecclesiasticae).

source_text:
ANNOTATIO V.
De Limitibus Consociationis Ecclesiasticae ad pag. 347.–352.
english: ANNOTATION V.
Concerning the bounds of church Consociation — Autor pages 347 through 352.

source_text:
§. I.
Limites, Obicibus oppositi, intelliguntur de Jure, uti Obices de facto. Quemadmodum limes injustus, obicis, ita obex justus, limitis naturam induit. Hinc limites Consociationis Ecclesiasticae hoc loco intelliguntur, non quales actu & de facto dantur, sed quales jure, & quidem Divinô ac Ecclesiastico, dari & possent, & debent.
english: §. I. Limits stand opposite Obstacles: limits are understood of right, obstacles of fact.
An unjust boundary acts like an obstacle; a just obstacle acts like a limit.
So here the limits of church consociation are not whatever happens to obtain in practice, but what by divine and church right can and ought to be set.

source_text: Ita verò intellecti, vel sumuntur Materialiter, pro rebus, seu Articulis Christ. Religionis, Consociationem Ecclesiasticam juste limitantibus, seu ad justos terminos redigentibus, intraque eosdem continentibus; vel Formaliter pro limitatione ipsâ, seu actu limitandi vario graduque.
english: Taken that way, limits are either Material — the things or articles of the Christian religion that justly bound church consociation and keep it inside those bounds —
or Formal — the limitation itself, the act of limiting in its various degrees.

source_text:
§. II.
Res Consociationem Ecclesiasticam limitantes, seu justos ei terminos figentes, non sunt Veritates Christianae quaecunque, sed Fundamentales, seu Fundamentalia Fidei Christianae dogmata, Annot. 2dâ descripta. Talia dari, ab aliis scilicet Fidei Christianae dogmatibus minùs fundamentalibus diversa, hisque contradistinguenda, probatum alibi, tùm ab Autore nostro Tract. de Fundamentalibus, Disp. 1. & 2. itemque Specim. Strict. contra Episcop. Condomiensem a. p. 63. ad 70. tùm à nobis, Dissert. de Pace Eccles. Cap. 7. & in Inquisit. in Arminianis. Annot. 17. omniumque Protestantium calculô confirmatum, etiam adversus Pontificios,
english: §. II. What sets just bounds for church consociation is not every Christian truth whatever, but the Fundamental dogmas of the Christian faith (described in Annotation 2).

That such fundamentals exist, distinct from less fundamental dogmas, has been shown elsewhere — by our Author’s Tract on Fundamentals (Disp. 1–2) and his Specimen against the Bishop of Condom (pp. 63–70), and by us in the Dissertation on Church Peace (ch. 7) and the Inquiry into the Arminians (Annot. 17) —
and all Protestants reckon the same way, even against the Roman party,

source_text: Fundamentales, sive auctoritate Divinâ eâque immediatâ, sive naturâ suâ talia, quòd fidem Christianam fundant, per se agnoscentes nulla, omnia verò Dogmata fidei Christianae maxima minimaque, tùm quà Veritatem, tùm quà Necessitatem, aut Fundamentalitatem, ab Auctoritate Ecclesiae Romanae suspendentes, quâ fit, ut quod vel fidem Christianam contingit minimum, vel fidei Christianae adversum est, illud nihilominus, hôc non obstante, per Constantiense quoddam, vel Papale Concilium, fidei Christianae essentiale evadat vel maximum,
english: who own no fundamentals in themselves — neither by immediate divine authority nor by their nature as founding the Christian faith —
but hang every dogma of the faith, great or small, as to truth, necessity, or fundamentality, on the authority of the Roman Church.
So what barely touches the Christian faith, or even runs against it, can still, through some Constance or papal council, become essential to that faith — even the greatest point.

source_text: eóque porrò illi, qui e. g. affirmat cum Paulo, in Eucharistiae Sacramento remanere substantiam Panis & Vini, 1. Cor. XI. 26. 27. 28. haut aliter, ac si fundamentum fidei Christianae integrum conculcâsset, anathema terribile per Concilium Tridentinum Session. XIII. Canon. II. annunciatum sit his verbis: Si quis dixerit, in Sacrosancto Eucharistiae Sacramento remanere Substantiam panis & vini unà cum Corpore & Sanguine Domini nostri Jesu Christi, negaveritque mirabilem illam & singularem Conversionem totius Substantiae panis in Corpus & totius substantiae vini in Sanguinem manentibus duntaxat Speciebus panis & vini: quam quidem Conversionem Catholica Ecclesia aptissimè Transsubstantiationem appellat, anathema sit. pag. m. 130.
english: Thus someone who affirms with Paul that in the Eucharist the substance of bread and wine remains (1 Cor. 11:26–28) is treated no milder than if he had trampled the whole foundation of the Christian faith:

Trent, Session XIII, Canon II, launches a terrible anathema in these words — if anyone says the substance of bread and wine remains with Christ’s Body and Blood, and denies that marvelous conversion of the whole substance of bread into the Body and of wine into the Blood (species alone remaining), which the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation, let him be anathema (pag. m. 130).
Stop before the proof that true divine Fundamentals make the limits — from Ephesians 4 (authoritative and ratiocinative).

source_text: Eadem verò Fundamentalia vera divinaque, Consociationis Ecclesiasticae limites conficere, probatur, tàm Autoritative, quam Ratiocinative.
english: That the same true, divine Fundamentals set the limits of church Consociation is proved two ways — by authority and by reason.

source_text: Autoritative ex Cap. 4. ad Ephes., rei probandae Loco quasi Communi reputando, totum insuper Fundamentum tàm Theoreticum à v. 1. ad 17. quàm Practicum à v. 17. ad fin. Cap. complexo, quando Apostolus v. 3. jubet servare unitatem Spiritûs in vinculo pacis, & unum Corpus Spiritumque, unum Corpus Spirituale constitui affirmat, ubi unus est Dominus, una fides, unum Baptisma, unus Deus & Pater omnium, qui est super omnes & per omnes & in omnibus v. 4. 5. 6.;
english: By authority: take Ephesians 4 as a standing commonplace for the point — covering the whole foundation, theoretical (vv. 1–17) and practical (v. 17 to the chapter’s end).

There the Apostle bids us keep the Spirit’s unity in the bond of peace (v. 3), and affirms one body and one Spirit — one spiritual body — where there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, above all, through all, and in all (vv. 4–6).

source_text: licèt deinceps & quod reliquum est, unicuique gratia data, etiam diversi gradûs, sit, secundum mensuram doni Christi v. 7. & alii constituti sint Apostoli, alii Prophetae v. 11. idque ad οἰκοδομὴν τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ad aedificationem Corporis Christi v. 12.
english: Yet afterward, and for what remains, grace is given to each — even in different measures — according to Christ’s gift (v. 7).
Some are set as apostles, others as prophets (v. 11), and that for the building up of Christ’s body (v. 12).

source_text: quò καταντήσωμεν οἱ πάντες εἰς τὴν ἑνότητα τῆς πίστεως καὶ ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ ὑιοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον, donec perveniamus omnes ad unam fidem [puta in omnibus & singulis] & in perfectum virum evadamus v. 13. non dimovendum vel circumagitandum omni ventô Doctrinae v. 14. intereà ἀληθεύοντες ἐν ἀγάπῃ in Charitate Veritati studentes v. 15.
english: The aim is that we all arrive at the unity of the faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a full-grown man (v. 13) — not tossed by every wind of teaching (v. 14) —
meanwhile speaking truth in love, studying truth in charity (v. 15).

source_text: Ratiocinative: Quia in Fundamentalibus eoque necessariis praecipuisque Christianae Religionis dogmatibus unanimes, licèt in aliis minus fundamentalibus minusque necessariis dissentientes, ad majorem intereà perfectamque Unitatem contendentes, in Charitate, unum idemque Spirituale Corpus magis sunt, quàm non sunt; vel (quod eodem recurrit) unius ejusdemque Ecclesiae Christianae Consociatione continentur magis, quàm non continentur: Quandoquidem à potiori fit denominatio.
english: By reason: those agreed on the fundamental — and so necessary and chief — dogmas of the Christian religion, though they still differ on lesser points, yet press on toward fuller unity in charity.
They are more one spiritual body than not.
Or, what comes to the same, they are more held in the Consociation of one Christian church than they are shut out of it — for we name a thing from its greater part.

source_text: Sicuti verò hominibus accensentur & societate humana eâdem contineri putantur, qui corpore & animâ rationali praediti sunt, licèt quandoque & animae rationalis vis virtusque exigua perquam, & Corporis membra nonnulla multum deformata inveniantur; ita ejusdem Consociationis Ecclesiasticae participes aestimandi, qui Ecclesiae Christianae essentialia, tàm Theoretica, quam Practica servant, licèt cum erroribus pariter atque peccatis Christianam Religionem haud evertentibus, etiam benè multis, colluctentur.
english: Just as people with a body and a rational soul still count as human and as members of one society — even when the soul’s force is weak and some bodily members are badly misshapen —
so those who keep the church’s essentials, theoretical and practical, should be counted sharers in the same church Consociation,
even while they wrestle with many errors and sins that do not overturn the Christian religion.
Stop before §. IV (consensus and Consociation judged from the same fundamental principle).

source_text:
§. IV.
Ex eodem oppidò fundamentalium Christianae Religionis dogmatum eorundem Principio tàm Consensus Christianorum, quam Consociatio, id est tam Unitas mentis seu Spiritus, quam Unitas Corporis, seu Ecclesiae, dijudicanda.
english: §. IV. From that same principle of the Christian religion’s fundamental dogmas we must judge both Christians’ Consensus and their Consociation —
that is, both unity of mind (or Spirit) and unity of body (or Church).

source_text: Secus, nec dabitur Consensus Christianorum catholicus ullus unquam, nec ulla Ecclesia Catholica, consensu istô copulata, ut & hanc frustra credamus & de istô mendaciter cantillemus: Die ganze Christenheit auf Erden / hält in einem Sinn gar eben.
english: Otherwise there will never be any catholic Christian consensus, nor any Catholic Church joined by that consensus.
Then we would believe that Church in vain, and sing falsely: “All Christendom on earth holds quite evenly in one mind.”

source_text: Nisi fortè, qui Orthodoxorum hodie nomine se jactitant, Catholicae quoque Ecclesiae titulum sibi solis quàm ridiculè vindicare, aut incogitanter ad se rapere attentent, utpote ne cum generibus quidem singulorum suorum, nedum cum singulis generum, quin ne cum uno quidem singulorum i. e. cum nemine ex suis secum ipsô, [admissâ locorum temporum aliorumque externorum, interna plurimùm mutantium, discriminatione ac mutatione] conciliandum.
english: Unless those who today brandish the Orthodox name try — how ridiculously — to claim the Catholic Church’s title for themselves alone, or snatch it without thinking.
They cannot even be reconciled with the kinds among their own people, still less with each person in those kinds — not even with one individual, that is, with none of their own at one with himself —
once you allow for shifts of place, time, and other externals that greatly change internals.

source_text: Unde porrò, uti jure meritoque Annot. superior. 2da consentientes in fide illos diximus, illosque solos, qui in Fundamentalibus omnibus consentiunt, in aliis licèt dissentiant; ita hôc locô omnes istos unam eandemque Ecclesiam Christianam constituere perhibemus, qui eadem Fundamentalia tenent.
english: So, as in Annotation 2 above we rightly called consenters in the faith only those who agree in all Fundamentals, though they differ elsewhere,
here we hold that all who keep the same Fundamentals make up one and the same Christian Church.

source_text: Quâ ratione Ecclesiasticâ Consociatione extorres arbitramur eos solos, qui in Fundamentalibus deficiunt, sive Theoreticis, quales sunt Sociniani, sive Practicis, quales sunt Pontificii, ad addititium suum fundamentum conscientias Christianorum quorumcumque, contra omnem charitatem Christianam, religioni Christianae quam maximè essentialem, sub anathematibus, obligantes.
english: By that measure we count as exiles from church Consociation only those who fail in the Fundamentals —
theoretical failures such as the Socinians, or practical ones such as the Pontificians, who under anathemas bind any Christian conscience to their extra foundation,
against all Christian charity, which is most essential to the Christian religion.

source_text: Vice versâ Protestantes Evangelicos, Reformatos atque Lutheranos, dissentientes licèt in nonnullis, ob Consensum tamen fundamentalem, eâdem jam tum Ecclesia Christiana contineri, Consociationeque Ecclesiasticâ copulatos esse: minimum hos, qui modos, quibus in tribus admodum dogmatibus quà Substantiam utriusque servatis, dissentiunt, fidei Christianae minus essentiales minusque fundamentales statuunt, eóque ab omni eatenus dissentientium damnatione non abstinent tantum, sed & abhorrent. De Arminianis strictè sic dictis jam pridem simile tulimus judicium, Inquis. in Armin. Annot. §. 1. 3.
english: Conversely, Evangelical Protestants — Reformed and Lutheran — though they dissent in some points, are already held in the same Christian Church and joined by church Consociation because of fundamental consensus.

At least those who treat the modes of dissent in about three dogmas (both sides keeping the substance) as less essential and less fundamental — and who not only refuse but abhor damning dissenters on that account.
On Arminians strictly so called we long ago gave a like judgment (Inquiry into the Arminians, Annot. §. 1. 3).
Stop before §. V (Hannekenius on truth and charity at the end of the Preliminary Questions).

source_text:
§. V.
Ut proinde tantum de Veritate Fundamentali intellecta ac exposita locum reperiant quae sub finem Preliminar. Quaestionum ad Declarat. Theol. de Vera August. Conf. estimatione, supra citatus Dn. Hannekenius ita disserit:
english: §. V. So those remarks apply only where Fundamental Truth is understood and laid out.
Toward the end of the Preliminary Questions on the Theological Declaration for a true estimate of the Augsburg Confession, Hannekenius (cited above) treats the point this way:

source_text: Non potest esse sana Unio mystici Corporis ejusque membrorum, cum Veritas laeditur: violatur enim protinus Vinculum Unionis, Charitas, quae è Veritate oritur.
english: Wound Truth, and the mystical Body with its members cannot stay in sound union.
Charity — the very bond of that union — is violated the moment it loses the Truth from which it springs.

source_text: Vana Charitas est cum laesione Veritatis, inanis Veritas absque exercitio Charitatis. Nemo aperiet veram charitatem sine professione solidâ Veritatis; neque quisquam audiet Confessor fidelis salutaris doctrinae, qui ruptâ Charitate scindit Unionem.
english: Charity with injury to Truth is vain; Truth without the exercise of Charity is empty.
No one shows true charity without a solid profession of Truth.
Nor is anyone heard as a faithful confessor of saving doctrine who, having broken Charity, splits the Union.

source_text: Conf. 1.Cor. I. 10.seq. II. 12. III. 6. VIII. 9.seq. IX. 27. X. 23. 24. 33. 34. XII. 4.seqq. 25.seq. XIII. toto, XIV. 3.seqq. 40. XVI. 13. 14. quam Epistolam finit fortissimo epiphonemate: Si quis Dominum Jesum non amat, qui una est vera Salus est, Salutaris Veritas, sit anathema, Maranatha.
english: He points to a long run of 1 Corinthians (chs. 1–3, 8–10, 12–14, and 16:13–14).
The letter’s strongest closing cry is: anyone who does not love the Lord Jesus — the one true Salvation and saving Truth — is anathema, Maranatha.

source_text: Ita ponens in Cognitione Veritatis salutem, ut amandum Jesum doceat, qui in Synaxi Unionis non potest adamari.
english: On that reading, salvation sits in knowing the Truth, and that knowledge teaches us to love Jesus.
Where the synaxis of union is already torn, that love cannot go deep.

source_text: Pestilens Charitas est absque Veritate, & maledicta omnis Ecclesiastica Unio, quae Jesum non amat in Veritate: 1.Joh. IV. 10. 11. 12.seq. pag. m. 39. Confer Tractatulum nost. Germanicum: Kurzer Entwurff der Einigkeit der Evangelisch-Lutherischen und Reformirten. §. 4. à pag. 21. ad 25.
english: Charity without Truth is pestilent, and every church union that does not love Jesus in Truth is cursed (1 John 4:10–12ff., p. m. 39).
Compare our German tract: Short Sketch of the Unity of the Evangelical-Lutheran and Reformed, §. 4, pages 21–25.
Stop before §. VI (limits of Consociation considered formally — Tolerance vs perfect Union).

source_text:
§. VI.
Hactenus de Limitibus Consociationis Ecclesiasticae, Materialiter consideratis, diximus. Formaliter considerati, seu quatenus limitationis hujus actum designant, duobus quasi gradibus conspicui fiunt,
english: §. VI. So far we have treated the limits of church Consociation on the material side.
Taken formally — as naming the act of drawing that limit — they show up in roughly two degrees.

source_text: quorum alter ad Tolerantiam duntaxat procedit, Consociatio partialis dicendus;
english: One degree reaches only as far as Tolerance.
That grade is rightly called partial Consociation.

source_text: alter ad perfectam Unionem exporrigitur, totalemque consociationem Ecclesiasticam conficit.
english: The other stretches out to perfect Union.
There it completes total ecclesiastical Consociation.

source_text: Dico duobus gradibus conspicuos fieri Consociationis Ecclesiasticae limites, scilicet ex vulgi opinione, quâ Tolerantia Politica cum Tolerantia Ecclesiastica confunditur;
english: I mark those two grades chiefly because common opinion mixes Political Tolerance with Ecclesiastical Tolerance.
That confusion is what makes the double ladder look sharp to the crowd.

source_text: alioquin, qui tolerandus Ecclesiasticè est, ei cum Fundamento Fidei & Fundamentalibus Christianae Religionis convenire necesse est:
english: Otherwise, anyone to be tolerated in the church must already agree with the Foundation of the Faith and the Fundamentals of the Christian religion.
Without that agreement, ecclesiastical tolerance does not even begin.

source_text: Cui autem convenit cum Fundamentalibus, hic idem eô ipsô, quòd tolerandus, eâdem quoque Ecclesiastica Consociatione copulandus copulatusque est.
english: But whoever does agree with the Fundamentals is, by that very fact that he is tolerable, also to be joined — and already joined — in the same church Consociation.
Stop before Annotatio VI (Classes of controversies among Evangelicals).

source_text:
ANNOTATIO VI.
De Controversiarum, quae Evangelicis intercedunt, Classibus ad p.353.356.
J. 1.
Citè admodum Autor noster in DUAS majores controversias dirimit, attendendo discrimen fere triplex, quô Classes istae duae inter se discriminantur, scilicet Autorum, Numeri, & Modi Controversias tractandi.
english: ANNOTATION VI. On the classes of controversies that stand between Evangelicals (pp. 353–356).
§. I. Our author quickly splits them into two major classes, marked off by a nearly threefold difference: authors, number, and the mode of handling the disputes.

source_text: Prior Classis juxta Autorem nostrum, Disputatores habet genuinos Lutheri, (puta placidioris, fidissimi charissimique Symmystae sui Philippi Melanchtonis variatam i. e. declaratam explicatamque August. Confessionem, etiam quod ad Xmum Articul. de Coena Sacra attinet,) si non à priori, à posteriori tamen, admittentis & approbantis, discipulos, vid. Annot. I. §.6.
english: The prior class, on his account, has as disputants Luther’s genuine disciples.
They admit Melanchthon’s milder, declared and explained Augsburg Confession — even Article X on the Sacred Supper — if not from the start, then afterward (see Annot. I. §.6).

source_text: Numerum, fere ad Unitatem redactum, non de reali corporis & sanguinis Christi in coena Praesentia & Manducatione supernaturalibus & spiritualibus utrinque concessis, sed de Praesentia, in, cum, & sub pane contingente, manducationeque orali, tàm indignorum quàm dignorum Communicantium.
english: The disputed number shrinks almost to one point.
Both sides already concede a real supernatural and spiritual presence and manducation of Christ’s body and blood in the supper.
What remains is presence in, with, and under the bread, plus oral eating by unworthy and worthy communicants alike.

source_text: Modum tractandi placidum & qualis decet, Controversiam Theologicam ab utraque contendentium parte habitam minus fundamentalem, ut scilicet charitati fraternae Christianaeque locus maneat reliquus.
english: The mode is peaceful — the kind that fits a theological fight.
Both parties treat the controversy as less than fundamental, so fraternal Christian charity still has room.

source_text: Haec controversiarum Theologicarum Classis, ad quemcunque tandem numerum extensâ, Lutheranos inter & Reformatos, quà rem, non alia est, quàm qualis inter ipsos vel Lutheranos, e. g. de Omnipraesentia & Multipraesentia Corporis Christi; Vel Reformatos, e. g. de Universali & Particulari Gratia, adhuc dum viget, Unioni Ecclesiasticae nihil quicquam derogans.
english: As to the matter, this class between Lutherans and Reformed is no different from disputes that still run inside each camp — Lutheran fights over the body’s omnipresence and multipresence, or Reformed fights over universal and particular grace.
While it lasts, it takes nothing away from church union.

source_text: Unde dubium non est, quòd sicuti Reformatis agnita quondam Lutheranorum horum secum inita Fraternitas, tùm in Germania inter Marpurgenses & Rintelenses, Cassellis, tùm in Polonia inter Augustana, Bohemica & Helvetica Confessionis, Sendomiriae est; Reformati etiam hodieque, ut semper aliàs, cum hujusmodi Lutheranis Fraternitatem Christianam sibi intercedere apertè profitentur; Ita non minus Lutheranos hos, corda animosque suos, cum Reformatis fraterno amore, etsi occultius conjunxisse, ab externa licèt Fraternitatis professione, metu Schismatis, quô reliqui Lutherani à se scinderentur, cohibiti.
english: So there is no doubt: the Reformed once recognized fraternity with these Lutherans — in Germany at Cassel among Marburgers and Rintelners, and in Poland at Sendomir among Augsburg, Bohemian, and Helvetic confessionists.
They still openly profess that Christian fraternity with such Lutherans.
These Lutherans have joined heart and mind to the Reformed in brotherly love, even if more secretly — held back from an external profession by fear of schism with the rest of their own.

source_text: Quod enim nullo omnino fundamentali errore Reformati à se diffideant, pridem tenent, non minus, ac Reformati Lutheranos hosce ab omni prorsus errore fundamentali immunes dudum agnoverunt & celebrarunt.
english: They have long held that the Reformed differ from them by no fundamental error at all.
The Reformed, for their part, have long acknowledged and celebrated these Lutherans as free of every fundamental error.
Stop before §. II (Posterior Class — Brenz, Andreae, Hunnius, Flacius / Formula of Concord).

source_text:
§. II.
Posterior Controversiarum Classis Autores ac disputatores habet, quà res maximè controversas, Joh. Brentii, ubiquitatis seu omnipraesentiae Corporis Christi; Jac. Andreae, oralis hujus Corporis manducationis superadditae, & Aegidii Hunnii, Praedestinationis ex praevisa Fide, praecipuorum ac famosissimorum Doctorum; quà modum autem controvertendi acerbiorem, Flacii Illyrici, inquietissimi hominis Ingenii, Discipulos: Verbô unô, eos, qui si non omnes, certè quàm plurimi, in verba Formulae Concordiae, etiam damnatoria, non minus, re ipsâ, quàm in verba ipsius Scripturae S. sibi jurandum ducunt.
english: §. II. The posterior class has, for the hottest points, Brenz on the ubiquity or omnipresence of Christ’s body, Andreae on oral manducation of that body added on top, and Hunnius on predestination from foreseen faith.
For the harsher style of fight it has Flacius Illyricus’s disciples — a most restless ingenuity.
In a word: those who (if not all, then most) bind themselves to the Formula of Concord’s words — even the damnatory ones — as tightly as to Holy Scripture itself.

source_text: Numerum habet, quà principales Controversias, Ternarium, seu tres potiùs dogmatum Christianorum articulos concernentem: De S. Coenâ primum; alterum, ex hoc enatum, de Persona Christi, tandemque adjectum tertium de Praedestinatione; Quà minus Principales, innumerum, & pro intempestivo zelo, quandoque etiam pro nuda Autorum libidine, indies augendum.
english: As to principal controversies the number is a ternary: first the Sacred Supper; then, sprung from it, the Person of Christ; and third, Predestination.
The lesser ones are countless, and they grow daily by intemperate zeal — sometimes by bare authorial whim.

source_text: Ut inde Autori nostro haec controversiarum Classis, in triplici differentia jure collocetur, quarum aliae nude confictae sint, quaestiones facti, non juris, quales Reformatorum nemini unquam in mentem venerunt, e. gr. Num Deus sit Autor Peccati? in Capite de Providentia Dei; Num omnipotens? in Capite de Praesentia Corporali in Coena; Num misericors? in doctrina de gratia, &c. Aliae minoris momenti, de ritibus & ceremoniis adiaphoris, in quibus facile Reformatos haberent obsequentes Lutherani: Aliae denique reales magis, ad tria dicta Capita Principalia pertinentes. Conf. in Annot. preced. cit. Tractatulum nost. Germanicum, Kurzer Entwurff der Einigkeit der Evangelisch-Lutherischen und Reformirten §.XIII. & seqq.
english: Our author therefore sorts this class into a threefold difference.

Some items are bare fabrications — questions of fact, not of right — that never entered any Reformer’s mind (Is God the author of sin? Is He omnipotent in bodily supper-presence? Is He merciful in the doctrine of grace?).
Others are lesser adiaphorous rites, where Lutherans would easily find the Reformed compliant.
Others again are more real and touch the three principal heads (see our German Short Sketch of Unity, §.XIII ff.).

source_text: Modum tractandi plerumque acerbiorem, omnibusque tàm piis Christianis quibuscunque, quàm ipsis Theologis cordatioribus exosum, ac res sacras, & Sacrum ordinem, & Causam Protestanticam, turpiter prostituentem, & tantum non pessimum in modum infamantem, etiam vel infra vulgi ipsarumque vetularum rixas, altercationes, calumnias, verba contumeliosa atque propudia projectum,
english: The mode of treatment is usually more acerbic.
Pious Christians and the more sober theologians alike hate it.

It foully prostitutes sacred things, the sacred order, and the Protestant cause — and nearly brands them with the worst infamy — sunk even below the quarrels, calumnies, and shameless abuse of the crowd and of old women.

source_text: praeterea cum Damnationibus opinionum adversantium, utut maximè innocuarum, verarum, seu falsarum, certè non fundamentalium, conjunctum promiscuè: quales damnationes in Epitome articulorum, de quibus Controversiae ortae sunt inter Theologos August. Confessionis, quam plurimae leguntur, tàm in opiniones Fratrum Luthericorum, ab eodem Lutheri nomine appellatorum, nonnullas, quam in Reformatorum plures latas, e. g. in has,
english: It is also promiscuously joined to damnations of opposing opinions — however harmless, whether true or false, and certainly not fundamental.

In the Epitome of articles on controversies among Augsburg Confession theologians, such damnations abound — against some opinions of Luther’s own-named brethren, and against more on the Reformed side — for example these:

source_text: Fidem non justificare sine bonis operibus, i. e. Fidem solitariam non justificare, Antithes. XI. ad Artic. 3. p. m. 560. Bona opera necessaria ad salutem esse, Antit. I. ad Art. 4. p. m. 563. Fidem in Christum non amitti, & Spiritum S. nihilominus in homine habitare, etiamsi sciens volens (puta actu duntaxat, non habitu, & semiplenâ voluntate) peccet homo. Ibidem, Ant. 3. Corpus Christi in S. Coena non corporaliter una cum pane sumi, sed tantum Panem & Vinum ore accipi, Corpus verò Christi spiritualiter, i. e. Fide sumi. Antit. 5. ad Art. 7. p. m. 574. Fideles Corpus & sanguinem Christi non in Pane & Vino Coenae Dominicae quaerere, sed oculos in Coelum attollere, & inde Corpus Christi petere debere. Ibid. Antith. 15. p. 575. Infideles & impaenitentes Christianos in Coena Domini, non verum Corpus & Sanguinem Christi, sed Panem tantum & vinum sumere. Antit. 16. p. m. 575. Christum secundum Humanitatem (eóque finitam Naturam) Omnipotentiae, aliarumque Proprietatum Divinae Naturae (eóque Infinitarum), prorsus non esse capacem. Christo, item, secundum humanitatem, datam quidem maximam potestatem in Coelo & in Terra, videlicet majorem & ampliorem, quàm omnes Angeli & Creaturae acceperunt, sed tamen cum Omnipotentia Dei nullam habere communicationem, neg. Omnipotentiam divinam illi (h. e. humanae Naturae) datam esse, Antit. 15. & 16. ad Art. 8. p. m. 582.
english: That faith does not justify without good works (i.e. solitary faith does not justify); that good works are necessary to salvation; that faith in Christ is not lost and the Spirit still dwells even when someone sins knowingly in act only.

That Christ’s body is not taken corporeally with the bread but only bread and wine by mouth, the body spiritually by faith; that the faithful must look to heaven rather than seek the body in the supper elements; that unbelieving communicants receive only bread and wine.

That Christ according to the humanity is incapable of divine omnipotence and the other infinite properties; that the greatest power given to His humanity still has no communication with God’s omnipotence (Epitome antitheses to Arts. 3–4, 7–8).
Stop before §. III (if Lutherans dropped this acerbic mode / swapped damnations for bare rejections, the door to fraternity would stand open).

source_text:
§. III.
Acerbiorem hunc Controversias tractandi modum si facessere juberent hodieque nominati Lutherani, vel saltem Damnationes suas, Anathematismis Tridentinis haud absimiles, in Rejectiones nudas falsarum sibi ita visarum Opinionum commutarent, quibus licèt, juxta se, perituris aliquando, Autores tamen Fautoresque earum (utpote, si omnino, certè bonâ fide errantes) salvandi sint maximè & cum his Fraternitatem Spiritualem colendi,
english: §. III. If today’s named Lutherans would drop this harsher way of handling controversies — or at least trade their damnations (not unlike Tridentine anathematisms) for bare rejections of opinions they judge false —

then even if those opinions may perish on their own view, the authors and favorers of them (erring, if at all, in good faith) are above all to be saved, and spiritual fraternity is to be kept with them.

source_text: Reformatis cupido esset, inque unam Ecclesiam cum iisdem coalescendi apertissima judicaretur janua, utpote sub hac Conditione, cum omnibus Fundamentum Fidei Christianae, tam Practica, quàm Theoretica servantibus dextram fraternitatis Spiritualis jungere quam paratissimis.
english: The Reformed would then desire it, and the door into one church with them would be judged wide open.
The condition is simple: they stand most ready to give the right hand of spiritual fraternity to everyone who keeps the Foundation of the Christian faith — practical and theoretical alike.

source_text: Factum jam tùm hujusmodi quid ab ipsis Patribus Bergensibus in Negativa Artic. XImi, quando ita scribunt: Rejicimus itaque (non autem damnamus) omnes, quos jam enumerabimus errores: (1.) Quòd Deus nolit, ut omnes homines paenitentiam agant & Evangelio credant. (2.) Quando DEus nos ad se vocat, quod non serio hoc velit, ut omnes homines ad ipsum veniant. (3.) DEum non velle, ut omnes salventur, sed quosdam, non ratione peccatorum suorum, verùm solô Dei Consilio, proposito & Voluntate ad exitium destinatos esse, ut prorsus Salutem consequi non possint. (4.) Quod non sola DEi Misericordia & Sanctissimum Christi Meritum; sed etiam in nobis ipsis aliqua Causa sit Electionis Divinae, cujus Causae ratione Deus nos ad vitam aeternam elegerit. p. m. 591.
english: The Bergen Fathers already did something like this in the Negative of Article XI.

They write: We therefore reject (but do not damn) all the errors we shall now list — that God does not will all to repent and believe; that His call is not serious for all; that some are doomed by bare counsel apart from their sins; that election’s cause lies partly in us, not only in God’s mercy and Christ’s merit (p. m. 591).

source_text: Ad simile quid faciendum in aliis suprà memoratis Antithesibus inducentur hodierni Doctores quàm facillimè, si recolant, omnes istas Antitheses suas similesque plures, in Scriptura S. nullibi, nec expressè, nec per Consequentiam obviam, damnatas legi; quin harum potius Antithesium Antitheses, si minus totidem verbis, certè per legitimas Consequentias, in verbo Dei asseri:
english: Today’s doctors would be led most easily to do the same on the other antitheses named above.
They need only recall that none of those antitheses — nor many like them — is read damned in Holy Scripture, either expressly or by ready consequence.
Rather, the antitheses of those antitheses are asserted in God’s word, if not in the same words, then by legitimate consequence.

source_text: e. g. Fidem solitariam non justificare. Jacob. II. integrô. Bona Opera ad Salutem esse necessaria. 1. Cor. VII. 19. Gal. V. 6. Hebr. XII. 14. Fidem in Christum & Spiritum S., non quovis actu peccandi utcunque quadantenus voluntario, amitti penitus. PS. LI. 13. 2. Sam. VII. 14. Corpus Christi non corporaliter unà cum Pane, idque Ore Corporis, sed Spiritualiter, & Ore fidei sumi, indeque non in Pane quaerendum, sed ex Coelo petendum esse; nec ab infidelibus, sed fidelibus tantum accipi; Joh. VI, 35. & v. 47.–59. itemque v. 63. inter se collatis. Christo, secundum Humanitatem, Omnipotentiam non competere Joh. X. Pater me (quà hominem considerato) major est; Ergo etiam respectu Potentiae: Christo autem, secundum humanam Naturam, finita omnia, infinita, vice versa, secundum Divinam Naturam, convenire, Rom. 1, 3, 4 Cap. IX, 5. 1. Pet. III, 18. C. IV, 1.
english: For example: solitary faith does not justify (James 2 entire); good works are necessary to salvation (1 Cor. 7:19; Gal. 5:6; Heb. 12:14).
Faith in Christ and the Spirit are not wholly lost by every partly voluntary act of sin (Ps. 51:13; 2 Sam. 7:14).
Christ’s body is taken spiritually by the mouth of faith, not corporeally with the bread by the body’s mouth — sought from heaven, received by the faithful only (John 6:35, 47–59, 63).
Omnipotence does not belong to Christ according to the humanity (John 10; Rom. 1:3–4; 9:5; 1 Pet. 3:18; 4:1).

source_text:
Faxit DEus O. M. ut sicuti Annotationibus in Protheoriam Autoris Historicam & Catallacticam Controversiarum cum Lutheranis, nunc finem impono, ita finis tandem imponatur odiis Evangelicorum mutuis, ut Historiae de his ansa omnis deinceps praescindatur, ipsi verò ad plenam perfectamque καταλλαγήν redeant, magis magisque Capiti suo Communi, Christo, conglutinandi.
TANTUM.
english: May Almighty God grant that, as I now end these Annotations on the Author’s Historical and Catallactic Protheoria of controversies with the Lutherans, so an end may at last be put to Evangelicals’ mutual hatreds.
Then every handle for a history of these fights may be cut off, and they may return to a full and perfect καταλλαγή — glued more and more to their common Head, Christ.
TANTUM. Stop before HEXAS Annotationum on the Prior Protestant Controversies De Coena Domini (Annotatio I).

source_text:
HEXAS ANNOTATIONUM IN CONTROVERSIAS PROTESTANTICAS PRIORES
DE COENA DOMINI, UNDE INITIUM SCHISMATIS,
ANNOTATIO I
De Sensu verborum Institutionis Sacrae Coenae, proprio ne, an figurato?
§. I.
Cur Controversiae Protestanticæ de Coena Domini, Autori nostro Priores dicantur, ipsemet haud obscurè subinnuit, quando subjicit: unde Schismatis initium.
english: Here begins the Hexad of Annotations on the earlier Protestant fights over the Lord’s Supper — the place where the schism took its start.
ANNOTATION I asks whether the Institution words of the Sacred Supper are to be taken properly or figuratively.
§. I. Our author himself shows why he calls those Supper controversies Priores when he adds the clause: whence the beginning of the Schism.

source_text: Scilicet priores audiunt, non prioritate Dignitatis, quòd fundamentalem quendam fidei Christianae articulum, aut principalem istorum concernunt qui sub disputationes incudem à Protestantibus, & inter se, revocantur; nec Prioritate Ordinis, quòd in Methodica, id est, juxta naturalem Systematis Theologici methodum disposita Controversiarum Protestanticarum tractatione, primum locum mererentur. Has enim prioritatis species vel Lutheranorum nonnulli deprecabuntur, per rationes plurimas ab And. Sennerto in unum collectas, Exerc. Theol. de articulis fid. fundamentalibus §. 64. & 65. p. Fasciculi exercitationum ejus 430. & 431.
english: They are not “prior” by dignity — as if they alone were some fundamental article of the faith, or the chief matter Protestants hammer out among themselves.
Nor by order — as if a methodical theological system would have to put them first.
Even some Lutherans deprecate those kinds of priority (Sennert, Exercises on fundamental articles §§. 64–65, fasc. pp. 430–431).

source_text: Sed verò prioritate partim temporis, quòd Babylone pontificiâ egressi, primò omnium, in nonnullis de Coena Domini quaestionibus, à se invicem dissentire coeperint Protestantes;
english: They are prior partly by time.
Once out of papal Babylon, Protestants first began to dissent from one another on some questions about the Lord’s Supper.

source_text: partim acerbitatis, quòd dissensus hic in nervum tandem erupit, ut schismati Protestantico turpe dederit initium.
english: They are prior partly by acerbitas.
That dissent at last erupted into the nerve and gave a foul beginning to the Protestant schism.

source_text: Prioris Prioritatis occasionem non insulsè annotat B. Georg. Calixtus hisce verbis: Sacramentum Eucharistiae multis & tetris abusibus & superstitionibus hactenus apud Pontificios deformatum erat & vix aliud religionis caput parem calamitatem expertum: Panem benedictum abusu remoto, quod nihil nisi ipsumissimum corpus crederent esse, adorabant & vulgò adorandum proponebant, quin & sacrificium propitiatorium (vocabulo hôc strictè & in formali significatione accepto) habebant & offerebant. Atque adeo Missas ut vocant solitarias, Communicantium expertes, frequentissimè celebrabant, rarò autem adhibitis Communicantibus. Hisce erroribus & pravitatibus abolendis intenti erant primi Reformationis duces & Autores, quod omnino rectè erat; quae est autem humani ingenii imbecillitas, quomodo id rectè fieret, non omnes in istis initiis providebant, Judic. de controversiis theologicis §.47. Batav. ed. p. 69. in fine & 70.
english: Calixtus notes the occasion of that first priority without tastelessness: among the Pontificians the Eucharist had been deformed by foul abuses and superstitions — scarcely any other head of religion had suffered equal calamity.
They adored the blessed bread as the very Body, set it out for adoration, and offered a propitiatory sacrifice; solitary Masses without communicants were frequent.
The first Reformation leaders rightly meant to abolish those errors — yet human ingenuity is weak, and not all foresaw at the start how it would be done rightly (Judic. §.47, Dutch ed. pp. 69–70).

source_text: Posterioris Prioritatis Causam Autoremque Lutherum vel ipse Lutheranus Dav. Chytraeus memorat, quando in actis suis cum Zwinglianis, colloquio Marpurgensi inter Protestantes, anno 1529. habito & à se plenè recitato tandem subjicit: Postquam igitur in colloquio Marpurgensi D. Lutherus, Zwinglium, Oecolampadium, Bucerum & eorum socios propterea quod in articulo de vera & essentiali praesentia corporis & sanguinis Christi in Coena Domini, diversum à sententia sua docerent, pro fratribus agnoscere & recipere noluit, Landgravius tamen & alii boni & pacis ac concordiae cupidi non destiterunt in eo elaborare, ut dissensio illa de Coena Domini piè componi & leniri & Christiana pax & fraternitas inter utramque partem constitui posset. p. mihi 647.
english: Even the Lutheran David Chytraeus records the cause and author of the second priority.

In his full account of the 1529 Marburg colloquy he adds: after Luther refused to acknowledge Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Bucer and their associates as brothers — because they taught differently on the true and essential presence of Christ’s body and blood in the Supper —
the Landgrave and other peace-seekers still did not stop laboring that the Supper dissent might be piously softened and Christian peace and fraternity set between both sides (p. mihi 647).
Stop before §. II (first controversy: interpretation of the Institution words Hoc est corpus meum — literal/κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν vs proper/improper).

source_text:
§. II.
Inter priores de S. Coena Controversias Protestanticæs, prima omnium est de Interpretatione verborum Institutionis Coenae horisticorum seu definitivorum: Hoc est corpus meum: Quae ut tanto amplior pinguiorque appareret, ab altera Protestantium parte in duas nequicquam discerpta est, quarum priori quaeritur: Num literaliter vel κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν? Posteriori: Num propriè, an verò impropriè verba S. Coenae, vel potiùs propositiones: Hoc est corpus meum, & Hic est Sanguis meus, capiendae sint.
english: §. II. Of the earlier Protestant Supper controversies, the first is how to read the definitive Institution words: This is my body.
One party has needlessly torn that question in two: whether literally / κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, and whether the propositions This is my body / This is my Blood are taken properly or improperly.

source_text: Ex una duas sic Controversias nequicquam constitui, ad oculum patet, si observetur: Τὸ κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν Propositionem accipere, triplici modô contingere posse, (1.) uti verba retineas, idque vel formaliter, vel aequipollenter, aequipollentia scil. formali, hoc est ea, quâ à formaliter retentis ne conceptu quidem distinguantur aequipollentia. (2.) Sensum verborum genuinum nativumque sequaris. (3.) Sensum verborum velis esse proprium.
english: That one fight should not be counted as two is plain once you see that taking a proposition κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν can mean three things.
First: keep the words — formally, or by formal equipollents that do not even differ in concept.
Second: follow the words’ genuine native sense.
Third: want that sense to be proper.

source_text: Enimverò de prioribus duabus significationibus τοῦ capiendi verba κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, vel τῷ ῥητῷ retinendi, litigium nullum inter Protestantes, utrâque parte persuasâ, tam Verba formalia & aequipollentia quaecunque, quàm verborum utrorumque sensum genuinum, h. e. semper unum eundemque, verum illum mentique Christi convenientem, tenendum servandumque esse, ut sola tertia in dubio maneat & controversa. Confirmatur: scil. literalem verborum, in propositione spectatorum, controversum sensum ad hoc recidere: Num Sensus literalis, proprius, an verò improprius sit?
english: On the first two meanings Protestants have no lawsuit: both sides hold the formal (and equipollent) words, and one genuine sense that fits Christ’s mind.
Only the third stays doubtful and contested.
So the disputed “literal” sense of the words in the proposition reduces to this: is that literal sense proper, or improper?

source_text: Quia literalis alicujus propositionis, etiam Biblicae, sensus, proprio impropriôque latior existit, & ad hos, etiam aequè perspicuos, perinde extensus: neque enim sensus alicujus propositionis biblicae minus literalis, i. e. minùs verus genuinus & dicentis menti ac intentioni minus conformis, quin & minus perspicuus, remanet, si impropria, quam si propria facta sit praedicatio, litera propositionis, unà cum perspicuitate sua, Improprietati non minùs, quàm Proprietati, obnoxia, vel ab ista non minus quam ab hac, afficienda. Unde rectissimè Scherzerus: Ad perspicuitatem, inquit, pertinet omnino sensus literalis seu Logicus, i. e. quem Spiritus S. per se primo & proximè intendit, sive propriis verbis, sive figurato sermonis genere efferatur. Si enim sensus literalis solùm propriis verbis proferretur, plures orationes Biblicae nullum haberent sensum literalem, quod absurdum, System. Theol. loc. 1. §. 24. p. m. 24. in fin.
english: A biblical proposition’s literal sense is wider than proper vs improper, and stretches equally to both with equal clarity.
An improper predication does not make the sense less literal, less true, or less matched to the speaker’s intent — the letter is open to impropriety no less than to propriety.

Scherzer puts it best: the literal or logical sense is what the Spirit first and proximately intends, whether in proper words or figurative speech; otherwise many biblical sayings would have no literal sense at all (Syst. Theol. I.§.24).

source_text: Cui adstipulatur, etiam quà applicationem ad propositionem S. Coenae de qua nunc quaeritur, Sebastian. Schmidius Tract. de principiis seu Fundamentis praesentiae corporis & Sanguinis Christi in S. Coena cap. 3. §. 17. Literalis sensus, seu τὸ ῥητόν, ait, est is sensus, quem verba ipsa immediatè, consideratis omnibus circumstantiis, reddunt: ubi libenter admittimus τὸ ῥητόν seu literalem sensum non tantùm esse, quem verba propriè sumta dare possunt, sed etiam quem tropicè accepta subministrant. Ut adeò literalem istum sensum, modò, verba propriè accepta, modò, verba tropicè usurpata, suggerant. Sic literalem sensum habent non tantum verba Petri, Matth. 16. vers. 16. Tu es Filius Dei viventis, sed & verba ipsius Domini Jesu, Joh. 6. vers. 51. Ego sum panis vivus; licet hic tropus sit, ibi nullus. Et hactenus inter nos & Calvinianos nihil erit controversiae, p. 18. in fin. & 19.
english: Sebastian Schmidius agrees for the Supper proposition itself: the literal sense / τὸ ῥητόν is what the words immediately yield when all circumstances are weighed.
He gladly allows that τὸ ῥητόν covers not only words taken properly but also words taken tropically.

So Peter’s You are the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:16) and Christ’s I am the living bread (John 6:51) are both literal — though only the second is a trope — and thus far there is no quarrel with the Calvinists (pp. 18–19).

source_text: Ibidem, postquam de literali sensu verborum, extra propositionem spectatorum, i. e. de horum proprietate, Reformatis nunquam non concedenda, frustraque quaedam subjecisset, etiam, contra omnem Reformatorum mentem, asseruisset, eos literalem verborum S. Coenae sensum, à se retentum, mystico solì seu allegorico oppositum velle, cùm hunc oppositum velint omni falso minusque genuino, vel cuivis à mente loquentis Christi & huius immediata intentione, abhorrenti, sponte suâ agnoscit, omnem disputationem de sensu literali verborum Coenae retento, vel minùs retento, quam Protestantes inter se agitant, huc recurrere: An verba (prout nempe propositionem Christi absolvunt) Hoc est corpus meum, propriè, an verò impropriè, capienda sint? Discrimen, inquit, (inter nos & Calvinianos) hôc loco est illud quod Calviniani à proprietate verborum, ubi non deberent, recedunt, reliquae vero sententiae Literam se sequi & premere confitentur: Quare verborum S. Coenae Hoc est Corpus meum, Hoc est sanguis meus (puta quatenus non singula in se verba considerantur, utpote eatenus propria sua significatione à Reformatorum nemine exuenda privandaque unquam, sed quatenus integram Christi propositionem conficiunt, de cujus proprietate & improprietate controvertitur) ῥητόν, litera, seu literalis sensus, is est (scil. Lutheranis) cùm verba ista omnia in propriis suis significationibus relinquuntur, nec ad tropum, quicunque ille tandem sit, disceditur. p. 19. in fin. & 20. Sic verò Reformatos Lutherani habent consentientes, cum hoc solùm negent Reformati: Verba Christi prout propositionem constituunt, sensumque suum literalem, verum genuinum, i. e. menti dicentis Christi exactè respondentem, propositioni impropriae propriaeque juxta communem, obtinent, propriè accipi. Vel, ut clariùs loquar: Propositiones has: Hoc est Corpus meum, & hic est sanguis meus, (in literali i. e. genuino veroque sensu suo acceptas) proprias negant esse Reformati (Vid. Gom. Tom. 3. Diff. 35. thes. 10.) quas vice versâ proprias contendunt Lutherani, alioquin, nullô omnino discrimine hîc à Reformatis distincti, vel distinguendi.
english: After needless talk of word-propriety outside the proposition — which the Reformed never refuse — Schmidius himself grants that the whole Protestant fight over a retained or less-retained “literal” sense of the Supper words comes back to one question: as they complete Christ’s proposition, are This is my body taken properly or improperly?

For Lutherans the ῥητόν of This is my Body / This is my blood (as one whole proposition, not the several words stripped of their own proper sense) is when every word stays in its proper signification and no trope is admitted.

The Reformed deny only that those propositions, taken in their genuine literal sense, are proper (Gomarus, Tom. 3, Disp. 35, th. 10); Lutherans contend they are — otherwise the two sides would not differ here at all.
Stop before §. III (Reformed proofs that the definitive Supper propositions are improper — generic/specific arguments).

source_text:
§. III.
Ceterum propositiones S. Coenae modò dictas definitivas, & sigillatim hanc (de qua communiter disputari solet) Hoc est corpus meum, non propriam, sed impropriam esse, probant Reformati argumentis ad duo genera revocandis, quorum prius GENERICAM, posterius SPECIFICAM propositionis, materialiter acceptae, naturam concernit.
english: §. III. The Reformed argue that the definitive Supper propositions — above all This is my body — are not proper but improper.
They reduce the proofs to two genera: the GENERIC and the SPECIFIC nature of the proposition taken materially.

source_text: GENERICA propositionis hujus natura (1) quà genus remotius, ostendit, Disparatum, in ea, de disparato praedicari, sive subjectum, τὸ hoc, solum panem, sive cum pane aliud praetereà, ipsum scil. Christi corpus, designet, dummodo exclusa explosaque maneat Carlstadiana Identica: Hoc Corpus est corpus meum, uti novitate & fictione, ita δισερημηνείᾳ & violentâ ab antecedentibus suis discerptione, utrique Protestantium parti merito suo exosa. Quatenus enim corpus Christi de pane, junctum licet sibi corpus Christi habente, praedicatur, praedicatur utique disparatum de disparato: At disparatorum natura, de se invicem praedicatorum, eò quòd disparata sunt, praedicationem impropriam infert, propriam respuit; sin minus, omnis praedicatio impropria è medio tollitur: Quaenam enim de se impropriè praedicabuntur, si non disparata? Certè, quicquam de seipso non potest impropriè dici: nec ulla potest dari metonymia, aut metaphora, nisi in Disparatis. Argumentum hoc si quisquam alius, acutissimè adstruxit deduxitque Doctissimus Gomarus, Operum Theol. Tom. 3. Disp. 35 a thesi 14. ad 20. inclusivè, in haec tandem Bellarmini verba definens: Non hic opus habemus Aristotele, cùm sensus communis sufficiat. Nam si liceat disparata de disparatis propriè affirmare, licebit eodem jure affirmare de nihilo aliquid, de aliquo nihil, de luce tenebras, de tenebris lucem, de Christo Belial, de Beliale Christum: neque fides nostra nos obligat ut defendamus quae contradictionem implicant pag. 139.
english: As remoter genus, the GENERIC nature shows a disparate predicated of a disparate — whether τὸ hoc is bread alone, or bread with Christ’s body besides — once Carlstadt’s Identica This Body is my body is exploded as a novel fiction both Protestant sides hate.

Body predicated of bread is disparate of disparate; disparates force improper predication and shut out the proper — otherwise no improper speech would remain, and no metonymy or metaphor could exist except among disparates.

Gomarus builds this sharply (Tom. 3, Disp. 35, th. 14–20), ending with Bellarmine: common sense suffices — if disparates may be affirmed properly of disparates, one may as well affirm nothing of something, darkness of light, Belial of Christ (p. 139).

source_text: Non juvat hôc loco personales objecisse praedicationes, utpote de quibus rectissimè praeceptor olim noster B. Johannes Vorstius, observat, in iis, non rem abstractam de abstracta, seu, quod idem est, disparatam naturam abstractam, de natura itidem disparata abstracta, sed concretum de concreto praedicare, cùm in sacramentali nostra, abstractum de abstracto, corpus de pane, eòque disparatum de disparato, praedicetur.
english: Objecting “personal” predications does not help here.
Vorstius notes that in those, a concrete is predicated of a concrete — not abstract disparate nature of abstract disparate nature.
In our sacramental saying, by contrast, abstract is predicated of abstract: body of bread, hence disparate of disparate.

source_text: Si instes cum Johanne Museo disp. peculiari de S. Coena, Vorstio oppositâ §. 99: In Sacramentali propositione etiam suo modo praedicari Concretum de Concreto, ita ut non dicatur: natura hujus panis est natura corporis Christi, sed tantùm, hic panis, scil. Eucharisticus, panis benedictus, non panis communis, sed Eucharistia, ex duabus rebus, terrena & caelesti, constans, est corpus Christi, citante Bajero Disp. de impanatione §.30., praeterquam quod (1) panem partim naturam abstractam relinquit esse, quatenus nempe Eucharisticus seu benedictus tantùm, nec communis ampliùs, per hoc, abstractam suam naturam nequaquam deserit, vel in concretam concedit: Neque enim panis (natura abstracta) per id, quòd ei benedictum & per benedictionem à communi usu separatus est, naturam abstractam cum concreta commutât, omni alioquin re abstractâ, & per benedictionem peculiarem à communi usu separata, per hoc ipsum in concretam convertenda; partim Eucharisticum panem, cum Eucharistia, confundit, de quorum posteriori rectè quidem dicas, ex duabus rebus, terrena & caelesti, constare, non item de priori, nisi ex sumta, nec adhuc dum probata, hypothesi, etiam (2) remanet adhuc, abstractam nihilominus naturam corporis Christi, seu abstractum corpus Christi, de concreto, seu de composito ex corpore & pane, praedicari, eòque personalibus propositionibus, (in quibus concretum, non verò abstractum, de Concreto praedicatur) praedicationem hanc sacramentalem dissimilem esse. Quando verò abstractum de Concreto directè praedicatur, uti adhucdum disparatum de disparato praedicatur, ita praedicatio non potest non esse impropria: praedicatur enim sic pars de toto, hacque ratione praedicatio conficitur synechdochica, per consequens, tropica seu impropria.
english: Musaeus (§.99 vs Vorstius) claims the sacramental line somehow predicates concrete of concrete — this Eucharistic bread / Eucharist of two things is Christ’s body — citing Bajer on Impanation.
But blessing does not turn bread’s abstract nature into a concrete; and he conflates Eucharistic bread with the Eucharist itself.

Even then an abstract body is still predicated of a composite of body and bread — unlike personal propositions — so abstract of concrete remains disparate of disparate, a synecdoche, and thus improper.

source_text: (II) GENERICA quà genus propius, exhibet propositionem sacramentalem, in qua signatum de signo praedicatur. Etsi verò sic praedicatio propria esse possit, quando nim. Signum cum signato materialiter idem est, tamen non potest non esse impropria, quandocunque signum & signatum materialiter differunt, sive signum nude significans, sive praetereà signati exhibitivum, habeatur: Utroque enim modo praedicatio evadit vel metonymica, vel synechdochica, eòque impropria. Priori quidem, per metonymiam signi pro signato; posteriori verò, vel per metonymiam continentis pro contento, vel per synechdochen partis pro toto. Confirmatur, sacramentalem propositionem ὁριστικὴν, suâ naturâ impropriam esse, Inductione etiam singularum Sacramentalium tam Veteris, quàm N. Testamenti, in ipsa quoque S. Coenae institutione, occurrentis.
english: (II) As nearer genus, the GENERIC view shows the sacramental proposition predicating the thing signified of the sign.

That can be proper only when sign and thing are materially the same; when they differ, the predication is metonymic or synechdochic — sign for thing, container for content, or part for whole — and so improper.
Induction from Old and New Testament sacramentals in the Supper’s own Institution confirms that a horistic sacramental proposition is improper by nature.

source_text: Quando enim (a) in Institutione Circumcisionis, Deus ita Abrahamum alloquitur: Hoc est foedus meum inter me & inter vos & semen tuum post te, quod servabis, ut circumcidatur vobis omnis mas Gen. 17, 10. foedus Dei de circumcisione non nisi impropriè praedicatur: Neque enim Circumcisio propriè foedus est, sed signum foederis, Deô ipsômet interprete versu proximè sequente 11. Debetis autem praeputium carnis praescindere, hocque ipsum foederis signum futurum est inter me & vos. Quando (b) in Institutione Paschatos, totum populum, Moses, nomine Dei, ita, informat: Agnus à vobis, in star festinantium, comedendus, est pascha Domini, Exod. 12, 11. item: Accipite agnum quilibet paterfamilias pro familia sua & mactate pascha, versu 21. Item: si quis ex vobis, agno mactato vescentibus, quaesiverit: quid rei seu officii hic peragitis? Respondebitis: est Pascha sacrificium Domini filios Israelis praetereuntis in Egypto, vers. 27. in propositionibus hisce cunctis, pascha, seu transitus, tam de agno, quàm de mactatione & comesione agni, nonnisi impropriè enunciatur, substantiâ agni nequaquam in actionem transeuntem, per praedicationem aliquam propriam, convertendâ, & quidem per ejusdem speciei tropum, per quem in N. T. ipse Christus pascha nostrum dicitur 1. Cor. 5. vers. 7. nec non petra, Israelitas in deserto secuta: Solet enim res quae significat, ejus rei nomine, quam significat, nuncupari, sicut scriptum est, septem spicae septem anni sunt & multa hujusmodi. Hinc est quod dictum est petra erat Christus: non enim dixit: petra significat Christum, sed tanquam hoc esset! Utique per substantiam hoc non erat, sed per significationem, sunt verba Augustini, quaest. supra Levit. 57.
english: (a) In circumcision’s Institution (Gen. 17:10–11) God’s covenant is predicated of circumcision only improperly — circumcision is the sign of the covenant, God Himself explaining in the next verse.

(b) In the Passover Institution (Exod. 12:11, 21, 27) passover / passage is predicated only improperly of the lamb and of its slaughter and eating — the same species of trope by which Christ is our passover (1 Cor. 5:7) and the desert rock was Christ by signification, not substance (Augustine, Quaest. Lev. 57).
Stop before §.III continuation (Baptism and Cup Institution inductions; SPECIFICA genus).

source_text: Adstringitur vis consequentiae si haec instantia ad Propositionem S. Coenae: Hoc est Corpus meum, applicetur, per id scil., quòd Christus S. Coenam immediàte post Pascha celebratum instituturus & commendaturus discipulis mysteriorum divinorum perquam ignaris, non potuit voluisse verba sua: Hoc, i. e. hic panis est corpus meum, aliter ab iis intelligi, quàm verba vixdum celebrati paschalis, Hoc, i. e. hic agnus est pascha seu transitus, ab iisdem intellecta hactenus erant, praesertim, cùm adderet Christus, quod pro vobis vel fractum est, vel frangitur, quôve sensu accipi debebat posterior propositio Christi Eucharistica: Hoc poculum est N. T. in sanguine meo qui pro vobis effunditur; Secus, & quodsi vel aliter intelligi verba sua à discipulis voluisse Christus, vel discipuli eadem aliter intellexissent, tam Christus iis admodum obscurè locutus fuisset, quam ipsis ansa suppeditata, ad miras quaestiones dilabendi, similes iis, quae leguntur Joh. cap. 14.
english: Tighten the consequence by applying that Passover instance to This is my Body.
Christ was instituting the Supper right after Passover for disciples still raw in the divine mysteries.

He cannot have meant This bread is my body to be heard differently from This lamb is the passover / passage — especially with broken for you and This cup is the N.T. in my blood poured out for you — or else He would have spoken obscurely and opened John-14-style puzzles.

source_text: Quando (y) in definitivis Baptismatis nonnullis: Baptisma est indutio Christi Gal. 3. 27. item, est ἐπερώτημα συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς εἰς Θεόν 1. Petr. 3. Spiritus S. sola Baptismatis Signata, de Signo, sive nudo, i. e. baptismate externo, sive exhibitivo, i. e. de integro baptismo, ex interna & externa parte constante, praedicat, negari nequit, vel Metonymicam vel Synechdochicam praedicationem fieri.
english: (y) In some baptismal definitives — Baptism is putting on Christ (Gal. 3:27); it is the appeal of a good conscience toward God (1 Pet. 3) — the Spirit predicates only Baptism’s signified things of the sign.
Whether the sign is bare external baptism or the whole exhibitive rite, the predication is metonymic or synechdochic; that cannot be denied.

source_text: Denique (d) Cùm in Institutionis S. Coenae parte altera propositio, tùm à Christo primum enunciata, apud Lucam cap. 22. vers. 20. tùm ab Apostolo 1. Cor. 11. vers. 25. repetita, occurrit: Poculum est N. T. in sanguine Christi, unô eam plures tropos spirare nemo facilè inficias ibit, ne quidem Pontificius Cajetanus in Luc. 22. ex Thoma de Aquino 1. Cor. 10.; quin potius Gregorius de Valencia etiam necessitatem tropi agnoscet de Eucharistia Libro I. cap. 9. th. 42. ita scribens: In propositione, Hic calix est N. T. in sanguine meo, oportere prorsus calicem accipi pro re contenta, quae est Christi Sanguis; & consequenter, de hoc sanguine testamentum, seu promissionem, non nisi figurate praedicari, quatenus promissionem videl. & Testamentum confirmat, ut explicat ille dicendi modus Matthaei & Marci in casu nominis obliquo, sanguis Novi Testamenti.
english: (d) In the other half of the Supper Institution — Luke 22:20 and 1 Cor. 11:25 — The Cup is the N.T. in Christ’s blood.
No one easily denies that one line breathes several tropes — not even Cajetan.

Gregory of Valencia grants the necessity: the cup must be taken for the contained blood, and testament/promise is predicated of that blood only figuratively (as Matthew and Mark’s blood of the New Testament shows).

source_text: Nec abnuet Lutheranus quivis, certè non Dominus Daniel Severinus Scultetus in Discussione Universalismi Reformati adhuc recenti, consequentiam interim abnuens: Ponam inquit, in his verbis (partis scil. Institutionis sacrae Coenae, secundae, seu posterioris) esse tropum, non sunt eam ob causam reliqua ad Sacrae Eucharistiae institutionem pertinentia tropicè accipienda. Proprius enim verborum sensus ubivis est retinendus, ni gravis obstet causa, quae hic, scilicet in propositione prioris Partis: Hoc est corpus meum, nulla est. Quibus verbis, uti mihi consenserit Clariss. vir, propositionem Eucharisticam: Hoc poculum est N. T. in sanguine meo, tropô non uno constare, tantôque magis consenserit, non nude posuerit, quantô ex Hebr. cap. 9. vers. 17. & 20. magis annotaverit, modum hunc loquendi aemulari formulam dicendi Mosis, cùm populum totum expiaret, & sanguine aspergeret, ita sonantem: Hic est sanguis N. T. à Deo injuncti;
english: Scultetus, in his recent Discussion of Reformed Universalism, grants a trope in those second-part Institution words, yet denies the consequence for the rest of the Eucharist Institution.
Proper sense, he says, is kept everywhere unless a grave cause blocks it — and in This is my body, he claims, there is none.
Strimesius notes he already agrees the Cup proposition is built of more than one trope, and all the more once Heb. 9:17, 20 shows it emulates Moses’ This is the blood of the N.T.

source_text: Ita vicissim me sibi duplici modo habuerit consentientem, tùm quod ex dictae propositionis (Hoc poculum est N. T. in sanguine meo) improprietate admissâ, non sequatur, omnia reliqua, ad S. Eucharistiae institutionem pertinentia verba, tropicè sumenda; tùm quòd proprius verborum sensus ubivis retinendus sit, nisi gravis obstet causa; dummodo praetereà observare haud gravetur Dominus Scultetus (1) me non ex propositione impropria hac: Hoc poculum est Novum Testamentum, inferre vel voluisse, vel etiamnum velle, omnia S. Coenae institutionis verba impropria esse, sed dicere duntaxat: Definitiva Sacramentalia adeo non abhorrere ab improprietate, ut ex omnium in universum (exceptis tantisper his solis; Hoc est corpus meum) improprietate, citra controversiam admittenda, probabilissimè saltem, & horum inferri queat improprietas. (2) Dictam modò improprietatem, postremis hisce necessariò transcribendam esse, quòd gravissima proprietati eorum causa obstet, quâ gravior dari nequit, ea scil. qua alioquin futurum est, ut Disparatum de Disparato, contra omnem hujus naturam sanamque hominum rationem, propriè praedicari dicendum fuerit.
english: So Strimesius consents on two points: admitting Cup impropriety does not make every other Institution word tropical; and proper sense stays unless a grave cause blocks it.

(1) He does not infer from This cup is the New Testament that all Supper Institution words are improper — only that definitive sacramentals so little abhor impropriety that from all the rest (This is my body set aside for now) one may most probably infer these too are improper.

(2) That impropriety must be written onto This is my body as well, because the gravest cause blocks propriety: otherwise a Disparate would have to be predicated properly of a Disparate against nature and sound reason.

source_text:
§. IV.
Argumenta, specificam propositionis, de qua adhuc disquiritur, naturam attingentia, istorum potissimum testimoniis conficiuntur, qui improprietatem ejus in specie, vel disertè atque explicitè, vel per interpretationes suas, sicque implicite, agnoscunt ac confitentur. EXPLICITE figuratam statuunt (1) PATRES ECCLESIAE ANTIQUIORES, quorum testimonia summâ industriâ collegit ex primis Reformatoribus Oecolampadius, in Dialogo, Melanchton, in consilio Epistolico, ad Fridericum Palatinum misso; Ex recentioribus Johannes Jonstonus Reformatus Syntag. de Commun. veteris Ecclesiae cap. 3. art. 3. §. 3. à pag. mihi 86. ad pag. 100. Et Petrus Picherellus Pontificius Opuscul. Theol. p. 28.
english: §. IV. Arguments for the specific nature of the proposition under debate are drawn chiefly from those who acknowledge its impropriety in species — expressly, or implicitly by their interpretations.
EXPLICITLY figurative: the more ancient Church Fathers (collected by Oecolampadius and Melanchthon), the Reformed Jonstonus, and the Pontifician Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. p. 28).
Stop before the Picherellus / Tertullian catalog and further SPECIFICA testimonies.

source_text: Hujus Verba recitare operae pretium duco, tùm quòd Opuscula viri in paucorum admodum manibus versantur, tùm quòd tantò majorem fidem meretur Autor, quantò Pontificii communiter proprietatem verborum Christi pressius urgere consuevere: Cum diceret Christus Joh. 6., inquit Picherellus, nisi carnem filii hominis manducaveritis &c. intelligit Tertullianus lib. de resurrect. carnis, num. marg. 28. non verè (i. e. improprie) dixisse edendam carnem suam, durum inquit & intolerabilem existimaverunt sermonem ejus, quasi verè carnem suam illis edendam determinasset. Voces hae quasi verè, faciunt ut Tertullianus intellexerit non verè. Cui adstipulatur Origenes in Lev. cap. 7timum, qui citatur de consecr. dist. 2 can. de hac. De hac hostia, quae in Christi commemorationem mirabiliter fit, edere licet: de illa verò, quam Christus in ara crucis obtulit, secundum se edere non licet. Ad eumque modum, quia videtur hoc dicto Christus facinus vel flagitium jubere, Augustinus ait figuratam esse locutionem, de doctr. Christ. lib. 3. cap. 16. & de fide contra Manich. cap. 37. 38. & figuratam etiam agnoscit Cyrillus in libro 7timo ad Leviticum.
english: Picherellus is worth quoting: few own his Opuscula, and a Pontifician witness carries extra weight when his own side presses Christ’s words as proper.

On John 6’s Unless you eat the flesh… he reads Tertullian as taking the eating not truly — i.e. improperly — because the hearers treated the sermon as hard as if He had truly set His flesh to be eaten (quasi vere → non vere).
Origen, Augustine, and Cyril likewise mark figurative speech for that hard saying.

source_text: (2.) REFORMATI DOCTORES ad unum omnes, qui τὸ Est, in propositione Christi, Hoc est corpus meum, vel cum Zwinglio, per τὸ significat, vel cum Oecolampadio, per τὸ Est signum seu figura corporis mei, interpretantur.
