english: (2.) The Reformed doctors as one interpret the Est in This is my body either with Zwingli as significat, or with Oecolampadius as Est the sign or figure of my body.

source_text: Ad quas tamen Reformatorum doctorum Interpretationes propositionis Eucharisticae, oppidò annotandum est: Non confundendam hic quaestionem de proprietate vel improprietate propositionis Christi Eucharisticae, cum quaestione, sive de praesentia, sive de manducatione corporis Christi, in Coena, reali ac substantiali: neque enim ex negata Priori, i. e. ex negata proprietate verborum, rectè infertur posterioris negatio i. e. negatio praesentiae & manducationis realis. Prior negatio verba spectat & terminos, seu propositionem ex verbis & terminis confiatam; posterior rem ipsam hujusque attributa. Prior, formaliter accepta, Logica magis, posterior verò magis Metaphysica. Propositio Christi: Hoc, i. e. hic panis est corpus meum, potest esse impropria, etiamsi corpus Christi, quod impropriè de pane hoc loco praedicatur, propriè, i. e. reverâ in Eucharistia & praesens sit & manducetur, supernaturali scilicet & spirituali nobisque imperceptibili modo. Sicuti enim, non per solam propositionis Christi assertam proprietatem, corpus ejus in Coena supernaturali modo praesens asseritur reque ipsâ manducari, ita nec per solam propositionis ejusdem negatam proprietatem, corpus ejus supernaturali modo vel praesens, vel re ipsâ manducari negatur. Praesentia pariter ac manducatio corporis Christi supernaturales & spirituales, eaeque quàm maximè reales & substantiales, (unicum illum à Christo definitum praesentiae & manducationis corporis sui, tàm intra, quàm extra Eucharistiam, modum designantes) ex cap. 6. Johan. & 1. Cor. 10. satis superque intelliguntur & citra omnem controversiam admittuntur, etiamsi propositio Institutionis S. Coenae definitiva: Hoc est corpus meum, ad modum definitivarum Sacramentalium omnium, impropria seu figurata ac tropica defendatur.
english: Do not mix the propriety of Christ’s Eucharistic proposition with the question of real substantial presence and manducation in the Supper.
Deny propriety of the words, and you still have not denied real presence or eating — the first fight is logical (words/terms); the second metaphysical (the thing).

This bread is my body can be improper while Christ’s body is truly present and eaten supernaturally and spiritually (John 6; 1 Cor. 10) — just as asserting propriety alone does not prove that presence.

source_text: (3.) LUTHERANI NON PAUCI, partim eorum, qui tropicam in genere, eorum partim, qui vel Metonymicam, vel Synechdochicam in specie, concedunt. Ex prioribus memoramus Marbachium contra Pezelium, p. 36. disertis verbis passum, in propositione: Hoc est corpus meum, non in universum omnem figuratam locutionem excludi, sed eam tantùm, quae à propria singularum vocum significatione nos cogit deflectere; In qua Marbachii determinatione facilè acquieverint Reformati, tropicam duntaxat locutionem urgentes, modum ejus non ita, sed promiscuè potiùs habentes, tropus ne in verbis, vel in praedicatione, collocetur.
english: (3.) Not a few Lutherans concede tropic speech in genus, or metonymy / synecdoche in species.
Marbachius against Pezelius allows that This is my body does not shut out every figure — only the kind that forces us off each word’s proper signification.
On that the Reformed easily rest, pressing tropic locution while caring less whether the trope sits in the words or in the predication.

source_text: Ex posterioribus, quà Synechdochen, praeter Selneccerum ipsumque Lutherum, innumeri alii, cum distinctione tamen inter Synechdochen Grammaticam & Rhetoricam, cujus Distinctionis applicatione ad praesentem materiam, quantum in Grammaticam peccetur, vel illi norunt, qui nondum aere lavantur. Nam ubi quaeso traditur in Grammaticis Synecdoche, pro quali contendunt Theologi hi? Quanquam Synecdoche, sive Grammatica dicatur, sive alio veniat nomine, tropus tamen ac figura remanet, juxta ac metonymia, metaphora aut ironia: Id quod docet tropi natura, nominis dissimulatione haud tollenda nec mutanda, cùm ipsa re obtinetur. Quà Metonymiam autem, Mansrafius in Erotematibus ad articulos quatuor Visitatorios, non minus in propositione definitiva partis prioris Sacrae Coenae, quàm posterioris ista: Hoc poculum, est N. T. in sanguine meo, metonymiam largiturus, sed sub distinctione satis ridicula inter Metonymiam Calvinianam de signo & signato, & Metonymiam Lutheranam, quâ uti effectus pro causa ponitur, in hac propositione: Poculum est Testamentum in sanguine meo, i. e. sanguis in poculo est illud quo sancitum est N. T., id est promissio remissionis peccatorum; ita Continens pro contento in hac: Hic panis est Corpus meum.
english: On synecdoche, Selneccer, Luther, and countless others distinguish Grammatical from Rhetorical synecdoche — a distinction that sins against Grammar for anyone not still wet behind the ears.
Call it Grammatical or not: synecdoche remains a trope, like metonymy, metaphor, or irony.

Mansfeld grants metonymy in both halves of the Institution, yet under a rather ridiculous split between Calvinian sign/thing-signified metonymy and Lutheran effect-for-cause / container-for-content metonymy.

source_text: IMPLICITE vero tropicam efficiunt propositionem quicunque hactenus aliter quam Reformati, eam interpretati sunt, tam Pontificii, quàm Lutherani, utrique tamen explicitè pro proprietate verborum, tanquam pro aris & focis, dimicantes. PONTIFICII propositionem: Hoc est corpus meum, interpretati per hanc: Id quod continetur sub speciebus panis & vini, est corpus meum, duplicem tropum ei inesse disertè ostendunt, primò Synechdochen, quum hoc (quod demonstrat substantiam cum accidentibus) ad accidentia propriè pertinere statuitur; deinde Metonymiam Continentis pro Contento. Taceo, dicentem, Propositionem, Hoc est corpus meum, tantundem significare, quantum, sub hisce speciebus seu accidentibus est corpus meum, re ipsâ negare verba illa propriè & ut sonant, accipienda, suâque ἐκθέσει hypothesin subvertere. Assertionis ratio solida est, quia hoc modo pervertitur (1) Subjecti & Attributi sedes: nam corpus meum fit Subjectum, & Hoc, Attributum. Deinde, sensus vocis, Hoc, falso & indoctè permutatur verbis istis, sub Hoc, vel sub hisce speciebus i. e. accidentibus, quae toto categoriae genere differunt, Gomar. loc. cit. p. 142. num. 63. 64.
english: IMPLICITE, whoever interprets the proposition otherwise than the Reformed also make it tropical — Pontificians and Lutherans alike — even while both fight explicitly for word-propriety as for hearth and altar.
The Pontificians’ That which is contained under the species of bread and wine is my body embeds a double trope: synecdoche (this → accidents) and metonymy of container for contained.

Swap This is my body for under these accidents is my body and you deny proper hearing in the act — subject and attribute seats flip, and This is falsely traded for under these species (Gomarus, p. 142).
Stop before Lutheran IMPLICITE readings (Luther’s in/cum/sub; Flacius’s duplex mass).

source_text: LUTHERANORUM famosior propositionis interpretatio duplex est. Altera Lutheri: Hoc, seu hic panis, est corpus meum, i. e. in, cum & sub hoc pane est corpus meum, Tom. II. Witteberg. sermone contra Fanaticos pag. 98. Laß sie / die Schwärmer / (ita suo more cognominat eos quos non habet in controversia sacramentaria ὁμοψήφους) fabren / und laß uns bey den Worten bleiben wie sie lauten: Daß IM BROD der Leib Christi und IM WEIN warhafftig sein Blut sey.
english: The better-known Lutheran reading of This is my body is twofold.
Luther’s: This / this bread is my body means in, with, and under this bread is my body (Wittenberg Tom. II vs the Fanatics, p. 98).
Let the Schwärmer go — his nickname for those not ὁμοψῆφος with him on the sacrament — and stay with the words as they sound: IN THE BREAD Christ’s body, IN THE WINE His blood truly.

source_text: Altera Flacii Illyrici: Hoc complexum, seu haec massa ex duabus rebus constans, est corpus meum; quorum utraque apertissimè tropica; prior metonymica, Continentis pro contento, posterior synechdochica, Partis pro toto.
english: Flacius Illyricus’s other reading: This complex / this mass of two things is my body.
Both readings are openly tropical — Luther’s as metonymy of container for contained; Flacius’s as synecdoche of part for whole.

source_text: Neque est, quod in gratiam posterioris, ceu famosissimae hodieque magis receptae, vel pro hujus proprietate, Sebast. Schmidius excipiat: τὸ Hoc, complexum denotans, cùm simul sit demonstrativum, prohibere, quò minus propositio tropica evadat.
english: Sebastian Schmidius tries to save Flacius’s more famous reading (or its propriety): τὸ Hoc names a complex and is demonstrative at once, so the proposition cannot turn tropical.
Strimesius will not let that exception stand.

source_text: Nam respondeo (1) Complexum nondum probatum esse, (2) Complexum Luthero improbari, per pronomen hoc nihil aliud quam panem intelligendum edicenti, tùm in libro contra Regem Angliae, ubi ait: Ex filo sermonis ostendi, pronomen hoc ad panem aptari & sic sonare aperta verba: Hoc est corpus meum i. e. hic panis est corpus meum: Nam Textus sic habet: accepit panem &c. vides hic quòd omnia illa verba: accepit, benedixit, fregit &c. de pane dicantur, & eundem demonstrat pronomen hoc, quia id ipsum quod benedixit, fregit & dedit, hoc inquam acceptum benedictum & fractum significatur, cum dicitur: hoc est corpus meum. Non praedicatum, sed subjectum demonstratur. Non enim corpus suum accepit, benedixit & fregit, sed panem. &c. hae sunt clara verba quae Rex nequitiosus occulit & nudam illam propositionem urget: Hoc est corpus meum, & pronomen hoc ad corpus propriè & immediatè aptat.
english: Reply (1): the Complex is not yet proved.
Reply (2): Luther himself rejects it — hoc means nothing but bread.

Against the King of England he threads the Institution verbs (took, blessed, broke) onto the bread: This is my body = this bread is my body; the pronoun shows the subject, not the predicate — the King hid those clear words and pressed the naked proposition onto the body.

source_text: Tum in Libro de captivitate Babylonica, Credo inquit, firmiter non modo corpus Christi esse in pane, sed panem esse corpus Christi. Sic enim me servabunt Verba, ubi dicit: accepit panem, gratias agens fregit & dixit: accipite, manducate. Hoc, i. e. hic panis, quem acceperat & fregerat, est corpus meum. Et Paulus, nonne panis quem frangimus participatio corporis Christi est? non dicit (NB.) in pane est; sed ipse panis est participatio corporis Christi, & paulò post ipse usus loquendi & sensus communis probat subjectum sic monstrativum panis (NB.) dum dicit, hoc est corpus meum.
english: In On the Babylonian Captivity Luther believes not only that Christ’s body is in the bread, but that the bread is Christ’s body — the Words keep him: This = this bread He took and broke.

Paul likewise: the bread we break is participation of Christ’s body — he does not say (NB.) it is in the bread, but the bread itself is that participation; common speech proves the demonstrative subject is bread when He says this is my body.

source_text: (3.) Positô, non concessô Complexô, partem sic praedicari de toto, & propositionem tropicam fieri. (4.) Demonstrationem non tollere complexum, Ergo nec tropum. (5.) Demonstrationem tantum ad illud pertinere, quod demonstrari sensibus poterat; & hoc vel erat corpus Christi, mensae assidens: sic verò propositionem enasci Carlstadianam, vel panis, quem in manibus gestabat Christus: sic verò nostram obtenturam metonymiam signi pro signato; vel denique aliud invisibile corpus Christi: sed hoc primò non poterat sensui demonstrari, quia ex hypothesi invisibile est; dein duo corpora Christi inducit, aliud visibile, aliud invisibile, praeterquàm quòd tertiò alterutrum corpus unà cum pane acceptum, tam Complexum, nondum probatum, quin Luthero improbatum, quàm proprietatem, magno molimine impugnatam, aegreque concedendam, reducem facit.
english: (3.) Grant the Complex only for argument: then a part is predicated of the whole, and the proposition is tropical.
(4.) A demonstrative does not cancel the complex — therefore not the trope either.

(5.) Sense can only point to what senses reach: the sitting body (Carlstadt), the bread in Christ’s hands (Reformed sign-for-signified metonymy), or an invisible second body — which cannot be shown to sense, doubles Christ’s bodies, and drags back both the unproved Complex Luther rejected and a propriety hardly to be conceded.
Stop before §.V (Bucer / Lutheran tropus-limits).

source_text: His omnibus altius pensitatis, Lutherani ipsimet, nec alia mente tropum, nec alium tropum quemcunque, propositione Christi exclusum, cupiunt, quàm eâ mente sola, solumque illum tropum, qui corporis Christi veram substantiam Eucharistia exterminat, attestante illud prolixius Bucero, Oper. Anglican. pag. 704. num. 26. itemque apud Chytraeum pag. 660. in med.
english: Weighed more deeply: the Lutherans themselves want only one tropus shut out of This is my body — the kind that drives Christ’s true substance out of the Eucharist.
Bucer (Opera Anglicana p. 704 §26) and Chytraeus (p. 660 mid) attest that limit at length.

source_text: Quòd verò Lutherus, inquit, nostrorum interpretationem rejecit, ex eo, quantum ego quidem ex scriptis ejus judicare possum, factum est, quòd praesentiam Christi per eam in Coena tolli & removeri fuit arbitratus. Nostri vero panem ejusmodi signum corporis Christi nequaquam esse dicunt, per quod corpus Christi abesse vel non sumi denotetur, id quod multis scriptis editis hactenus notum fecerunt.
english: Bucer: Luther rejected our interpretation, so far as his writings show, because he thought it removed Christ’s presence from the Supper.
Our doctors deny that bread is a sign meaning the body is absent or not taken — and they have said so in many books.

source_text: Deinde & hoc manifestum est ex hac locutione, qua panis figura & signum corporis Christi esse dicitur, nequaquam sequi quòd corpus Christi propterea non adsit: aliàs enim de Augustino quoque dici posset, quòd nudum panem in Coena esse senserit, cum tamen contraria sententia in libris ipsius ubique reperiatur: nam contra Adamantum scribens his verbis usus est: Christus non dubitavit dicere, hoc est corpus meum, cùm daret signum corporis sui. Cùm igitur nostrae partis Doctores per interpretationem suam Christi praesentiam tollere aut negare nequaquam voluerint, sed in omnibus scriptis & libris suis eam sint testati, nec aliud quidpiam quam hoc planum facere & obtinere interpretatione sua studuerint, quòd panis non sit substantialiter corpus Christi, hac ratione vulgum à pane visibili ad Christum invisibilem adducere volentes, equidem non de re, sed tantum de verbis contentiones esse reperio. Epist. Buceri ad Pontanum non procul ab initio.
english: Calling bread a figure and sign of Christ’s body does not prove the body is absent — else Augustine too would be read as teaching bare bread, though he wrote against Adamantus: Christ did not hesitate to say this is my body when giving the sign of His body.

Our doctors never meant to deny presence; they only press that bread is not substantially the body, to lead people from visible bread to invisible Christ — so the fight is about words, not the thing (Bucer to Pontanus).

source_text: Idem prorsus videtur Calixtus Senior innuere Judicio de controversiis num. 81. pag. m. 136., metonymicam Reformatorum propositionem ibidem Ecclesiasticam phrasin appellando quae admitti posset.
english: Calixtus Senior points the same way (Judgment on the Controversies §81, p. 136): the Reformers’ metonymic proposition is an ecclesiastical phrase that could be admitted.

source_text: Hoc verò pacto Controversia tota cessat omnino & evanescit, Reformatis tropum quidem defendentibus, sed qui corpus Christi Coenâ abesse haud patitur, nedum facit; Lutheranis verò tropo adversantibus, qui corpus Christi Coenâ movere ejusque praesentiam ex ea tollere minus verecundatur.
english: On that pact the whole controversy ceases and vanishes.

The Reformed defend a tropus that will not let Christ’s body be absent from the Supper — still less make it so; the Lutherans fight a tropus that is less shy about moving the body out and stripping presence from the meal.

source_text: Quod reliquum est, sensum verborum institutionis figurativum variis modis contra Pontificios probatum videas apud Mortonum, Episc. quondam Dunelmensem de Eucharistia, parte secunda Classe 1. cap. 2. 3. & 4.
english: For the rest, see Morton (sometime Bishop of Durham), On the Eucharist II Class 1 chs. 2–4, for figurative Institution proofs against the Pontificians.
Stop before Annotatio II (Consubstantiation history).

source_text: ANNOTATIO II. De Consubstantiatione, Historia ejus Compendiolum complexa ad pag. Aut. 34. & 36. in fin. §. I. IN atque bello Eucharistico, à velitatione verbali rhetorica, de verborum Christi, hoc est corpus meum, interpretatione, propriâ, an impropriâ, ad realem, de ipsius corporis Christi in Sacra Coena praesentia, seu praesentiae potiùs modo, deventum est Disceptationem.
english: Annotatio II opens On Consubstantiation — a short history at Author pp. 34 and 36 fin.
§.I: the Eucharistic war has moved from the verbal fight over whether This is my body is proper or improper to a real debate on Christ’s bodily presence in the Supper — or rather its mode.

source_text: Istam cum alii Corporalem pani copulent; Alii annihilatae panis substantiae substituant; Alii denique corporali negatâ, Spiritualem Spiritibus fidelium contingere credant; universi etiam Veritatem sententiae suae ab antiquitate petant & ex ea adstruere fatagant.
english: Three camps: some join a corporal presence to the bread; others put Christ’s body in place of annihilated bread-substance; others deny the corporal and credit a spiritual presence to the spirits of the faithful.
All three hunt antiquity to prove their side.

source_text: Triplicis hujus Sententiae cùm triplex Denominatio, tum triplex Historia, Consubstantiationis puta, Transsubstantiationis, & Spiritualis Praesentiae, postliminiò enata est, per compendium à nobis recitanda.
english: From that triple opinion came a triple name and a triple history: Consubstantiation, Transubstantiation, and Spiritual Presence.
Strimesius will run them in a short compendium.

source_text: Ab istâ tamen ejus parte facto initio, quae nobis in hoc Controversiarum Elencho potissimum opposita est, inque nostra, ceu illius antithesi, postremò defituri, mediam verò, ob solam cum prima cognationem, authore Spanhemio memoratam, duabus nominatis interferturi.
english: Order: start with Consubstantiation — the part chiefly opposed to us in this Elenchus; end with ours (Spiritual Presence) as its antithesis.
Insert Transubstantiation in the middle only for kinship with the first, as Spanhemius notes.
Stop before §.II (Consubstantiation crassior vs subtilior).

source_text: §. II. Consubstantiatio, quae, vi etymi, duarum Substantiarum, per se sejunctarum Conjunctionem, vel in actu, vel in statu considerandam, significat, alia Crassior est, alia Subtilior. Prior corporis Christi naturalis & localis, vel in pane inclusionem localem, vel unionem interiorem commixtioni physicae, seu miscibilium alteratorum elementorum unioni haud absimilem, denotat.
english: §.II: Consubstantiation, by etymology, is the joining of two substances kept apart in themselves — considered in act or in state.
It comes in a crasser and a subtler form. The crasser means either local enclosure of Christ’s natural body in the bread, or an interior union like a physical mixture of altered elements.

source_text: Hanc, utroque modo conceptam, à Luthero, post rejectam ab eo Transsubstantiationem, edoctam contendunt ejus Adversarii. Carlstadius, priorem modum Luthero impingit, ipsummet ita allocutus: Du wirst mich lang nicht überreden daß GOtt im Brod sey? Item: Wie kan man Christum ins Brod und Wein bringen?
english: Adversaries say Luther taught that crasser mode after he rejected Transubstantiation.
Carlstadt pins local enclosure on him: You will not long persuade me that God is in the bread — and How can one bring Christ into bread and wine?

source_text: Posteriorem, Unionem scil. corporis Christi cum pane personalem, eoque intimam & perichoristicam, Lutherum inculcasse in duobus sensibus, prolixius exponit Becanus, Manual. Controv. lib. 2. cap. 2. quest. 2. p. 330. Et sanè vero Lutherus utriusque modi à se asserti, formulis suis loquendi, haud levem suspicionem genuerit, quando ex una parte, verba Christi, hoc est corpus meum, tùm in prosa oratione, per tres has particulas, In, Cum, & Sub hoc pane est corpus meum, tum in ligata Cantione à se composita: JEsus Christus unser Heyland &c. / per hunc rythmum, verborgen im Brod so klein / gab Er uns seinen Leib zu essen / explanavit, hancque suam Explanationem Impanationis & Companationis titulis gravandi ansam dedit amplissimam.
english: Becanus (Manual Controv. II.2.2 p. 330) charges Luther with a personal, intimate, perichoretic union of body with bread.

Luther’s own speech feeds the suspicion: In, With, and Under this bread is my body, plus his hymn line hidden in the bread so small / He gave us His body to eat — ample handle for Impanation and Companation labels.

source_text: Ex altera parte, Unionem panis & Corporis Christi in Eucharistia cum Unione humanae Christi naturae, & personae ejus divinae, in libro de Captivitate Babylonica Tom. 2. mihi p. 265. eum in modum comparat, ut huic per omnia similem fecisse visus sit; tamen, quia tum ipse Lutherus posteriorem Unionis modum, seu personalem, conceptis verbis in Confessione sua majore de Coena, negat; in Libro autem de Captivitate Babylonica, Transsubstantiationem pontificiam refutaturus, panisque in Coena praesentiam adstructurus, inter propositiones has duas: Hoc, seu, hic panis est corpus meum, Et, Deus est homo, nudam duntaxat earum comparationem instituisse deprehenditur & ostendere gestivisse, quô modô utrobique Disparatum de Disparato praedicetur; (Quô nomine etiam inter nostrates Wolfgangus Musculus, Lutherum à personali corporis & sanguinis Christi Unione absolvit Loci commun. p. m. 354.)
english: In On the Babylonian Captivity he compares bread–body union with the hypostatic union (Deus est homo), which looks personal.

Yet his Greater Confession on the Supper denies a personal mode, and the Captivity comparison is only bare Disparate-of-Disparate predication — so Musculus (among ours) absolves him from personal union of body and blood.

source_text: Tùm verò formulis loquendi, priorem Unionis modum invehentibus, nil aliud sibi voluisse à Lutheranis perhibetur, quàm inexplicabilem Coëxistentiae corporis Christi cum pane rationem, denotare, eandem ob causam nunquam unâ vel alterâ ex tribus particulis, In, Cum, & Sub, separatim acceptâ, sed universis simul sumtis, usus (cujus tamen contrarium vidimus Annot. praeced. §. 3. 4.); Nec non in rythmo, solam Imperceptibilitatem modi praesentiae corporis Christi in Eucharistia, vocabulo germanico hoc, Verborgen / exprimere sat egisse, hunc in sensum rythmo integro exponendo: JEsus gab uns in dem so kleinen Brod / seinen Leib / verborgen / das ist / auf verborgene unbegreifliche und geheime Weise / zu essen; idcirco (utut expositiones ac excusationes Lutheri ejusque formularum loquendi, satis violente contortaque maneant) non tamen vel Luthero ipsi, quantum ad hactenus ab eo dicta attinet, vel Lutheranis hodiernis, Crassiorem istam Consubstantiationem rectè tribui posse arbitramur.
english: Lutherans say the crasser-sounding formulas only mark inexplicable coexistence — hence In/Cum/Sub used together, never apart (though Annotatio I §§.3–4 showed the contrary).
Verborgen in the hymn means only that the mode of presence is imperceptible — hidden, incomprehensible, secret.
However forced the excuses, Strimesius will not rightly pin that crasser Consubstantiation on Luther or today’s Lutherans.

source_text: Posterior, seu Subtilis Consubstantiatio, solam dicit duarum Substantiarum, panis scil. & Corporis Christi in S. Coena Coëxistentiam Unionemque quandam exteriorem, ac παραστατικήν, dicendam equidem Substantialem, Corporalem, Localem, at non Formaliter, seu quoad Unionis modum, sed solum Materialiter & quoad ipsa Unienda, quae omnino Substantiae & quidem Corporeae sunt, indeque porrò suum quaelibet locum proprium, localitatemque intrinsecam, obtinent. Hujus Definitionem, seu essentiales conceptus jamjam nominatos, cùm Lutherani nulli dubitaverint suos facere, etiam Definitum sive latino Consubstantiationis, sive graeco συνουσίας termino expressum, facilè admiserint, uti colligere datur ex Kronmayeri Theol. Posit. p. 703. & 714. & Bayeri Dissert. de Impanatione p. 31. quanquam ab admisso Definito hoc, nulla Synusiastas eos appellandi justa procedat consequentia, nec diffitendum sit, si genuinum & patristicum συνουσίας & συνουσιαστῶν usum sequaris, Lutheranos non συνουσιάστας, sed ἐνουσιάστας rectius appellari, sic merito monente Suicero, Thesaur. Eccles. p. 1183. & 1184.; Justius verò Becanus cit. a pag. 331. inferat, datâ Consubstantiatione quacunque, etiam Lutherana tantum, & subtiliori, propriae praedicationi verborum Christi locum ampliùs nullum relinqui.
english: Subtler Consubstantiation: bread and Christ’s body coexist in the Supper with an exterior, παραστατική union — substantial/corporal/local materially as to the things united, not formally as to union-mode; each keeps its own place.
Lutherans own the definition and the name Consubstantiation / συνουσία (Kronmayer; Bayer) — yet Suicer would call them ἐνουσιάσται, not συνουσιάσται.
Becanus’s sharper point: grant any Consubstantiation, even the Lutheran subtler kind, and proper predication of Christ’s words has nowhere left to stand.
Stop before §.III (history: conception / nativity / duration).

source_text: §. III. Utriusque Consubstantiationis Historiam, per Compendiolum aliquod tradendum, tribus admodum momentis comprehendemus, quorum primum Consubstantiationis CONCEPTIONEM; Secundum, NATIVITATEM; Tertium, PERDURATIONEM enarrat.
english: §.III: both kinds of Consubstantiation get a short history in three moments.
CONCEPTION, then NATIVITY, then DURATION.

source_text: CONCEPTIONEM locandam arbitramur in triplici errore eorum, qui Consubstantiationem alterutram enixi tandèm sunt. Horum errorum PRIMUM absolvunt malè intellecta Patrum primorum Dicta, vel, ex duabus rebus, id est Substantiis, terrena, & cælesti, vel ex una tantum terrena substantia, at Accidente quodam Cælesti, sive Externæ Sanctitatis, sive Virtutis Divinæ Intrinsecæ, adaucta, Eucharistiam sacram constare innuentium.
english: CONCEPTION sits in a triple error of those who finally pressed either Consubstantiation.

FIRST error: early Fathers badly read — as if the Eucharist were two substances (earthly + celestial), or one earthly substance plus some celestial accident of external holiness or intrinsic divine virtue.

source_text: (1) Duas hîc Substantias memorat unus omnium instar Irenæus Anno Dni. 160: Panis, inquit, qui est à terra, percipiens invocationem Dei, jam non communis panis est, sed Eucharistia ex duabus rebus constans, terrena & cælesti, libro 4. contra hæres. cap. 34.; Sed libro 5. cap. 12. idem ferè repetens, adjicit tamen, se verba sua ad usum sacræ Eucharistiæ restricta velle, in quo fiat, ut quemadmodum animæ cælestes, cælesti substantia, ceu alimento sibi proprio, sic corpora terrestria substantia terrestri nutriantur & augescant: Eum, inquit, Calicem, qui est creatura, suum sanguinem, & eum panem, qui est creatura, suum corpus confirmavit: Quando ergo calix & panis percipiunt verbum Dei, fit Eucharistia sanguinis & corporis Christi ex quibus augetur & consistit Carnis nostræ substantia.
english: (1) Irenaeus (A.D. 160) is the stock witness for two things, earthly and celestial, in the Eucharist after invocation.

But bk. 5 restricts the saying to use: celestial souls feed on celestial substance; earthly bodies on earthly — the creature-cup and creature-bread confirmed as His blood and body when they receive God’s word.

source_text: (2) Substantiam terrenam sanctitate quadam affectam, Irenæo paulò vetustior Scriptor, S. Justinus Martyr, saltem implicitè inducit, quando Apol. secunda ad Anton. Imperat. prope finem, Christianorum sui temporis consuetudinem celebrandæ Cænæ hisce recenset: Postquam Præses gratias egit & acclamavit populus, illi, qui à nobis dicuntur Diaconi, seu Ministri, dant cuique præsentium quod sumant de pane & vino; & hoc alimentum à nobis vocatur Eucharistia; non enim ut vulgarem panem, neque ut vulgare poculum ea sumimus. Eundem in sensum Greg. Nyssenus in Orat. de Baptis. Christi: Panis, ait, initio communis est, sed per mysterium consecratus, vel sanctificatus, dicitur corpus Christi. Utrumque verò de nuda externa sanctitate verba facere, prior, appellatione vulgaris panis, i. e. destinato separatoque, per verbum & preces ad sanctum usum, contradistinguendi; posterior verò adjectis mox Similitudinibus nonnullis, à Sanctitate olei ad sanctum usum, aquæ in baptismate, quin templi lapidumque, ex quibus templum exstruendum est, petitis, disertè satis explicat.
english: (2) Justin (near Irenaeus’s senior) describes deacons giving bread and wine called Eucharist — not taken as common bread or cup.

Gregory of Nyssa: bread starts common, then consecrated is called Christ’s body — both mean bare external holiness (set apart by word and prayer; like oil, baptismal water, temple stones), not a second metaphysical substance.

source_text: Denique (3) Substantiam terrestrem, singulari virtute divinâ, i. e. Spiritus Sancti efficacia, imprægnatam quasi, in S. Coena sistunt Theodoretus seu potiùs Clemens in Epitome Stromat. quæ desiderantur, dicens: Panem & oleum sanctificari τῇ δυνάμει τῶν ὀνομάτων, non eadem manentia κατὰ τὸ φαινόμενον, sicut in speciem assumpta sunt, sed δυνάμει εἰς δύναμιν πνευματικὴν μεταβάλλεσθαι — virtute in virtutem spiritualem mutari. Hæc Clementis dicta fusiùs declarat Victor Antiochenus ad illa Marci: Et cænantibus ipsis: Deus sese accommodans nostris infirmitatibus immittit propositis speciebus virtutem vitæ & ea transmutat in efficaciam ipsius carnis, ut in participationem vivificam eam habeamus. Prorsus ad mentem Liturgiæ Græcorum quam S. Marci vocant, utpote in qua rogatur Deus, ut immittat super panes & calices Spiritum Sanctum suum, & eos sanctificet & perficiat tanquam Deus omnipotens & faciat panem quidem corpus calicem autem sanguinem. Cujus quoque vestigia legit S. Cyprianus, Spiritum Sanctum non Autorem duntaxat Rei Sacramento debitæ esse, sed & sacramento plenitudinem gratiæ suæ infundere dicit, de Baptismo Christi. At, omnes hi, effatis his suis, Corporis Christi in S. Coena praesentiam, non aliam, quam spiritualem, tum per Autorem Spiritum, tum per Autoris hujus operationem, effectumque spiritualem, introducunt.
english: (3) Clement (via Theodoret’s Stromata epitome): bread and oil change by the power of the names into spiritual power — not same in appearance.

Victor of Antioch, the Liturgy of St. Mark, and Cyprian speak of the Spirit sending life-virtue into the species — yet all introduce only a spiritual presence of Christ’s body, by the Spirit’s authorship and effect.

source_text: Itaque recitata hactenus dicta Patrum aliaque similia quàm plurima, quibus equidem Eucharistiam sacram duplici substantia constare illi dixerunt, sed de legitimo tantùm usu intellexerunt, in quo, dignè accedentes, non terrestrem solum panem, sed & Cælestim participant, panem Eucharisticum precibus quidem sanctificari, sed ea sanctificatione, quâ omnia alia, perhibente Apostolo 1. Tim. 4. virtutem quidem ac efficaciam divinam, pani, vel affundi, vel infundi, à Spiritu Sancto, sed respectu duntaxat eorum qui pane sacramentali ritè vescuntur (utpote qui soli, non autem panis, δυνάμει εἰς δύναμιν virtute in virtutem spiritualem, per spiritualem corporis Christi participationem, transmutantur); Hæc inquam dicta Patrum, Rhetoricô præterea elata stylô, nec ad Metaphysicum rigorem exigenda, illuc, per errorem, traxerunt Consubstantiationem enixuri & interpretati sunt, acsi Patres Corporalem Unionem panis & corporis Christi, in Coena Sacra, etiam ante, & extra usum, seu perceptionem panis fidelem, fieri inculcassent, ex opere operato, vescenti cuivis, virtutem spiritualem, quin ipsam corporis Christi substantiam, corporali modo, conciliaturam ac communicaturam.
english: Those Father-sayings meant legitimate use: the worthy receive earthly and celestial; 1 Tim. 4 sanctification; Spirit’s virtue toward communicants, not a changed bread-substance.
Rhetorical, not metaphysical — yet consubstantiation-pressers twist them as if the Fathers taught corporal bread–body union before and outside faithful use, ex opere operato to any eater.
Stop before §.IV (SECOND error — middle-ages Fathers after Chalcedon).

source_text: §. IV. Errori primo successit SECUNDUS, perversa scil. intelligentia ac interpretatio Patrum Mediorum Seculorum, post Chalcedonense scil. seu postremum Concilium Oecumenicum, Eutychi oppositum, istius hæresin verò impugnantium argumento inter alia eô quoque, quô humanam Christi naturam ne exaltatam quidem, post Unionem cum divina personalem, à Divina magis absorberi statuerunt, quàm panis absorbetur à corpore Christi, in legitimo Eucharistiæ usu, isti uniendo.
english: §.IV: after the first error comes a SECOND — middle-ages Fathers after Chalcedon, read askew.
Fighting Eutyches they said Christ’s exalted human nature is not absorbed by the divine more than bread is absorbed by Christ’s body in legitimate Eucharistic use.

source_text: Loca hujusmodi aliquot, eademque omnino, in medium adducunt Reverendissimus Burnetus in Expositione 39. articulorum Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ pag. 330. & doctissimus Picherellus Opuscula Theol. p. 176, Chrysostomi scil. ad Cæsareum Monachum scribentis: Sicut antequam sanctificatur panis, panem nominamus: Divina autem illum sanctificante gratiâ, mediante sacerdote, liberatus est quidem ab appellatione panis, dignus autem habitus est Dominici corporis appellatione, & signatura panis in ipso permanfit. THEODORETI in Dialogo ita loquentis: Neque signa mystica post sanctificationem recedunt à sua natura: Manent enim in priore substantia & figura & forma & videri & tangi possunt, suntque panis &c. intelliguntur autem ea quæ sunt & creduntur, Dialogo secundo.
english: Burnet (39 Articles p. 330) and Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. p. 176) stack the same loci.
Chrysostom to Caesarius: after sanctification the bread is worthy of the Lord’s-body name, yet the bread-signature remains.
Theodoret’s Dialogue II: the mystical signs keep prior substance, figure, and form — still bread to sight and touch, understood as believed.

source_text: GELASII denique contra Eutychen ita disputantis: Sacramenta, inquit, quæ sumimus, divina res est, & tamen non desinit esse substantia & natura panis & vini. His adjicimus PROSPERUM, Scriptorem per omnia Catholicum, disertè docentem: Eucharistiam duabus constare visibili elementorum specie & invisibili Dn. nostri sanguine & carne (hoc est Sacramento & re sacramenti) sicut persona Christi constat ex Deo & homine, Distinct. secunda de consecratione cap. Hoc est.
english: Gelasius against Eutyches: what we take is a divine thing, yet does not cease to be the substance and nature of bread and wine.
Prosper: Eucharist = visible element-species + invisible Lord’s flesh and blood (sacrament and res), as Christ’s person is God and man.

source_text: Quæ loca omnia, in id Primariò intenta, ne crederetur, post spiritualem corporis Christi, cum pane, in Eucharistia, ritè debitèque celebrata, Unionem, panis abolitionem quandam seu absorbitionem contingere, istuc flectere sustinuerunt quotquot ad Consubstantiationem sibi aditum pararunt, ut post consecrationem panis, cum hoc ipso, etiam ante usum ejus, Corpus Christi non alio modo uniri sibi imaginarentur, quàm, post benedictam inter mulieres ab Angelo salutatam matrem Christi, in hujus utero, conceptæ humanæ Christi naturæ divina persona, substantiali sese modo, sociavit cumque ista in unum idemque ὑφιστάμενον unita est.
english: Those texts first meant to block belief that after spiritual bread–body union the bread is abolished or absorbed.
Consubstantiation-seekers bend them instead: after consecration, even before use, they imagine union like the divine person joining Christ’s human nature in Mary’s womb into one ὑφιστάμενον.

source_text: Accessit tandem TERTIUS error, Seculo nono & undecimo subnatus, ex partim crudè intellectis Bertrami, alias Ratramni, in libro de corpore Christi ad Carol. Calvum, de figura corporis Christi in S. Coena, ad mentem antiquiorum Patrum, enunciatis, alibi recitandis integris; partim crudè nimis, de eadem figura corporis Christi, Berengarii effatis, utut non ita crudè ab ipso acceptis, debitus: His enim sese opponentium plurimi, ita panem corporis Christi figuram negarunt in Eucharistia sacra esse, ut Corporalem hujus cum isto Unionem urserint, sicque conceptum fotumque hactenus Consubstantiationis embryonem, vel crassiorem, vel subtiliorem, in lucem publicam prodire fecerint.
english: THIRD error (9th–11th c.): crudely heard Bertram/Ratramnus on the figure of Christ’s body (to Charles the Bald), plus Berengar’s figure-sayings taken too raw.
Opponents denied figure so hard they urged corporal union — and so forced the long-fostered Consubstantiation embryo, crass or subtle, into public light.
Stop before §.V (Paschasius Radbertus as alleged first author).

source_text: §. V. Enimverò sunt, tàm ex Reformatis Franciscus Burmannus, Synops. Theol. Tom. 2. p. 401. quàm ex Lutheranis, Joh. Wilhelm. Bajerus, Theol. Histor. p. 593. qui illo tempore PASCHASIUM RHADEBERTUM, Abbatem Corbeiensem, Bertrami adversarium Coævum, in libro ejusdem cum Bertrami libro nominis, primum Consubstantiationis Autorem Patremque constituunt.
english: §.V: Reformed Burmann (Synopsis Theol. II p. 401) and Lutheran Bayer (Theol. Histor. p. 593) both cast Paschasius Radbertus, Abbot of Corbie — Bertram’s coeval adversary — as Consubstantiation’s first author and father.
They point to his book under the same title as Bertram’s.

source_text: Rectiùs multo à Bellarmino Conversionis, Transsubstantiationis rudimenti, Propagatorem habitum, cùm Tom. Controv. de Eucharist. p. m. 579. tùm in libro de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis p. 150., probante idem calculumque adjiciente suum Nostrate Viro Celeberrimo Wilhelmo Caveô, Script. Eccles. Hist. literaria p. 376., suffulciendo hac in parte ipsis Rhadeberti enunciatis quàm plurimis in libro de corpore & sanguine Domini cap. 20.
english: Bellarmine is nearer the mark: Paschasius propagates Conversion, the seed of Transubstantiation (Eucharist Controversies; Ecclesiastical Writers).
Cave adds his vote; Paschasius’s own On the body and blood of the Lord ch. 20 props that reading.

source_text: Et tantùm non extra dubium idem ponente Bertramô, quando duarum duntaxat, tempore suo, de praesentia corporis Christi in sacra Coena, sententiarum meminit, initio libri sui pag. m. 3. 55. quarum alteram, de Spirituali praesentia, ipsemet, cum Patribus omnium seculorum, fovet, alteram, de Corporali, per Conversionem panis, adductam, in Paschasio Rhadeberto, oppugnat; Tertiam, si quae fuisset novitiamque, silentio haud praetervecturus, praesertim apud adversarium reperiundam.
english: Bertram nearly settles it: in his day he knows only two opinions — spiritual presence (his own, with the Fathers of every age) versus corporal presence by conversion of the bread (Paschasius), which he attacks.
Had there been a novel third (consubstantiation), he would not have passed it in silence — least of all in his adversary.

source_text: Quanquam interea illud allegato Bajero concedendum sit Paschasium Rhadebertum, primum fuisse, qui propriè dictum Corpus Christi, in S. Coena, Ore corporis, accipi docuerit, & quidem citra lacerationem, dentibus instituendam, libro de corpore & sanguine Christi cap. 4. restricta tamen etiam Orali acceptione ad solos fideles, lib. eodem cap. 6., cibum istum (nempe carnem Christi) non nisi solis amicis & fratribus Christi porrigi, disertis verbis cap. 10. professus.
english: Concede to Bayer this much: Paschasius is first to teach oral reception of Christ’s proper body in the Supper without tooth-laceration.
Even then he restricts oral reception to the faithful alone — that food only for Christ’s friends and brothers.

source_text: Quemadmodum similiter Burmanno largiendum, docuisse Rhadebertum, Carnem Christi etiam spiritualiter manducari in Sacramento Coenae, & sanguinem spiritualiter potari, cap. 5. 6. 10. 20.
english: Concede to Burmann likewise: Radbertus also teaches spiritual eating of the flesh and spiritual drinking of the blood in the Supper sacrament.
Stop before Berengar’s confuters as inventors of crassior/subtilior (Rupert of Deutz &c.).

source_text: Ceterum inter Berengarii Confutatores tam Crassioris, quam Subtilioris Consubstantiationis Inventores, nullo negotio repereris. PRIORIS quidem RUPERTUM TUITIENSEM Abbatem, fassô Johanne Gerhardô, Patrolog. p. 551. nequicquam ergò vel Reformatis, à Reverendiss. Forbesio, vel Lutheranis, nisi in contumeliam, a Bajero Disput. de Impanat. num. 11. 21. & 22. annumeratum, cum ipse Rupertus semet crassum Impanatorem expositione sententiae suae prodat.
english: Among Berengar’s confuters you easily find inventors of both crasser and subtler Consubstantiation.
Of the crasser: Rupert, Abbot of Deutz — Gerhard owns him; Forbes and Bayer list him only as insult — because Rupert’s own exposition brands him a crass Impanator.

source_text: Tum Commentario in Genesin Lib. 6. cap. 32. his verbis tradito: Quomodo, inquit, panis, qui videtur, est Christus? ad hæc inquam, quomodo qualibet metalli species v. g. aurum sive argentum (nota tamen hîc similitudinem Fratribus Augustanae confessionis usitatam, praecipuè de ferro) valido igni conflatum atque resolutum, re vera & aurum est, & ignis quoque dicitur & est? Etenim aurum videtur & est, quod erat, & tamen verissimè ignis dicitur & est, quod non erat: Idcirco sic omnino panis admotus vel immersus terribili atque ineffabili mysterio passionis Christi, adhuc panis videtur esse, quod erat, & tamen in veritate Christus est, quod non erat.
english: Genesis commentary (VI.32): how is visible bread Christ? Like gold in strong fire — still gold to sight, yet truly called and is fire.
So bread brought into Christ’s passion-mystery still seems bread, yet in truth is Christ — a similitude Augsburg brothers later use of iron.

source_text: Tum Commentario in Exodum, Lib. 2. cap. 10. expositione auctiori: Sicut, inquit, humanam naturam non destruxit, cùm illam operatione sua ex utero virginis DEUS verbo in unitatem personae conjunxit; Sic SUBSTANTIAM panis & vini, secundum exteriorem speciem, quinque sensibus subactam, non mutat aut destruit, cum eidem Verbo, in UNITATEM corporis ejusdem, quod in cruce pependit, & sanguinis ejusdem quem de latere suo fudit, ista CONJUNGIT. Ibidem: Proinde sicut hominem, ait, qui de virgine sumtus in cruce pependit, rectè & Catholicè Deum confitemur, sic veraciter hoc, quod sumimus de sancto altari, Christum dicimus, agnum Dei praedicamus.
english: Exodus commentary (II.10): as God did not destroy human nature when joining it into personal unity from the virgin’s womb, so He does not destroy bread-and-wine substance when joining it to the Word into unity of the crucified body and shed blood.
What we take from the altar we truly call Christ, the Lamb of God — as we confess the virgin-born man on the cross to be God.

source_text: CUNONEM etiam Abbatem Sigebergensem, complicem & fautorem sententiae suae nactum, utpote de quo, in praefatione, libris suis, de operibus Trinitatis in Genesin & Exodum, praefixa, inter alia scribit, quòd solus CUNO, imò per Cunonem, (ut ait) Christus praesidio sibi adfuit contra eos, qui molesti fuere huic operi, & qui tùm dictis tùm factis, fremuerunt in ipsum, quasi paxillus sibi Cuno factus sit, positus in loco fideli, in quo spei suae possit vasculum suspendi.
english: Rupert names Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg, accomplice and patron of his sentence.
In the Genesis/Exodus preface Christ stood by him through Cuno alone against those who roared at the work — Cuno a peg in a faithful place for the vessel of his hope.

source_text: Sed & reperias vice versâ, eodem seculo undecimo, qui sententiam hanc hæresin appellarunt & in ipsa herba suffocare annisi sunt, GUITMUNDUM scil. Aversanum, de exortu modò dictae sententiae, ita scribentem, libro 3. de veritate corporis & sanguinis Domini contra Berengarium: Nunc, inquit, contra illos habenda est ratio qui Ecclesiae rationibus expugnati, jam quidem negare nequeunt substantiam corporis Christi cibo inesse Dominico; panem tamen & vinum per verba Salvatoris in carnem ejus & sanguinem verti nequaquam credentes, sed Christum PANI ET VINO COMMISCENTES, tanquam subtiliori ratione, HÆRESIN ALTERAM condiderunt. … Quapropter … nec alias ipsi afferant, quae insania est, ut Christum, ut ita dixerim, sua autoritate IMPANENT ET INVINENT. … At IMPANARI & INVINARI Christum, nulla … expetit ratio, nec Prophetae praedixerunt, nec Christus ostendit, nec Apostoli praedicaverunt, nec mundus, exceptis his paucissimis HÆRETICIS, credidit. … Christus enim isti IMPANATUM ET INVINATUM annunciant … Hos IMPANATORES suos ipse Dominus Jesus ore suo interficit cum accipiens panem … ait, Hoc est Corpus meum; non ait: IN HOC LATET corpus meum; nec dixit: IN HOC vino est sanguis meus.
english: Same eleventh century, the other way: Guitmund of Aversa calls the sentence a heresy to smother in the blade.
Beaten from denying Christ’s body in the Lord’s food, some mix Christ with bread and wine and found another heresy — Impanate and Invinate by their own authority.
No prophet, Christ, apostle, or world taught Impanation; the Lord kills Impanators with This is My Body — not In this lies My body.

source_text: Guitmundo meritò adjungimus ALGERUM ex Scholastico & Ecclesiastico monachum, eandem Impanationis sententiam, novae hæreseos, hisce postulantem: Quamvis, inquit, Sacramentum à re Sacramenti tanquam figura à veritate satis distinctum sit, errantes tamen quidam, de quibusdam sanctorum verbis dicunt ita personaliter IMPANATUM Christum, sicut in carne humana, personaliter incarnatum Deum, quae HÆRESIS, quia nova & absurda est, rationibus & autoritatibus radicitus est exstirpanda.
english: Alger joins Guitmund: some erring readers make Christ personally Impanated as God is personally Incarnate — a new absurd heresy to root out by reason and authority.
Stop before §.VI (SUBTILIOR inventor Ascelinus).

source_text: §. VI. POSTERIORIS seu SUBTILIORIS CONSUBSTANTIATIONIS Autor primus non Berengarius est, ex mera incertitudine & aliena relatione, à Guitmundo habitus, quem cæcum ducem secutus est Bajerus Disput. de Impan. num. 15. 16; Sed ASCELINUS, MONACHUS quidam, Wilhelmo Caveo memoratus, multis verò, ut & Bajero ignoratus.
english: §.VI: first author of the subtler Consubstantiation is not Berengar — Guitmund guessed that from hearsay, and Bayer followed him blind.
It is Ascelinus, a monk Cave remembers and Bayer (with many) never knew.

source_text: Ascelinus enim, in Epistola ad Berengarium ipsum, per Dacherium ex antiquis membranis Abbatiæ Casalis Benedicti, editâ, etiamsi confiteatur, se Paschasii sententiam sequi (nempe quantum ad corporalem carnis Christi praesentiam in sacramento attinet) tamen de pane consecrato & modo praesentiae corporis Christi in Eucharistia longè aliter, ac ille, scribit, non Conversionem panis in Corpus Christi, sed tamen ad minimum Coëxistentiam Corporis cum pane benedicto, defendens.
english: Ascelinus’s letter to Berengar (Dacherius, from Casale Benedicti membranes) owns Paschasius on corporal presence of Christ’s flesh in the sacrament.
On consecrated bread and the mode of presence he writes far otherwise: not conversion of bread into body, but at least coexistence of the Body with the blessed bread.

source_text: Verba ejus hæc sunt: Neque vero mirari vel diffidere debemus, Deum facere posse ut hoc quod in Altari consecratur (nempe panis & vinum) virtute Spiritus Sancti & ministerio sacerdotis, UNIATUR corpori illi, quod ex Maria Virgine Redemtor noster assumsit, utrumque substantia corporea, utrumque visibile.
english: His words: do not marvel that God can make altar-consecrated bread and wine, by Spirit and priest, be united to the body our Redeemer took from Mary.
Both are corporeal substance; both visible.

source_text: Addit, pro illustratione Unionis duarum Substantiarum, non item, pro illustratione Modi Unionis, Similitudines: quòd & nos ipsi, inquit, ex corporea & incorporea, ex mortali & immortali substantia sumus compacti; & in Christo divina humanaque natura convenit in unam personam. Vide hanc Epistolam ad Berengarium apud Dacherium in notis ad vitam Lanfranci pag. 24. & 25. Edit. Paris. anno 1648. allegante Otrokocsi in Irenico pag. 79. & 80. Hæc Asceliniana, praesertim cùm Unionem panis & corporis Christi promiscuè inculcent, citra omne discrimen respectûs ad pios & impios, tam genuina sunt modernæ sententiae Lutheranae, quàm Ovum Ovo.
english: Similitudes illustrate the union of two substances, not the mode: we are compacted of corporeal/incorporeal and mortal/immortal; in Christ divine and human meet in one person.
Letter at Dacherius on Lanfranc (Paris 1648); Otrokocsi cites it.
These Asceliniana — union of bread and body without pious/impious distinction — match modern Lutheran sentence as egg to egg.
Stop before §.VII (Nativitas summary / Lateran XIII).

source_text: §. VII. Ita habet Nativitas utriusque Consubstantiationis, Seculo 13, in Concilio Lateranensi, sub Innocentio III., rursus denatae, quod Concilium, Consubstantiationis, ceu jam tum explosæ & antiquatæ opinionis, mentionem, hisce injicit:
english: §.VII: both Consubstantiations have their Nativity reborn in the 13th century — Lateran Council under Innocent III.
That council already treats Consubstantiation as an exploded, antiquated opinion, and names it thus:

source_text: Fuerunt, inquit, qui dicerent, quòd sicut post Consecrationem, vera panis remanent accidentia sic & vera panis substantia: quia sicut subjectum non potest subsistere sine Accidentibus, sic Accidentia non possunt subsistere sine subjecto.
english: Some said: after consecration, as true bread-accidents remain, so true bread-substance remains.
For a subject cannot stand without accidents, nor accidents without a subject.

source_text: Sed panis & vini substantiis permanentibus ad prolationem illorum verborum CORPUS ET SANGUIS CHRISTI, veraciter incipiant esse SUB ILLIS (nempe sub panis & vini substantiis) ita quòd sub eisdem Accidentibus UTRUMQUE verè suscipitur PANIS ET CARO, VINUM ET SANGUIS, quorum alterum probat sensus, reliquum credit fides.
english: With bread and wine substances still there, at Body and Blood of Christ those start to be under them.
Under the same accidents both are truly received — bread and flesh, wine and blood — sense proves one, faith the other.

source_text: Postquam jam tum Berengariana sententia, cui sese Consubstantiatores ex professo opposuerant, inque nimia ejus oppugnatione Consubstantiationem suam progenuerant, in ipsa Berengarii persona censuram publicam passa fuisset. Quo de in sequentibus Annotationibus commodior dicendi locus fuerit.
english: By then Berengar’s sentence had already taken public censure in his person.
Consubstantiators had openly fought him — and in over-fighting him had begotten their own Consubstantiation.
More on that in the Annotations that follow.
Stop before §.VIII (PERDURATIO / revival after apparent extinction).

source_text: §. VIII. Etsi verò hoc pacto extincta visa est Consubstantiatio, exiguo satis tempore & à paucioribus edocta; Waldensibus etiam (in quorum doctrina de S. Coena, Consubstantiationis subtilioris sententiam conservatam nonnulli gloriantur) diversum prorsus à Consubstantiatione profitentibus, id quod Annotatio nostra quarta ad oculum ostendet; tamen resuscitata quasi è mortuis postliminio fuit, sub finem Seculi supra dicti XIII., per Johannem Parisienfem, Monachum ex ordine Dominicano.
english: §.VIII PERDURATIO: Consubstantiation looked extinct — short-lived, few teachers; Waldenses (some claim) keep a subtler line, but they actually teach something else (see Annotatio IV).
Yet it rose again near the end of the 13th century through John of Paris, Dominican.

source_text: Non-improbata Scholasticis nonnullis, sigillatim Scoto, subtili doctori, initio seculi XIV, famosissimoque Durando, Anno 1320, quorum testimonia lege apud Franciscum Foris Otrokocsi in Irenico Cap. 6. §. 27. & seq. non item Thomæ Aquinati, à Dorschæo, hoc locô, neutiquam in Consensum trahi merito, quanquam fassus introducatur Transsubstantiationem ex verbis Institutionis probari haud posse.
english: Some Scholastics did not reject the revival — Scotus early in the 14th century, and Durandus in 1320 (Otrokocsi, Irenicum VI.27ff.).
Aquinas is not to be dragged into this consent by Dorsche, even if he grants Transubstantiation is not proved from the Institution words alone.

source_text: Donec tandem Petrus de Aliaco Cardinalis Cameracensis, qui Concilii Constantiensis tempore floruit, cujusque manu & consiliis Johannes Hussus & Hieronymus Pragensis, Viri Dei Christique martyres, miserè periêre, initio Seculi XV. Anno scil. 1414. apertius illi favere cœpit, à quo etiam D. Lutherus eandem hausisse fatetur ipsemet Lib. de Captiv. Babyl. Tom. 2. Operum Latinorum Jenensium fol. 263.
english: Peter d’Ailly, Cardinal of Cambrai, at Constance (1414) began to favor it more openly — the same whose hand and counsel saw Huss and Jerome of Prague perish.
Luther himself confesses he drew that line from Cambrai (Babylonian Captivity, Jena Latin II fol. 263).

source_text: Dedit inquit, mihi quondam, cùm Theologiam Scholasticam haurirem, occasionem cogitandi, Cardinalis Cameracensis Libro sententiarum quarto acutissime disputans: Multò probabilius esse & minus superfluorum miraculorum poni, si in altari verus panis verumque vinum non autem sola accidentia esse astrurentur, nisi Ecclesia determinasset contrarium. Postea videns, quæ esset Ecclesia, quæ hoc determinasset, nempe Thomistica, hoc est Aristotelica, audacior factus sum & qui inter saxum & sacrum hærebam, tandem stabilivi conscientiam meam sententia priori: esse videlicet verum panem verumque vinum, in quibus Christi vera caro verusque sanguis non aliter nec minus sit, quam illi sub accidentibus suis ponunt. Quod feci, quia vidi, Thomistarum opiniones, sive probentur à Papa, sive à Concilio, manere opiniones, nec fieri articulos fidei, etiamsi Angelus de Cœlo aliud statueret. Nam quod sine scripturis asseritur aut revelatione probata, opinari licet, credi non est necesse &c.
english: Luther: Cambrai’s Sentences IV gave him leave to think true bread and wine on the altar likelier than bare accidents — unless the Church had ruled otherwise.
Seeing that Church was Thomist/Aristotelian, he fixed his conscience: true bread and wine, with Christ’s true flesh and blood no less than under accidents.
Thomist opinions stay opinions, not articles of faith — even if an angel from heaven said otherwise; without Scripture or proven revelation, opinion is free, belief not owed.

source_text: Unde non potest non oleum & operam perdere Bajerus, in id annisus, ut ostendat, Lutherum & diversam à Cameracensi opinionem, & præter Cameracensem, pluribus communem, fovisse, Disput. de Impan. num. 50.
english: So Bayer wastes oil and labor trying to prove Luther both differed from Cambrai and shared a wider common opinion (Disput. de Impan. §50).
Stop before §.IX (Marburg determination; difficulties of corporal-in-bread presence).

source_text: §. IX. Quicquid verò de Luthero ejusque Sententia fiat, istaque vel eadem, vel diversa, à Cameracensis, æstimetur, nobis sufficit, ad non imputandam Cameracensis opinionem hodiernis Lutheranis, hos eam nolle sibi adscriptam.
english: §.IX: whatever one makes of Luther versus Cambrai, today’s Lutherans will not wear Cambrai’s opinion as theirs.
That refusal is enough — we do not impute it to them.

source_text: Utut nulli assequamur, quomodo Lutheri Determinatio Colloquii Marpurgensis, his scil. concepta verbis: (Etsi autem, an verum corpus & Sanguis Christi corporaliter in pane & vino Coenæ Domini præsens sit, hoc tempore non concordavimus &c.) à Corporis Christi præsentia in vel cum pane, corporali, adeoque à subtiliori Consubstantiatione, expediri possit; cum verba ista non præsentiam duntaxat veri Corporis Christi in Coena, sed & modum præsentiæ corporalem, quin corporalem hunc præsentiæ modum, in ipso pane, disertissimè profiteantur. Eoque non possumus non colophonis locô, tribus quod aiunt verbis, innuere, quibus Difficultatibus Corporalem corporis Christi in pane præsentiam, sive soli Crassiori, sive & Subtiliori, saltem Lutheri, Consubstantiationi vindicandam, pressam advertamus.
english: Marburg’s determination (we have not agreed whether the true body and blood are corporally present in the bread and wine) does not free Luther from corporal presence in or with the bread — nor from subtler Consubstantiation.
Those words confess not presence alone but a corporal mode in the bread itself.
Colophon: watch the difficulties that press corporal-in-bread presence for crassior or subtilior (at least Luther’s) Consubstantiation.

source_text: Enimverò Consubstantiatio quæcunque etiam Subtilior, maximè Lutheri recitata modò, subtiliori utut, quin subtilissima, nobis haud invitis, accensenda, adversa conspicitur: (1) Expressis Scripturæ ipsiusque Institutionis Sacræ Coenæ verbis, quibus panis quidem corpus Christi dicitur esse, non autem Corpus Christi pani præsens, minus, pani corporaliter præsens, minimè omnium, in ipso pane, corporaliter præsens esse. Certè Corporalis præsentia corporis Christi in pane, præterquam quòd Localem præsentiam inferit, quatenus Corporalis esse dicitur (Corporalitate cum Localitate, saltem intrinseca, æquè latè patente) & inclusionem dicit, quatenus in pane, licèt & extra eum, Corpus Christi corporaliter præsens perhibetur, & eo ipso panis non est Corpus Christi, quia corpus Christi duntaxat in pane corporaliter præsens existere dicitur.
english: (1) Scripture and Institution say the bread is Christ’s body — not that the body is present to the bread, less corporally present to it, least of all corporally present in it.
Call presence corporal and you import locality and inclusion; then the bread is not the body, because the body is only said to exist corporally present in the bread.

source_text: (2) Circumstantiis primæ Institutionis: Corpus enim Christi fuit tum temporis corporaliter ad mensam, seu mensæ corporaliter accubuit, adeoque Corporaliter in pane non fuit. Item, quòd si corpus Christi corporaliter in pane tum fuit, cùm Christus Sacramentum Coenæ instituturus, ipsemet panem cum discipulis edit. Matth. 26. 29. Marc. 14. 25. sequetur, eundem in & sub pane, suam propriam carnem comedisse; adeoque totum suum corpus & animam, tum temporis in ore habuisse: hincque adeo, vel multiplicationem esse factam ejusdem corporis Christi, vel duo Christum habuisse corpora, unum continens & comedens, alterum contentum & comesum.
english: (2) At the first Institution Christ’s body was corporally at the table — so not corporally in the bread.

If it was in the bread while He Himself ate with the disciples (Matt. 26:29; Mark 14:25), He ate His own flesh in and under the bread — whole body and soul in His mouth — hence either multiplication of one body, or two bodies (one eating, one eaten).

source_text: (3) Naturæ omnium Sacramentorum, quorum nullum tale signum est, quod rem signatam, secundum suam essentiam, in sese comprehendat. i. e. corpus Christi corporaliter in se contineat: neque enim Sacramenta definiuntur δοχεῖα latibula & vasa includentia res signatas, uti dolium aut cantharus includit vinum, aut marsupium pecuniam, aut cunæ infantem, quibus similibus nonnulli utuntur, ipse etiam Lutherus in Confessione Majore Tom. 2. Witteb. pag. 185. confer etiam Colloquium Maulbrunense Anno 1564. die 15. April. habitum, p. 108. 109.; Sed definiuntur, juxta Augustinum, esse Signa visibilia invisibilis gratiæ. Signi autem natura non est, corporaliter continere, sed signare & significare. Hinc nec Lutherani audent hactenus dicere: Sanguinem Christi corporaliter in aqua Baptismi præsentem esse, vel in hac corporaliter includi.
english: (3) No sacrament is a sign that contains the thing signified in its essence — sacraments are not δοχεῖα jars enclosing what they signify (cask, purse, cradle), though Luther and Maulbronn use such likenesses.
Augustine: visible signs of invisible grace — a sign signifies; it does not contain corporally.
Hence Lutherans dare not say Christ’s blood is corporally in baptismal water.

source_text: (4) Naturæ Corporis Christi, quod corporaliter in uno tantum loco est, & uti tempore institutæ Coenæ, ad mensam corporaliter, non autem simul supra mensam, in pane, vel in manibus Christi panem sumentibus & frangentibus, fuit; Ita tempore celebratæ adhuc & celebrandæ Coenæ, corporaliter in cælis est & in cælis manet teste Spir. S. Act. 3, 21. ipsôque Christô, etiam in Institutionis Coenæ verbis Matth. 26, 29. 1. Cor. 11, 26. Quemadmodum verò caro Christi, dum in terra fuit corporaliter, non utique erat in Cœlo; ita nunc quia in cælis est corporaliter, non est utique in terris, ait B. Vigilius Lib. 4. Hinc Lutherus ipse, postremis verbis præfationis suæ in Biblia, sic scribit: Des Hohen Priesters Söhne / Die mit dem täglichen Opfer umgehen / sollten auff uns Christen deuten / die wir für unserm Vater Christo / im Himmel sitzend / hie auff Erden / mit dem Leibe wohnen / und nicht hin Durch sind bey ihm / ohne mit dem Glauben geistlich. Ubi observa Lutherum tria dicere (1) Christum sedere in Cœlo, nos corpore esse in terra. (2) Nos corpore non esse cum Christo. (3) Non aliter, quam spiritualiter & per fidem, nos esse cum Christo.
english: (4) Christ’s body is corporally in one place only — at the Institution at the table, not also in the bread in His hands; now corporally in heaven (Acts 3:21; Matt. 26:29; 1 Cor. 11:26).
Vigilius: as when on earth it was not in heaven, so now in heaven it is not on earth.
Luther’s Bible preface: we dwell on earth with the body before Christ seated in heaven, and are with Him only spiritually by faith — three points Strimesius marks.

source_text: Denique (5) Consubstantiatio adversa est Determinationi tam qualitatis internæ, quàm conditionis externæ corporis Christi, sub qua, in pane, corporaliter præsens, & olim, in prima Institutione fuisse, & modò, in omni cœnæ administratione, adhuc esse, credendum est, puta: Num exinanitum & crucifixum? an verò exaltatum & glorificatum? Num animæ rationali junctum? an verò ab hac anima separatum? Num sanguine turgidum; an verò exsangue? Num uti in pane cum sanguine, ita sanguis in vino cum corpore? Num in utraque Coenæ parte, i. e. specie utraque, tàm panis, quàm vini, totum? an pars totius? Dubio determinationis protinus, nec aliter tamen, terminando, quàm si corpus Christi præsens quidem, non tamen corporaliter, verum supernaturaliter ac spiritualiter duntaxat in Coena præsens, sed non in pane, verùm in anima solius credentis ac vera fide manducantis, confiteamur.
english: (5) Consubstantiation cannot settle the body’s internal quality or external condition if it is corporally in the bread — emptied or exalted? with soul or without? bloody or bloodless? whole in each species or part?
The doubt ends only if we confess the body present in the Supper supernaturally and spiritually — not in the bread, but in the soul of the true-faith eater alone.
Stop before Annotatio III.

source_text: ANNOTATIO III. De Transsubstantiatione ad pag. 36. in fine. Historia Transsubstantiationis Compendiolum complexa. §. I. Transsubstantiatio, si non quà nomen, certè quà rem, Consubstantiatione antiquior, rem absurdissimam, quam designat, apto satis, etsi serò admodum invento terminô, quà genericum saltem conceptum, expressam exhibet.
english: Annotatio III opens on Transsubstantiation (to p. 36 end): a short History-compendium.
§.I: as rem (if not yet as name) it is older than Consubstantiation; the rem it names is most absurd; the term itself came late but fits the generic concept.

source_text: Quemadmodum enim Transmutatio rei cujuscunque, transformatio vel exterioris, vel interioris formæ; sic Transsubstantiatio unius præcisè substantiæ in aliam (remanentibus sensibusque expositis prioris, seu transmutandæ, posterioris verò, seu in quam transitio fit, absorptis, nulli saltem sensui obviis Accidentibus) mutationem inaudito prorsus exemplo significat. Hujus Historiam, ob cognationem solùm cum Consubstantiatione, hoc locô, per compendium, tradituri, duas quasi Tractationis partes, constituemus, quarum Prior ORTUM Transsubstantiationis in caussis suis rimabitur: Posterior PROGRESSUM ejusdem in modis gradibusque conspicuum reddet.
english: Transmutation reshapes form; Transsubstantiation turns one substance into another while sense-exposed accidents of the former remain and those of the latter are absorbed — a mutation without precedent.
Plan: ORTUS (causes) then PROGRESSUS (modes and degrees), treated here only for kinship with Consubstantiation.

source_text: §. II. Inter Ortûs CAUSAS attendere quoque juvat Occasionalem, quam causam per accidens vocant. Hujusmodi alia Generalior, Specialior alia est. GENERALIOREM existimavero, Hyperbolicas, quin quandoque catachresticas Patrum, tam Græcorum, quàm Latinorum de Symbolis Eucharisticis, locutiones, quibus, nisi dextrè capiantur, incauti facile in errores abducuntur.
english: §.II Ortus causes: also the Occasional (cause by accident).
GENERALIOR: hyperbolic — sometimes even catachrestic — Father-speech on Eucharistic symbols; mishandled, it leads the unwary into error.

source_text: Inter Græcorum Patrum dicta eminent ista CHRYSOSTOMI, Orientalium Patrum disertissimi: Conspicies ait, in sacra Eucharistia Dominum immolatum. Qui cum Patre sursum sedet in illo ipso temporis articulo, omnium manibus pertractatur. Ipsum vides, ipsum tangis, ipsum comedis. Neque enim Angelos neque Archangelos, sed ipsum horum omnium Dominum Tibi ostendo. In mysteriis sanguis ex Christi latere hauritur; hoc admirabili sanguine lingua cruentatur. Hom. 5. & 83. in Matth. Hom. 24. in 1. ad Corinth. Et rursus: Nos in unam secum massam reducit, nec se tantùm videri permittit, sed & tangi & manducari & dentes carni suæ infigi, adeo ut per cibum, quem nobis largitus est, in carnem suam convertamur. Hom. 45. in Johan.
english: Chrysostom (Eastern Fathers’ most eloquent): in the Eucharist you behold the immolated Lord — seated with the Father yet handled, seen, touched, eaten; blood from His side stains the tongue (Hom. Matt. / 1 Cor.).
Again: He knits us into one mass with Himself; teeth are fixed in His flesh so that by the food given we are turned into His flesh (Hom. 45 on John).

source_text: Ex Latinis, eloquentissimi AUGUSTINI verba hæcce adduxisse suffecerit Conc. 1. in Ps. 33. Ferebatur, inquit, Christus in manibus suis, quando, commendans ipsum corpus suum, ait: Hoc est Corpus meum; Ferebat enim illud corpus in manibus suis. Quibus omninò parallelum PROSPERI AQUITANICI de promis. & prædicat. part. 2. cap. 25. assertum: Dominus ait, suum corpus in sanctificato pane gestans manibus suis, dixit: Hoc est corpus meum. Hæc aliaque hujus farinæ Patrum hyperbolice satis enunciata, quibus una ex parte mysterii dignitatem amplificare atque extollere; Ex parte altera verò communicantes ab externorum symbolorum contemplatione ad res significatas tantò devotiùs meditandas convertere allaborarunt, nonnulli propriè nimis acceperunt, non attendentes, quibus iidem Patres hyperbolas suas haud rarò per restrictivas particulas QUASI, QUODAMMODO similesque, mitigarunt ac emolliverunt, annotante id ipsum perquam accuratè pontificio Autore eruditissimo Petro Picherello Opusc. Theol. à pag. 19. in fin. Si cui volupe est, plures Patrum hyperbolicas expressiones legere, haud frustra fuerit famigeratissimum Petrum de Marca Dissert. Posthuma de Euchar. Sacrament. p. 15. evolvere, quanquam in usum suum pontificium, i. e. abusum attractas, ideoque à B. Witakero vindicatas Tom. I. pag. 9.
english: Augustine (Serm. 1 on Ps. 33): Christ was carried in His own hands when He said ‘This is My Body’; Prosper parallels Him bearing His body in the sanctified bread.
Such hyperboles aimed to exalt the mystery and turn communicants from outward symbols to the things signified — yet some took them too properly, missing QUASI / QUODAMMODO softenings (Picherellus).
More samples: de Marca’s posthumous Eucharist dissertation (pontifical abuse) — vindicated by Whitaker.

source_text: §. III. SPECIALIOR Transsubstantiationi ansa data fuit per varios Patrum, maximè Græcorum ἐμφατικωτέρας, pro genio linguæ, excogitatos terminos, quibus in specie mutationem istam, relativam partim, respectu scil. rei signatæ, partim mysticam, respectu communicantium fidelium, pani Eucharistico per & post consecrationem copulatam, designare soliti sunt, quales Autori nostro observati recitantur p. 450 & 480 necnon Salmasio in Tractat. de Transsubst. p. 1. μεταβολή scil. μεταμόρφωσις, μεταποίησις, μεταστοιχείωσις, μετατύπωσις, μεταρρυθμισμός, μετασκεύασις; singuli præterea propriis suis Autoribus tribuuntur à Joh. Jonstono de Communione c. 3. p. 113. Hi termini de morali & σχετικῇ mutatione à Patribus intellecti, substantialis mutationis opinionem aliis, procedente tempore, ingenerarunt.
english: §.III SPECIALIOR handle: Greek emphatic change-terms (metabole, metamorphosis, metapoiesis, metastoicheiosis, metatyposis, metarrhythmismos, metaskeuasis) for a mutation relative to the thing signified and mystic for communicants — cited via our Author, Salmasius, Johnston.
Fathers meant moral and schetic (relative) change; later readers bred a substantial-mutation opinion from those words.

source_text: A Patribus interim nullam extra dictam Mutationem intellectam fuisse, probant, præter cætera, rationes hæ quatuor: (1) quòd expressè Patres docent, idque constantissimè, panes Eucharisticos post consecrationem manere semper idem, quòd ante fuerant. (2) quòd identidem panes post Consecrationem, Signa, Figuras, Symbola, Icones seu imagines, Typos, Antitypos, Similitudines, Metaphoras, Formas, Census, Species, appellant, sicque implicitè eorum versionem in corpus Christi inficiantur. Utramque rationem pluribus Patrum testimoniis confirmatam vide apud Jonston. citato tract. cap. 3. à pag. 82. ad 100. (3) quòd iisdem terminis utuntur Patres, quando fidelium cum Christo Unionem, per Sacræ Eucharistiæ usum debitum, describunt, probante ibidem eodem Jonstono cap. 5. à pag. 216. ad 225. (4) quòd adhuc terminos eosdem adhibent de aliis rebus variis locuti, quibus Conversionem Substantialem adscripsisse eos, nemini in mentem venerit. Pertinent huc verba Joh. Dunelmensis Histor. Transsubst. Papalis: Quid quod ipsi, inquit, Patres has easdem μεταβολῆς μεταποιήσεως & μεταστοιχείωσεως voces usurpant, cùm de Rebus aliis loquuntur, quæ substantiam suam, minimè vel amittunt vel mutant?
english: Four proofs Fathers meant no mutation beyond that: (1) consecrated breads remain what they were; (2) they are still called signs/figures/symbols/types — so conversion into Christ’s body is implicitly denied (Johnston).
(3) Same terms describe the faithful’s union with Christ by due Eucharist use; (4) same terms on other things no one takes as substantial conversion — Dunelm on that metabole vocabulary.
Stop before §.IV vera causa (idolatry and tyranny of Papism).

source_text: §. IV. Cæterùm à Causa non causa oriundæ Transsubstantiationis ad VERAM ORTUS EJUS CAUSAM deveniendum est, in Idololatria & Tyrannide, Papismi vera anima huicque summum Antichristianismi dedecus conciliaturis, locatam.
english: §.IV: leave the non-cause; the TRUE CAUSE of Transsubstantiation’s Ortus sits in Idolatry and Tyranny.
That pair is Papism’s true soul, and will win it Antichristianism’s highest disgrace.

source_text: Enimvero accidit, ut exactis Seculis Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Apostolicis, verè Episcopalibus atque Patristicis, saltem fine hisce cunctis imminente, Seculo admodum sexto imaginum sacrarum usus cultusque in templis invalescere inciperet, superioribus temporibus non tantùm inauditus prorsus, sed etiam ex omnium Protestantium Confess. publica majorem in modum exosus.
english: When the Apostolic / Episcopal / Patristic centuries were spent (or nearly ended), about the sixth century sacred-image use and cult began to strengthen in temples.
Earlier ages had never heard of it; Protestant public Confessions hate it still more.

source_text: Hinc facilè inventi sunt qui novæ idolomaniæ sese opponerent in Constantinop. IV. Concilio, vulgò dicto Oecumenico septimo, sub Leone Isauro & Constant. Copronymo, celebrato, decreto Patrum 380. unanimiter facto, imagines nullas, minimè omnium Dei Christique figuras in templis tolerandas esse.
english: Opponents of the new idolomania gathered in Constantinopolitanum IV (popularly ‘Seventh Oecumenical’) under Leo the Isaurian and Constantine Copronymus.
380 Fathers unanimously: tolerate no temple images — least of all figures of God and of Christ.

source_text: Subnexâ ratione disertissimâ, quòd veræ Christianæ Ecclesiæ de nulla alia Christi Figura, quicquam unquam innotuisset, præterquam ea, quæ in S. Eucharistia detur, inque Pane consecrato conspicua sit. Sic enim Conciliorum Epitomator Sagittarius Constantinopolitanorum mentem ac Constitutionem edisserit.
english: Annexed reason, most express: the true Church never knew any other Figure of Christ than the one given in the Sacred Eucharist and seen in the consecrated Bread.
Sagittarius (council epitomator) reports the Constantinopolitans’ mind and constitution so.

source_text: Quòd dixerint: Quænam est hæc insana opinio pictorum, ut lucri turpis & miseri causa ea quæ efficere nequeunt, studeant conficere, ut & ea quæ ore & corde sunt tantummodo confessa, impiis manibus figurare intendant? Damnati autem à cordatis viris in eo quòd incomprehensibilem & incircumscriptibilem Divinam Christi naturam ipsi depingere studuerunt, ad aliam aliquam pravâ inventione apologiam confugiunt, quòd solius carnis, quam vidimus & palpavimus & cum qua versati sumus, illius, inquam, imaginem exhibeant: quod sane impium est & Nestoriana Diabolica inventio.
english: Sagittarius’s quote: what insane painters’ opinion — for base gain they try to figure with impious hands what mouth and heart alone confess?
Condemned for painting Christ’s incomprehensible, uncircumscribable Divine nature, they invent a flesh-only image apology — impious, and a Nestorian diabolic invention.

source_text: Et paucis intersertis: Exultent & lætentur & libertate linguæ fruantur, quicunque veram Christi imaginem sincerissimâ mente facientes desiderant & venerantur & ad salutem animæ corporisque adferunt, quam ipse Dominus noster Deus summus sacerdos, ex nobis integrè massam assumens, circa passionis tempus, in typum & recordationem efficacissimam, suis sacerdotibus & mystis tradidit: nam cum se sponte morti objiceret, gloriosa inquam illi & vivificanti, sumens panem benedixit, postquam gratias egisset & fregit tradensque discipulis dixit: accipite, manducate: Hoc est corpus meum. Ecce igitur vivificantis corporis illius imaginem quæ honorificè & gloriosè exhibita est. Quia quemadmodum id quòd è nobis assumsit, materia sola est substantia humana, juxta omnia non perfectè expressa, quæ per se existit persona, ne adjectio in Divinitate accidat; ita & imaginem totam electam, videlicet panis substantiam, mandavit apponi, ne scil. humanâ effigie figurata induceretur idololatria. Similiter etiam panem Eucharistæ veluti imaginem veram naturalis carnis per Sancti Spiritus aggressionem sanctificatam, divinum corpus esse voluit, illique sic placuit &c. &c. Lege ipsum Sagittarium p. m. 354. 355. & seq.
english: The true image of Christ they honor is what the High Priest Himself handed at the passion as type and efficacious remembrance: blessed, broken bread — ‘This is My body’.

As the assumed humanity is material substance (lest Divinity get an addition), so He commanded bread’s substance as the whole chosen image — lest a human effigy breed idolatry; Eucharist bread, Spirit-sanctified true image of natural flesh, He willed a divine body (Sagittarius pp. 354–355).
Stop before §.V (Nicaea II overturn).

source_text: §. V. At verò, vix ac ne vix quidem salutare hoc verboque Dei exactè congruum Judicium Patrum Constantinopolitanorum, cum subnixa ratione suâ haud indecedente, exauditum fuerat, cum imaginum Patroni graviter illi irascerentur ac inviderent, donec, elapsis præter propter annis 30. ira eorum ac indignatio ita cresceret, ut alio in Concilio, Nicææ habito, & ab hac Civitate Nicænum secundum dicto, ab idololatris Pontificiis verò, haud secus ac Constantinopolitanum ab Orthodoxis, Oecumenicum septimum nuncupato, Patribus Constantinopolitanis Decreto adversô contradictum fuerit.
english: §.V: the Constantinopolitans’ salutary, Word-congruent judgment was barely heard before image-patrons grew angry.

After ~30 years their indignation forced Nicaea II — called Second Nicene from the city, but by pontiffs ‘Seventh Oecumenical’ (as the Orthodox had styled Constantinopolitanum) — and an adverse decree contradicted those Fathers.

source_text: Sequenti modô: Imaginum usum cultumque in templis haud aspernandum esse, in specie Christi imagines crucifixi pro nobis, memoriam ejus resuscitare.
english: Nicaea II: temple image use and cult are not to be despised.
In particular, images of Christ crucified for us revive His memory.

source_text: Rationem verò in contrarium, ab Eucharistiæ imagine & figura petitam, usque adeo falsam esse, ut censendum omnino sit, panem consecratum in S. Coena neutiquam Figuram corporis Christi, sed ipsum potius corpus Christi existere.
english: The counter-reason from the Eucharist as image/figure was judged so false that consecrated supper-bread must be held not a Figure of Christ’s body but the body itself.

source_text: Hoc tamen ipsum, cum propriè accipi non posset, panis substantia, à substantia corporis Christi, totâ specie diversa remanente, nec uno disparatorum integro residuôque, alterius naturam essentiamque specificam participaturo, Conversionem panis in corpus Christi implicitè insinuabat, i. e. Transsubstantiationis pullum, ovi cortice, ceu involucro suo, obtectum, fovebat, mox fractô cortice lucem adspecturum postque octiduum quasi circumcidendum etiam, nomineque proprio insigniendum.
english: Taken properly that cannot stand: bread’s substance remains wholly diverse in species from Christ’s body, and neither disparate shares the other’s specific essence.
So it implicitly fostered Conversion — Transsubstantiation’s chick under the egg-shell, soon to break into light and after an octave be named.

source_text: Ab eo tempore, puta à tempore habiti Concilii Niceni secundi, non certe citius (sunt verba Bellarmini) GRÆCI PATRES SÆPE, (non tamen semper) MONUERUNT, (non verò expressè inculcarunt) EUCHARISTIAM NON ESSE FIGURAM, SED CORPUS CHRISTI, Tom. 3. de Eucharist. p. m. 579. Ingolstad. edit. Modum interim, quô Eucharistia corpus Christi esset, per 200. circiter annos, in totum adhuc ignorabant inque medio relinquebant.
english: Bellarmine: from Nicaea II (not sooner) Greek Fathers often — not always — warned the Eucharist is not a figure but Christ’s body (Tom. 3 de Eucharist. p. 579 Ingolstadt); they did not expressly inculcate it.
