For ~200 years they still left the mode wholly unknown, in the middle.

source_text: Usque dum Seculo demum IX. exurgeret præced. annot. memoratus Paschasius Rhadebertus, Bertramum, panem Eucharisticum cum Veteribus, etiam Figuram corporis Christi contendentem, oppugnaturus, assertis autem hujusmodi, decertans, quæ Conversionem panis in corpus Christi, disertè profitebantur: e.g. cùm diceret: Sub specie panis visibilis, nihil aliud quam caro Christi porrigitur. Item: Panis in carnem, & vinum in sanguinem convertitur. lib. de corpore & sang. domini, cap. 10. & 20., allegante Francisco Foris Otrokocsi in Irenico cap. 6. §. 1. p. m. 69. ac sequenti modô in posteriorem Paschasii propositionem commentante: Scil. de crassiusculâ & substantiali conversione, ex mente Paschasii, secus quam aliqui veterum atque etiam ipse Bertramus, de sacramenti & mystica locutione & immutatione, locuti sunt nonnulli.
english: Ninth century: Paschasius Radbertus rises against Bertram (who with the Ancients kept the bread a Figure) and expressly professes conversion — under visible bread-species only Christ’s flesh is offered; bread into flesh, wine into blood (De corp. & sang. Dom. 10 & 20).
Otrokocsi: Paschasius means a crasser substantial conversion, unlike ancients/Bertram’s sacramental-mystic speech.

source_text: Hoc tamen observandum de Paschasio, quòd etsi propriè dici nam Christi carnem contendat perpetuò porrigi à Sacerdote sub specie panis & naturalem sanguinem sub specie vini, neget tamen ab ullo quàm A VERO FIDELI percipi carnem & sanguinem: negat etiam ullo modo dentibus vorari carnem Christi, quæ sanè mira sunt, atque in his multum differt ipse à posteris suæ sententiæ sequacibus. Contenderet manibus tractari carnem Christi, eamque sub specie panis, in os mitti, NON tamen DENTIBUS ATTERI. Scilicet, nondum ille subtilitatem figmenti tunc adhuc recentis tâm operosè edisseruit, sicut Lombardus, aliique post ipsum de Solorum Accidentium fractione & attritione. Hucusque Otrokocsi dicto loco.
english: Paschasius quirks: flesh and blood under the species, yet received only by a true believer; not chewed by teeth — marvels that already distance him from later followers.
Hands may handle and mouth receive under bread-species, but teeth do not wear the flesh; he had not yet spun Lombard’s accident-only fraction/attrition subtlety. Hucusque Otrokocsi.
Stop before §.VI (public Ortus / Berengar XI).

source_text: §. VI. Hoc pacto quidem Ortum suum nacta est Transsubstantiatio, sed obscurum privatumque, publicâ autoritate olim in lucem publicam emittenda, id quod Seculo demum XI. contigit.
english: §.VI: Transsubstantiation has its Ortus — but still obscure and private.
Public authority will push it into public light only in the eleventh century.

source_text: Cùm Berengarius Bertrami Orthodoxam quidem de Eucharistia Opinionem, multis etiam cum complicibus & asseclis secutus, crudè tamen nonnihil, panem consecratum, corporis Christi Figuram propemodum nudam, dicere visus est.
english: Berengar follows Bertram’s orthodox Eucharist opinion (with many allies).
Yet he seems to speak crudely: consecrated bread almost a naked Figure of Christ’s body.

source_text: Ob id, privatorum pariter atque publicorum Doctorum cumprimis Lanfranci Cantuariensis, seu istorum Antesignani, calamis confossus, à Papis Leone IX. anno 1049. & Nicolao II. anno 1059. non solum in judicium vocatus, sed & carceri mancipatus & ad recantationem his conceptam verbis adactus.
english: Private and public doctors — Lanfranc of Canterbury foremost — pierce him with their pens.
Leo IX (1049) and Nicholas II (1059) haul him to judgment, prison, and a forced recantation.

source_text: Quibus omninò tùm Paschasii Rhadeberti de Convers. panis in corpus Christi, publicè confirmatur, quàm absurdissima ipsi Paschasio visa Laceratio corporis Christi dentalis solenniter introducitur.
english: That recantation publicly confirms Paschasius’s conversion of bread into Christ’s body.
It also solemnly introduces the dental laceration of Christ’s body — which Paschasius himself had found most absurd.

source_text: Ego Berengarius consentio S. Romanæ & Apostolicæ sedi & ore ac corde profiteor, de Sacramento Dominicæ mensæ eam fidem me tenere, quam Dominus & venerabilis Papa Nicolaus & hæc sacra Synodus Autoritate Evangelica & Apostolica tenendam tradidit mihique firmavit: panem scil. & vinum quæ in altari ponuntur post consecrationem non solummodo sacramentum, symbolum, sive figuram, sed etiam verum corpus & sanguinem Domini nostri Jesu Christi esse & SENSUALITER non solum sacramento, sed veritate manibus sacerdotum tractari, frangi & FIDELIUM DENTIBUS ATTERI, apud Gratianum de Consecr. dist. 2. c. 42.
english: Ego Berengarius: after consecration the altar bread and wine are not only sacrament/symbol/figure but the true body and blood.
And SENSUALLY — in truth, not only in sacrament — priests’ hands handle and break them, and the faithful’s teeth wear them (Gratian De Consecr. dist. 2 c. 42).

source_text: Quin tandem, cum Berengarius, ob negatam veritatem, sibi malè conscius, ad seipsum rediisset, & suam ipsius revocationem non minus absurdam quam impiam, scripto editô revocasset, eamque per vim sibi extortam esse ab Ecclesia malignantium & vanitatis Concilio, significasset, ab Hildebrando, aliis Hellenbrando, Gregorio VII. appellato, ad Romanum Concilium evocatus virgisque cæsus ad novam recantationem, trium mensium concessis induciis, coactus postliminio est, obtrusâ palinodiæ seu professionis ejusmodi formulâ, quâ panem mysticum substantialiter converti in veram & propriam carnem Christi, sub gravissimo Papæ præcepto, deinceps confitendum erat.
english: Berengar, conscience-struck, published a revocation of that forced palinode as absurd and impious, calling the council a church of the malignant and of vanity.
Hildebrand (Gregory VII) summoned him to Rome, beat him with rods, and after a three-month truce forced a new formula: mystic bread substantially converted into Christ’s true proper flesh.

source_text: Formulam Recantationis affert Thom. Waldensis, Tom. 2. cap. 24. & Abbas Uspergensis in Chronico ad annum 1080; Integram verò de Berengario historiam, ex doctissimi Usserii libro de successione Ecclesiarum cap. 7. à parag. 28. ad fin. capitis, in summam redactam evolve, in elaboratissima Historia Transsubstantiationis jam suprà commendati Johannis Dunelmensis cap. 7. §. 4. & seqq. à p. m. 134. ad pag. 143.
english: Recantation formula: Thomas Walden Tom. 2 ch. 24; Abbot of Ursperg Chronicle at 1080.
Full Berengar history: Ussher De successione Ecclesiarum ch. 7 §§28–end, summarized in John of Durham’s Historia Transsubstantiationis ch. 7 §.4 ff. pp. 134–143.
Stop before §.VII (public monster seated by papal decrees / Lateran name).

source_text: §. VII. Protruso hac ratione in publicam lucem Transsubstantiationis monstro horrendo (cui lumen tamen ademtum adhuc omne erat, quòd post aliquod demum temporis spatium, nomine tandem suo proprio se exornatum vidit) Decretis summorum Paparum, ex ipsa etiam Romana Petri sede pronuntiantium, in thronum firmiter satis collocatum stabilitumque est.
english: §.VII: by this path the horrible Transsubstantiation-monster is thrust into public light — yet still without its proper name.
Papal decrees from Peter’s Roman seat plant it firmly enough on a throne.

source_text: Postquam nempe de vero Conversionis in Eucharistia Modo, à Scholasticis & horum principe Petro Lombardo lib. 4. dist. 11. pag. m. 311. 312. 313. subtiliter æquè atque acriter disputatum esset.
english: That seating follows Scholastic dispute on the true Conversion-mode in the Eucharist.
Lombard (bk. 4 dist. 11 pp. 311–313) leads — subtle and sharp alike.

source_text: Nam tum, Seculo nempe XII. medio, per Petrum Blesensem Epistola 140, juxta Caveum p. 471, juxta alios per Stephanum Æduensem vel Augustodunensem Episcopum, de Sacramento Altaris in Bibliotheca Patrum (cujus tamen Autoris & ætas & scripta valdè incerta sunt) Transsubstantiationis nomen adinventum.
english: Mid-twelfth century: the name Transsubstantiation is invented.
Cave points to Peter of Blois Ep. 140; others to Stephen of Autun On the Sacrament of the Altar (Bibliotheca Patrum — author and date very uncertain).

source_text: Et Seculo seq. XIII. anno 1215. ab Innocentio III. Papa, in Lateranensi Concilio suo canonizatum est.
english: Next century, 1215: Pope Innocent III canonizes that name in his Lateran Council.
So the invented term Transsubstantiatio becomes a canon of the faith under Lateran IV.

source_text: Auctor tantæ Canonizationis se sermonibus suis, ceu sorex voce, prodit, hunc in modum suos allocutus: Mihi, inquit, dicitur in Propheta: Constitui te super gentes & regna &c. &c. Has Innocentii allocutiones omnes cum laudatissimus Dunelmensis pag. 149. recensuisset, subjicit pag. 150: Hæc ille Christi jam factus, non Vicarius modo, sed etiam Rivalis, quæ nunc commemoro, ut videamus qualis fuerit rerum conditio & Latinæ Ecclesiæ facies, quando Transsubstantiatio pro fidei articulo ab Innocentio Papa proposita est & obtrusa.
english: Innocent betrays the author of the canonization in his own sermons — ‘To me it is said in the Prophet: I have set you over nations and kingdoms…’ (as a shrew by its voice).
Dunelm (pp. 149–150): commemorate this already Rival of Christ, not mere Vicar, to see the Latin Church’s face when Transsubstantiation was thrust as an article of faith.

source_text: Canon Canonizationis in Extravag. de Fide & summ. Trinit. Firmiter credimus &c. his verbis legitur: Una verò est fidelium universalis Ecclesia, extra quam nullus omnino salvatur. In qua idem ipse sacerdos & sacrificium Jesus Christus; hujus corpus & sanguis in Sacramento Altaris sub speciebus panis & vini veraciter continentur: TRANSSUBSTANTIATIS pane in corpus & vino in sanguinem, potestate divina, ut ad perficiendum mysterium unitatis accipiamus ipsi de suo, quod ipse accepit de nostro. Et hoc utique Sacramentum nemo potest conficere, nisi Sacerdos fuerit ritè ordinatus secundum claves Ecclesiæ, quas ipse concessit Apostolis & eorum successoribus Jesus Christus. Vide etiam Sagittar. retrò citatum, p. 495. in fin.
english: Firmiter (Extravag. De Fide & summa Trinitate): one universal Church; Christ’s body and blood truly under bread and wine species.
Key clause: bread TRANSUBSTANTIATED into body and wine into blood by divine power — only a duly ordained priest may confect (Sagittarius p. 495).
Stop before §.VIII (still on the Scholastic anvil after canonization).

source_text: §. VIII. Neque tamen adhuc dum canonizata sic Transsubstantiatio, extra omne concussionis & eversionis periculum posita fuit, quin licentiosæ Scholasticarum Disceptationum incudi subjiceretur ab ipsis quoque Scholasticorum Doctorum Antesignanis, genuinum Conversionis modum in omnem partem & quaqua versum disquirendo versantibus.
english: §.VIII: even after canonization, Transsubstantiation is not past concussion or overthrow.
Scholastic standard-bearers still hammer the genuine Conversion-mode on a licentious disputation-anvil — every part, every which way.

source_text: À Johanne Parisiensi, semet illis associante & à pag. 30. & 50. ad 77. Copiosiori numero adductis, opinionibus.
english: John of Paris joins those Antesignani.
From his pages 30 and 50–77 a more copious heap of opinions is adduced.

source_text: Verò eorum ad duodenarium redactis numerum per Werenfelsium nostratetem, Concione de Sacra Coena Germ. p. 30.
english: Our Werenfels trims that heap to a dozen.
Source: his German Concio on the Sacred Supper, p. 30.

source_text: Quinimo ex Reformatoribus Pontificiæ Idolomaniæ, tàm XIV. quàm XV. Seculo exsurrexerunt, qui partim Ruperti Tuitiensis & Ascelini, de Consubstantiatione, vel Crassiori, vel Subtiliori, partim Veterum pristinæque Ecclesiæ de Supernaturali & Spirituali Corporis Christi in S. Coena præsentia, reducem fecerunt, inque hodiernum usque diem servant, haud morati fulmen brutum expelvi Tridentina.
english: Fourteenth- and fifteenth-century reformers of pontifical idolomania also rose.

Some restore Rupert of Deutz and Ascelinus on Consubstantiation (crasser or subtler); others restore the pristine Church’s supernatural and spiritual presence of Christ’s body in the Supper — and keep it to this day, undeterred by Trent’s brute thunderbolt.

source_text: Quô Transsubstantiationi ita cautum legitur Sessione XIII. cap. 4. Can. 2. p. m. 130. initio: Quoniam Christus Redemptor noster, corpus suum, id quod sub specie panis offerebat, verè esse dixit; ideo persuasum semper in Ecclesia Dei fuit, idque nunc hæc sancta synodus declarat, per consecrationem panis & vini Conversionem fieri totius substantiæ panis in substantiam corporis Domini nostri & totius substantiæ vini in substantiam sanguinis ejus, quæ Conversio convenienter & propriè à sancta Catholica (Romana) Ecclesia TRANSSUBSTANTIATIO est appellata.
english: Trent Sess. XIII cap. 4 Can. 2 (p. 130): because Christ said what He offered under bread-species was truly His body, consecration converts the whole substance of bread into His body and of wine into His blood.
That conversion the holy Catholic (Roman) Church conveniently and properly calls TRANSUBSTANTIATION.

source_text: Proinde, si quis dixerit in SSmo. Eucharistiæ Sacramento remanere substantiam panis & vini unà cum corpore & sanguine Domini nostri Jesu Christi, negaveritque mirabilem illam & singularem Conversionem totius substantiæ panis in corpus, & totius substantiæ vini in sanguinem, manentibus duntaxat speciebus panis & vini, quam quidem Conversionem Catholica (Romana) Ecclesia aptissimè Transsubstantiationem appellat, Anathema sit. Nec morati Papæ definitionem, Conciliiq; injustam Confirmationem, ut juxta hanc Transsubstantiationis, non aliam formam, professio & juramentum fidei fiat, utque unus hic è novis Symboli Romani articulis sub tenore & pœna frequenti hujusmodi exaudiatur: Ego N. firma fide credo & profiteor omnia & singula, quæ continentur in symbolo fidei, quo S. Romana Ecclesia utitur; … profiteor pariter in Missa atque in Eucharistiæ Sacramento esse verè realiter & substantialiter corpus & sanguinem unà cum anima & divinitate Domini nostri Jesu Christi, fierique conversionem totius substantiæ panis in corpus & totius substantiæ vini in sanguinem Christi, quam Conversionem Catholica (Romana) Ecclesia Transsubstantiationem appellat: vide Bullam Pii IV. Confirm. Concil. Trident. super forma juramenti professionis fidei unà cum eodem Concilio editam.
english: Anathema if anyone says bread and wine substance remain with body and blood, or denies that singular conversion with species alone remaining.

Nor do they delay the Pope’s definition and the Council’s unjust confirmation: profession and oath must follow this Transsubstantiation form — Ego N. … truly, really, substantially body and blood; conversion of whole substances — Pius IV’s bull on the Trent faith-oath.

source_text: Nec denique morati articulum insuper hunc, Symboli Romani XIIItium tali Epiphonemate & interminatione Papæ claudi: Nulli ergo omnium hominum liceat hanc paginam nostræ voluntatis & mandati infringere vel ei ausu temerario contraire. Si quis autem hoc attentare præsumpserit, indignationem omnipotentis Dei ac beatorum Petri & Pauli Apostolorum ejus, se noverit incursurum. Datum Romæ ap. S. Petrum, Anno Incarnationis Domini 1564. Idibus Novembris.
english: That thirteenth Roman-Symbol article closes with Pius IV’s threat: none may infringe this page; presumers incur God’s and Peter and Paul’s indignation.
Dated Rome at St. Peter’s, 13 November 1564 (Ides).
Stop before §.IX (Form from Lombard / Aquinas / Hoc est corpus meum).

source_text: §. IX. Ita habet Historia Transsubstantiationis, cujus Formam ex Magistro Sententiarum Lib. IV. Dist. VIII. c. p. m. 307. hujusque Commentatore præcipuo Thoma Aquinate, Summ. Theol. part. 3. Quæst. 78. Artic. 1. p. m. 292. reponunt.
english: §.IX: so the History stands; they lodge its Form in Lombard Sent. IV Dist. VIII (p. 307).
Chief commentator: Aquinas ST 3 q.78 a.1 (p. 292).

source_text: In Enunciatione verborum Christi: Hoc est Corpus meum, Hic est sanguis meus, vel, Hic est calix sanguinis mei, utpote quorum verborum Enuntiatione, à Sacerdote facta, Sacramentum Transsubstantiationis conficiatur.
english: Form = enunciation of Christ’s words: Hoc est Corpus meum; Hic est sanguis meus; or Hic est calix sanguinis mei.
By the priest’s speaking those words, they say, the Sacrament of Transsubstantiation is confected.

source_text: Contendentibus tamen nonnullis pro interferenda verbis hisce conjunctione Causativa, ENIM, quippe Matth. 26. 28. reperta, eoque nullibi non in dictis verbis utriusque partis Eucharistiæ subaudienda.
english: Some insist on inserting the causative conjunction ENIM into those words.
It stands in Matt. 26:28, so they would have it understood under both Eucharist parts everywhere.

source_text: Ceu ætiologica partim, rationem reddente, quare illud, quòd porrigebatur, edendum bibendumque fuerit, partim promissiva, quòd promissio omni Sacramento propria, in Baptismate disertis his verbis expressa legatur: Quicunque crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvabitur.
english: ENIM is partly aetiological — why what was offered was to be eaten and drunk.
Partly promissive — like Baptism’s own promise: whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved.

source_text: Vid. Picherellum Opusc. Theol. §. 8.; Quin, tantam interferendæ dictæ voculæ conjunctivæ necessitatem opinantibus aliis, ut citra ejus adjectionem Sacramenti Formam incompletam, i. e. Transsubstantiationem haud plenè confectam dicant.
english: Picherellus (Opusc. Theol. §.8) is cited on this.
Others press the little word so hard that without adding ENIM they call the Form incomplete — Transsubstantiation not fully done.

source_text: Id quod paucis abhinc annis Reverendiss. Stillingfleedio, coram Jacobo II. M. Britanniæ Rege, cum Jesuita White, disputanti, ansam dedit monendi, Pontificiorum alios, ab aliis celebratæ scil. cum omissione particulæ Enim, Missæ, adstantes ac venerabile, quod ajunt, adorantes, non posse, vel ex propria hypothesi, ab idololatria, saltem materiali, propriè interim dicta & Israëliticæ in deserto per omnia simili, immunes manere, cùm Latriæ Cultu prosequerentur id, quod, vitio omissæ voculæ enim, nondum in verum corpus Christi transiisset.
english: Stillingfleet, disputing with Jesuit White before James II, used that to warn: standers at a Mass that omits Enim, adoring the ‘venerable,’ cannot escape even material idolatry on their own hypothesis.
By latria they would worship what — for want of enim — has not yet become Christ’s true body (Israel-in-the-desert parallel).
Stop before §.X (Transsubstantiation unworthy of Christ’s banquet; eliminate from the Church).

source_text: §. X. Quicquid interim de Pontificiæ Transsubstantiationis Forma, sive quatuor, sive quinque verborum pronuntiationi, temerè satis & citra omnem Scripturæ S. authoritatem, affixa, fiat; Ipsa certè Transsubstantiatio, præsertim in omni suo ambitu concepta acceptaque, Sacro à Christo instituto Epulo prorsus indigna, dignissima verò est, quæ Ecclesiâ Christi totâ eliminetur.
english: §.X: leave the four- or five-word Form fight — rashly pinned on without Scripture’s authority.
Transsubstantiation itself, taken in full scope, is utterly unworthy of Christ’s instituted banquet and most worthy to be wiped from Christ’s whole Church.

source_text: Transformatura alioquin hanc, (maximè omnium Necessitatem sui pluribus Anathematibus stabiliens) in verè Antichristianam, tam Revelationi divinæ de credendis pariter atque faciendis, quam Rationi humanæ, quin Sensibus omnibus, tyrannice insultans eorumque Vim infringere, atque abolere conata.
english: Otherwise it remakes the Church truly Antichristian — especially by staking its own Necessity on many Anathemas.
It tyrannizes divine Revelation (belief and practice), human Reason, and all the Senses, trying to break and abolish their force.

source_text: Enimvero Transsubstantiatio adversatur (1) Scripturæ S. cujus autoritas hoc commentum tùm alibi evertit, tùm eô maximè loco, ubi Sacramenti hujus Institutio traditur, id quod ex Antithesi, duodenaria numerosiori, manifestissimè emergere facit insigne Ecclesiæ Reformatæ lumen B. Hottingerus Eucharistiæ defens. Sect. VIII. à p. m. 79. ad 84.
english: (1) It is adverse to Holy Scripture — overthrown elsewhere and above all where the Sacrament’s Institution is given.
Hottinger (Eucharist Defense VIII, pp. 79–84) shows that from an antithesis denser than a dozen.

source_text: Reverendiss. Guil. Forbesius præter multos ex Doctissimis Protestantibus, qui dogma Transsubstantiationis Scripturis adversari luculentissimè demonstrarunt, obsecrat quoque lectorem, adire, ex pontificiis ipsis, eruditam Picherelli Expositionem verborum Institutionis Coenæ Domini & ejusdem Dissertat. de Missa legere diligentissimeque considerare, necnon Archi-Ep. Spalatinum l. 5. de Republ. Eccles. cap. 6., fusissime hoc dogma impugnantem & refellentem Edit. Fabrician. noviss. p. 600. in media.
english: Forbes, with many learned Protestants, has shown the dogma adverse to Scripture.
He also begs readers to weigh Pontificians against themselves: Picherellus on the Institution-words and the Mass, and Spalatinus De Republ. Eccles. 5.6 (Fabricius p. 600) refuting it at length.

source_text: (2.) Analogiæ fidei Divinæ, quà multos symboli Apostolici Articulos, plurimasque de Corporis Christi natura, nostris corporibus per omnia substantialia simili, Scripturæ assertiones. Contradictio hæc, Analogiæ Fidei intentata, usque adeò non tollitur per conficta hoc locô miracula, ut augeatur magis, quippe fidei quoque Analogiam, de Miraculorum natura ac scopo, infestans atque lacertans.
english: (2) It clashes with the divine Analogy of faith — Creed articles and Scripture on Christ’s body as substantially like ours.
Forged miracles here do not heal that contradiction; they worsen it, tearing also the analogy of faith about what miracles are for.

source_text: Cum enim miracula rarò admodum, non temerè nec alio fine, à Deo patrari credenda Christianis sint, quam ut per ea, ceu omnem creatam finitamque potentiam supergressa opera, sensibus humanis clarissimè exposita, de veritate ejus, quod creditu difficile, planè convincantur; Hic quidem, seu in Missa papistica, è contrario quotidie innumeris vicibus, in innumeris locis, eadem repeti atque recurrere miracula, contra luculentissima sensuum humanorum de contrario plenissimè convictorum testimonia, credenda imperantur. Confer. Tillots. Volum. 3. Concionum p. m. 364. & 365. Ut hoc nomine perquam ingeniose B. Joh. Melchioris, non ita pridem Doctor Theologus Herbornensis, Transsubstantiationem, non nisi per Enthusiasmum, credibilem demonstraverit, Operum Theol. part. 2. à p. m. 467. ad 840.
english: Miracles should be rare, not rash, to convince the senses of what is hard to believe; the papistic Mass instead commands the same ‘miracle’ daily in countless places against the senses’ clearest contrary witness (Tillotson Sermons 3, pp. 364–365).
Melchior of Herborn ingeniously showed Transsubstantiation credible only by Enthusiasm (Opera Theol. 2, pp. 467–840).
Stop before (3) Praxis Christiana (first table / latria; cup withheld).

source_text: (3.) Praxi Christiana, quà priorem Legis Divinæ Tabulam, (a) Naturali de toto Triuno Deo religiosâ veneratione colendo: quandoquidem in Missa illud ipsum, quod sensus omnes testantur panem ac vinum esse (speciebus seu accidentibus horum, non tantùm substantias suas oculis exponentibus, sed, ceu particulas, eorum constitutionem ingredientibus) summus Deus & creditur, & prædicatur esse, & illo ipso cultu, qui summo Deo proprius est, quique à pontificiis ipsis, per λατρείας nomen ab omni alio inferiori cultu discriminatur, Communicaturis, quin Missæ Celebrationi adstantibus quibusvis, adorandum præbetur atque edicitur.
english: (3)(a) Christian praxis vs the first table: religious worship of the Triune God.

In the Mass what every sense calls bread and wine (accidents showing and composing the thing) is believed and preached as the highest God, and commanded to communicants and bystanders under latria — the cult Pontificians themselves wall off from every lesser cult.

source_text: Hôcque ipso summa Idololatriæ species incurritur, ne Pontificiis quidem ipsis, sub hypothesi haud facta Transsubstantiationis, negata unquam, sed nec neganda citra hanc hypothesin, tùm quod hypotheseos suæ nullo vel Revelationis vel Rationis argumento, certiores fieri possint, multis è contrario utriusque argumentis, saltem dubii de ista reddantur, si non omnino ab eadem abducantur; tùm, quod Idololatriæ natura ac admissio, neutiquam ab hypothesi opinioneque humana, sive vera ista sit, sive falsa, sed verò à determinatione seu definitione Dei, dependeat, quâ toties idololatriam propriè sic dictam committi novimus, quoties id, quod summe Deus non est, sive ex errore, sive citra errorem, vel æstimatur, vel salutatur talis, nedum religioso summôque cultu afficitur.
english: That is the highest species of idolatry — which even Pontificians never deny if Transsubstantiation is not supposed, and must not deny without that hypothesis.

They cannot make their hypothesis certain by Revelation or Reason; and idolatry turns on God’s definition, not on whether a human opinion is true or false — whenever what is not the highest God is estimated, saluted, or given highest cult as if it were.

source_text: (b) Praxi Institutæ, quatenus hæc à Christo immediatè originem trahit, quâque non minùs ad Calicis vinique, quam panis usum, singulos Communicantes obstringit, per Missam interim & Transsubstantiationis rationem, Laicis cunctis eripiendum. Hoc pacto Transsubstantiatio etiam in posteriorem Divinæ Legis Tabulam impingit, Proximo id subducens, quod illi tribuendum expresso Christus mandato voluit per τὸ: Hoc facite, S. Coenam administraturis id omne designandum injungens, quod ipse administrans designaverat.
english: (3)(b) Instituted praxis from Christ binds every communicant to the cup and wine no less than to the bread.
Mass and Transsubstantiation’s rationale snatch that cup from all the laity — so it also hits the second table, withdrawing from the neighbor what Christ ordered by ‘Do this.’

source_text: (4.) Tàm Fidei, quam huic superstructæ praxi, primorum, per multa secula Christianorum: Quodsi enim primævi Christiani Transsubstantiationem professi fuissent, nemine eorum tùm temporis, veri sensus Christi verborum: Hoc est corpus meum, hic est sanguis meus, ignaro existente, quî fieri unquam potuisset, quò minùs ab his, præfervidis alioquin Mysteriarum Religionis suæ propugnatoribus, fama dogmatis, ad eos, quos inter vivebant, Judæos pariter atque Ethnicos, quam velocissimè transiisset citra omnem moram, non contradictiones horum ferias duntaxat, sed & exsibilationes quascunque expertura?
english: (4) Faith and praxis of the first centuries: if the earliest Christians had professed Transsubstantiation, none then mistook ‘This is my body / blood.’
That dogma’s rumor would have flown at once to neighboring Jews and Gentiles and met not only contradiction but every hiss — from such fervent mystery-defenders it could not have stayed quiet.

source_text: Id quod tamen, vel semel, vel ab ullo hostium Christianæ sectæ infestissimorum, factitatum esse, nullibi, nec in ipsorum (Tryphonis puta, Celsi, Juliani, Porphyrii, omnem profectò ansam Dogmata Christiana calumniosissimè traducendi, quàm studiosè captantium) nec in cujuspiam ex diligentissimis Christianarum veritatum Assertoribus (quales Justinus Martyr, Tertullianus, Origenes, Arnobius & Minutius Felix memorantur) Scriptis Apologeticis expositum legimus.
english: Yet we nowhere read that even once from the fiercest enemies — Trypho, Celsus, Julian, Porphyry — who hunted every handle to calumniate Christian dogmas.
Nor from the careful apologists Justin, Tertullian, Origen, Arnobius, Minucius Felix.

source_text: Thyesteas Coenas, quarum quandoque Christiani arguebantur, ad Gnosticos solos (non nisi per apertissimam malitiam Christianis annumeratos) pertinuisse, à veris autem Christianis, citra omnem Eucharistiæ S. mentionem injectam, nedum Mysterii hujus expositionem defensionemque susceptam vel minimam, pro mera calumnia habitas explosasque fuisse, notius est, quàm ut hoc loco prolixius dici debeat. Quin Praxios Rituumque, Transsubstantiationi indissolubiliter annexorum (quales sunt Sacramenti Adoratio, Elevatio, Circumgestatio) recentioribus seculis adinventæ, apud veteres Christianos constans atque perpetuus defectus, de Transsubstantiatione ab his penitus ignorata prolixè satis testari censendus est.
english: Thyestean banquet charges stuck to Gnostics alone (maliciously counted as Christians); true Christians never even mentioned the Eucharist there, much less explained or defended this mystery — mere calumny, exploded.
And the ancients’ constant lack of later Transsubstantiation-rites (Adoration, Elevation, Circumgestation) amply shows they utterly ignored Transsubstantiation.
Stop before (5) Natura Sacramentorum.

source_text: (5.) Natura Sacramentorum, nomine ad minimum triplici.
english: (5) Transsubstantiation assaults the Nature of the Sacraments under at least three heads.
Strimesius marks the assault as at minimum triple — three named wounds to what a sacrament is.

source_text: (1.) Quòd Signum Materiale, alteram sacramenti partem essentialem, ex Eucharistia submovet, panem nempe & vinum, solis remanentibus harum substantiarum accidentibus, ut substantialitate omni, ex sententia Pontificiorum, ita & Materialitate, casssis. (2) Quòd Signatum Sacramenti Eucharistici (Corpus nempe & Sanguinem Christi) in ipsum Signati Sacramentum Corporis & Sanguinis Christi, commutat.
english: (1) It removes the material Sign — bread and wine — leaving only accidents, void of substantiality and (on their view) of materiality too.
(2) It turns the Signatum (Christ’s body and blood) into the sacrament of that Signatum itself — sign and thing collapse.

source_text: (3) Quòd propositionem sacramentalem ipsâ hujus pronuntiatione, sacramento Eucharistiæ eliminat, pane non amplius superstite, dum de pane sacerdos propositionem hanc finit: Hoc, seu hic panis est Corpus meum.
english: (3) By the priest’s pronunciation it kills the sacramental proposition.
Bread no longer survives while he finishes of bread: ‘This, or this bread, is My Body.’

source_text: (6.) Rationi Emaculatiori, i. e. Philosophiæ, tùm Theoreticæ, tum Practicæ. Priori quidem, dum primarum ac præcipuarum rerum, Substantiæ puta & Accidentis, Spiritus & Corporis, Penetrabilitatis & Impenetrabilitatis, Extensionis & Localitatis essentiales Ideas ac Definitiones invertit ac concutit, Substantiam Finitam definitamque accidentibus suis essentialibus exuendo, Accidentia ab Inhæsione, in substantia, actuali absolvendo, corpus & sanguinem Christi in spiritum commutando, per negatam iisdem tum extensionem, tùm impenetrationem tùm localitatem, humanis corporibus essentialiter debitas, indeque nec per miracula, ab essentiarum ad unum omnium finitarum Autore, etsi pro Lubitu suô Annihilatore quoque potentissimo, contradictoria interim nulla, idque per & propter omnipotentiam suam, admissuro, destituendas.
english: (6) Cleaner Reason / Philosophy — theoretical first.

It overturns essential ideas of substance and accident, spirit and body, penetrability, extension, locality: strips finite substance of essential accidents, frees accidents from inherence, spirits Christ’s body by denying extension, impenetrability, and place — which even omnipotence will not admit as contradictories via miracle.

source_text: Prætereà Species & Accidentia Signorum, panis & vini, admittendo tales, quæ tamen signorum horum substantias necessariò ingrediuntur, e.g. Panis quantitatem ab Extensione ejus definita, ipsôque, adeo pane, realiter haud diversam; Vini Motum in Calice, Accidentibus nudis i. e. omni substantialitate orbis, minimè competentem, visum verò in subtilioribus vini, calice comprehensi, particulis, exhalaturis cum tempore, vinique massam substantialem, evolutione suâ imminuturis. Practica verò Philosophiæ inimica imminet Transsubstantiatio, quando etiam pietatem, in Deum, naturalem, & naturalem humanitatem arietat. PIETATEM IN DEUM, afferendo, Deum oraliter manducari: Ecquemnam tam amentem esse putas, qui id, quô vescitur, Deum esse credat? quærit Cicero de Natura Deorum Lib. 3. Cui respondet Averrois judicium sententiaque de Christianismo: Omnes regiones peragravi, nec Christianâ gente deteriorem ullam reperi: Quia quem Deum adorant, hunc dentibus devorant. vid. Dionys. Carthus. in 4. Dist. 10. Art. 1. Confer B. Hotting. Eucharist. defens. pag. 214. & seqq.
english: It also admits bread/wine species that must enter those substances (bread’s quantity not really other than the bread; wine’s motion in the cup unfit for bare accidents, yet seen in exhalable particles that shrink the wine-mass).

Practical philosophy too: it butts natural piety — oral God-eating. Cicero: who is mad enough to think what he eats is God? Averroes: no worse race than Christians, who devour with teeth the God they adore (Hottinger pp. 214ff).

source_text: Dein HUMANITATEM QUOQUE NATURALEM Communemque, statuendo jubendoque Carnem Christi humanam, corporali ore manducandam & sanguinem ejus humanum, ore corporali hauriendum bibendumque, Actiones hoc pacto imperando, à quibus humana Natura, nondum in brutam degenerata, sponte suâ abhorret & ut abhorreret tantò certiùs, olim, in gente Judaica, ab omni animantium sanguine abstinendum esse, disertô à DEO præcepto cautum fuisse legitur, Lev. 7. vers. 27. & cap. 17. 14.
english: It also butts natural common humanity: commanding Christ’s human flesh chewed and His blood drunk with the corporal mouth — acts unfallen human nature spontaneously abhors.
God once expressly barred the Jewish people from all animal blood (Lev. 7:27; 17:14) so that abhorrence would be the surer.
Stop before §.XI (7) Sense.

source_text: §. XI. (7.) Sensui emunitiori nec uni tantum, sed pluribus: Enimvero panem & vinum in S. Eucharistia non annihilari, nec in horum locum, corpus & sanguinem Christi, corporaliter substitui, tàm visus & tactus, quàm gustus & olfactus, distinctè evincunt; Quorum distinctum testimonium præsertim ab omnibus unà perhibitum, in dubium vocandum haud esse.
english: §.XI (7): cleaner Sense — not one only but several.

Sight, touch, taste, and smell distinctly prove bread and wine are not annihilated in the Eucharist, nor Christ’s body and blood corporally put in their place; their joint distinct testimony is not to be doubted.

source_text: Ipsa revelata Scriptura S. non unô modô edicit (1) Semet ipsam sensibus nostris, i. e. Lectioni & Auditioni commendando, id quod temere faceret, si sensibus fides habenda non sit. (2) Imperium in Sensus Rationi, præsertim illuminatæ, deferendo certisque limitibus circumscrivendo, in quod frustra niteretur, si Sensuum actus fallibiles sint.
english: Revealed Scripture itself backs that: (1) it trusts itself to our senses in reading and hearing — rash if senses deserve no faith.
(2) it gives Reason empire over the senses within limits — pointless if sense-acts are fallible.

source_text: (3) Ad Sensuum testimonium, in Veritate à se confirmanda stabiliendaque, provocando, tùm per Christum ipsum: Vide manus meas & pedes meos, nam ego ipse sum, Contrectate me & videte, nam Spiritus Carnem & OSSA non habet, sicut me conspicitis habere Luc. 24. 39. tùm per dilectissimum Christi Apostolum: Quod erat à principio &c. 1. Joh. 1, 1. Quod si verò vel uni Sensui benè constituto, nec requisito ullo ad sentiendum destituto, fides meritò habenda, quantò magis pluribus: Cùm, quò plures species, inter se conspirantes, variis modis excitantur, eò perceptio, quæ est earum contemplatio, certior sit. Unde omnium hominum usu frequentatum, ut pluribus Sensibus magis credant, quàm uni atque alteri.
english: (3) Christ and John appeal to sense to confirm truth: Luke 24:39 (handle me; a spirit has not flesh and bones); 1 John 1:1 (that which was from the beginning).
If one well-constituted sense deserves faith, how much more several conspiring species — all men trust many senses more than one.

source_text: Denique (8.) Sui ipsius Nomenclaturæ, quâ Transsubstantiatio dici cupit i. e. Conversio Substantiæ in substantiam, qualis tamen Conversio neutiquam obtinet, suppositô, ex pane & vino per eandem nihil remanere, ut rectius eô nomine Annihilatio substantiæ unius, & alterius substantiæ Creatio, quam Transsubstantiatio, dici mereatur.
english: (8) By its own name: it wants ‘Transsubstantiation’ = conversion of substance into substance.
But if nothing of bread and wine remains, the truer name is annihilation of one substance and creation of another — not Transsubstantiation.

source_text: Scilicet, si istos audiamus, quibus solis datum est hæc βάθη callere (sunt verba Matthæi Wreni in Increpatione Bar Jesu, seu Refutatione Catechismi Racoviensis p. m. 342.) Substantia Panis neutiquam transiit in Substantiam corporis, sed exterrit a (ut par est,) ad Divina illa vocabula, Hoc est corpus meum, tam subito, prorsusque evanuit, ut nè durare quidem tantisper ausa fuerit, dum & Accidentia sua convasare, Speciesque misellas secum auferre posset. Quanto minus opinandum est, Substantiam Divini Corporis transiisse in eam, quæ evanuit, Panis Substantiam?
english: Wren (Increpatio Bar Jesu / Racovian Catechism refutation p. 342), on those who alone know these ‘depths’: bread-substance did not pass into body-substance.

Terrified at ‘This is my body,’ it vanished so fast it dared not even pack its accidents and drag the poor species along — still less did divine-body substance pass into that vanished bread-substance.

source_text: Cui igitur Substantia, aut unde suum Trans? Qua heic Transsubstantiatio est? Translocatio quidem ista est; Succedere enim volunt Corpus de Cælo in Locum Substantiæ Panis; Et Transfiguratio est; Submittere enim se aiunt Sanctum Corpus Figuræ, quam profugus Panis in Speciebus suis (satis inclementer post se relictis) gesserat. Sed ecquid est aliud? Rogandi igitur sunt Romani Correctores, ut & Augustodunensem istam ἀκυρολογίαν corrigere jam velint, & (si fatalis necessitas sic ferat, Error Errori Errorem ut semper pariat, atque Prodigium Dogmatis & nominis stribiligine æternum insigniatur,) ut ab altera porrò literula orsi, appellari hanc nunc jubeant, pro Transsubstantiatione, Vicesubstantiationem.
english: So where is the Trans? This is translocation (body from heaven into bread’s place) and transfiguration (holy body under the fugitive bread’s leftover figure) — not Transsubstantiation.
Ask the Roman correctors to fix Autun’s misnomer: if error must breed error, start from another letter and call it Vicesubstantiation.
Stop before Annotatio IV (true Eucharistic sentence through the ages).

source_text: ANNOTATIO IV. De Vera circa Eucharistiam S. Sententia, per omnia æræ Christianæ secula ad hunc usque diem, edocta. ad pag. 37.
english: ANNOTATIO IV opens: On the True Sentence concerning the Sacred Eucharist.
It is the sentence taught through every age of the Christian era down to this day (Autor p. 37).

source_text: §. I. Tandem Historiæ de vera Sententia Eucharistica per compendium condendæ, accingimur, cujus ut primordium, ita fundamentum in ipsis Institutionis S. Cœnæ verbis & collocandum arbitramur, & à Christo ipso collocatum advertimus, dicente, Hoc est corpus meum, Hic est sanguis meus.
english: §.I: we now briefly write the history of that true Eucharistic sentence.
Its beginning and foundation sit in the Institution words themselves — This is my body, This is my blood — placed there by Christ.

source_text: Hæc enim verba Christi de pane ab eo accepto, benedicto, fracto, sicque discipulis suis dando, de calice item benedicto similiter, discipulisque porrigendo, enunciata, etsi ob expositas Annotatione Ima rationes, quatenus propositionem plenam ac integram absolvunt, Tropum includant eòque propositiones figuratæ dicendæ sint, non inficiatis omnino vel ipsis Lutheranis, quin paucioribus quidem explicitè, implicitè omnibus idem ipsum admittere necesse habentibus, tamen talem tropum minimè omnium continere eòque sensu figuratas constituere propositiones à quoquam Orthodoxorum, Lutheranorum pariter ac Reformatorum perhibebuntur, quæ corpus & sanguinem Christi Cœnâ S. eliminant.
english: Those words (bread taken, blessed, broken, given; cup blessed and offered) do include a trope as full propositions — Annotatio I’s reasons; even Lutherans must admit it, a few explicitly, all implicitly.
But no Orthodox — Lutheran or Reformed — will say the trope is the kind that eliminates Christ’s body and blood from the Sacred Supper.

source_text: At verò Corpus & Sanguinem Christi, verè ac realiter, propriè & citra omnem figuram, in S. Eucharistia, & præsentia esse, & ab omnibus, juxta Institutionem Christi S. Cœnâ utentibus, participari, veræ, genuinæ & orthodoxæ de S. Cœna sententiæ animam expedit.
english: The soul of the true, genuine, orthodox Supper sentence is this:
Christ’s Body and Blood are truly and really present in the Eucharist — properly, not by bare figure — and are participated in by all who use the Supper per Christ’s Institution.

source_text: Unde rectissimè Reverendissimus Cosinus Historiam suam Transsubstantiationis papalis, his verbis auspicatur: Quæ à Christo Domino, in solenni hujus augustissimi sacramenti Institutione, ad perpetuam sui memoriationem, prolata sunt verba, nempe, Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur, Hic est sanguis meus qui pro vobis effunditur, omnino infallibilia atque verissima esse, universa per orbem terrarum sancta confitetur Ecclesia. Si quis autem contrarium affirmaverit, aut veracitatem Christi in dubium vocare ausus fuerit, dictisve ejus fidem derogaverit, nec iis assensum suum præbuerit, nisi per figmentum & nudam figuram expositis & detortis, illum in Ecclesiis nostris nec tolerare, nec excusare vel possumus, vel debemus.
english: Cosinus (Most Reverend) rightly opens his History of papal Transsubstantiation with the Institution words: This is my body given for you; This is my blood poured out for you — the whole Church confesses them infallible and most true.
Anyone who twists them into a fiction and bare figure, denying Christ’s truthfulness, we neither can nor ought to tolerate or excuse in our churches.

source_text: Quicquid enim sacrosancta docet Scriptura, id nobis verum ac indubitatum esse oportet. Verum igitur nec minùs indubium esse fatendum est, quod dixit Christus: Caro mea verè est cibus & sanguis meus est potus; quæ juxta B. Paulum per panem & poculum nobis communicantur: eundem enim panem communionem corporis Christi, itidemque poculum, sanguinis ipsius poculum, appellavit.
english: Whatever Holy Scripture teaches must be true and undoubted for us — so also Christ’s My flesh is truly food and my blood drink, communicated through bread and cup per Paul.
Paul called the bread the communion of Christ’s body and the cup the cup of His blood.
Stop before §.II (John 6 and Paul as the mode-commentaries on Institution).

source_text: §. II. Oportunè admodum Doctiss. Episcopus cùm Sermonis Christi de manducanda carne sua, & bibendo sanguine suo Joh. 6. tum Sermonis Paulini, de panis & poculi Eucharisticorum communione cum corpore & sanguine Christi, mentionem hôc locô injicit.
english: §.II: Cosinus (Most Learned Bishop) aptly brings in two discourses here.
John 6 — eating Christ’s flesh and drinking His blood; and Paul — communion of Eucharistic bread and cup with Christ’s body and blood.

source_text: Quandoquidem etiam Institutionis S. Cœnæ verba corporis & sanguinis Christi tùm præsentiam, tum participationem satis distinctè insinuant, de Modo tamen utriusque speciali decernunt nihil, ut hic totus ex dictis Christi & Pauli sermonibus, ceu unicis quidem sed plenissimis ac luculentissimis Commentariis, petendus ac addiscendus veniat.
english: Institution words clearly enough hint presence and participation of body and blood — but decide nothing about the special Mode of either.
That whole Mode must be sought from Christ’s and Paul’s discourses as the only, fullest, most lucid commentaries.

source_text: Equidem de Joh. 6., id diu satis & acriter disceptatum est, etiam inter ejusdem Sectæ Christianæ Theologos: Num in eo, de Cœna Domini, de præsentia & manducatione carnis & bibitione sanguinis Christi Sacramentalibus agatur? Aliis affirmativam, negativam aliis, tenentibus magnoque tuentibus conatu. At litigium istud facilè ita componitur, ut utraque pars verum dixisse intelligatur.
english: Long sharp fight even within the same Christian camp: does John 6 treat the Lord’s Supper and sacramental eating/drinking of Christ’s flesh and blood?
Some yes, some no — both sides can be true once the dispute is composed.

source_text: Enimverò de Cœna S. deque præsentia & manducatione corporis ac bibitione sanguinis Christi sacramentalibus, agitur alicubi, vel plenè & quà totum horum, vel semiplenè & qua partem aliquam. Priori modo de Cœna deque præsentia & participatione corporis & sanguinis Christi sacramentalibus, ditô loco non agi, in propatulo est, quia non agitur de pane & vino Eucharisticis, nec de horum vel præsentia, vel participatione, quæ interim Sacramenti S. Cœnæ nec non sacramentalis præsentiæ ac participationis partes integrantes, quin essentiales, constituunt; at posteriori modo de iisdem agi, non minus in aprico est, quia agitur de manducatione carnis & bibitione sanguinis Christi, eòque tùm de præcipuo S. Cœnæ & proprio & proximo Objecto, carne & sanguine Christi, tum de præcipua eaque sacramentali, Sacræ Cœnæ celebrationis imperata à Christo actione, scil. manducatione corporis & bibitione sanguinis ejus.
english: Supper-talk can be full (the whole) or semi-full (a part). John 6 is not full: no Eucharistic bread and wine, which are essential integrating parts of the sacrament.
It is semi-full: it does treat eating flesh and drinking blood — the Supper’s chief nearest object and the commanded sacramental action.

source_text: Ceterum hôc posteriori modo cap. Joh. 6. de S. Cœna deque Sacramentali & carnis & sanguinis Christi tùm præsentia, tùm participatione, ita specialtim agitur, ut quis hic modus sacramentalis utriusque, & qualis censendus sit, omnium disertissimè inibi exponatur, quô proinde nomine sermonem Christi, Joh. 6. cap. habitum, antecedaneum verborum Institutionis Christi eumque luculentissimum Commentarium arbitramur esse, i. e. Commentarium non de jam tum instituta, sed de paulò post instituenda S. Cœna, tantam huic facem præferentem, tantumque luminis, concisis Institutionis Christi verbis: Hoc est Corpus meum, & Hic enim sanguis meus, fæneratum, ut Discipulis Christi, per Magistri sui sermonem istum, objectionibus & dubiis suis omnibus plenissimè liberatis, nullum amplius scrupulum ista vel moverint, vel quiverint movere.
english: So read, John 6 specially exposes what the sacramental Mode of presence and participation is — the antecedent, most lucid commentary on the Institution words.
Not on a Supper already instituted then, but on the one soon to be: torch and light for ‘This is my Body’ / ‘This is my blood,’ clearing the disciples’ scruples.

source_text: Est verò hic Modus tàm præsentiæ, quàm participationis carnis & sanguinis Christi, mere Spiritualis, Supernaturalis, Cælestis, corporali, naturali, carnali localique, ceu vel magis, vel minus Capernaitico, oppositus.
english: That Mode of presence and participation is merely Spiritual, Supernatural, Celestial.
It stands against corporal, natural, carnal, local presence — Capernaite in greater or lesser degree.
Stop before §.III (four proofs that John 6 inculcates the spiritual mode).

source_text: §. III. Spiritualem, Supernaturalem, Cælestemque Modum præsentiæ pariter atque participationis corporis & sanguinis Christi, non alium quempiam, certè non Corporalem, Naturalem ac Terrestrem, Joh. 6., à Christo inculcari, quadruplici argumento probatur.
english: §.III: four proofs that in John 6 Christ inculcates the Spiritual, Supernatural, Celestial Mode of presence and participation of His body and blood.
Not any other mode — certainly not the Corporal, Natural, Earthly one.

source_text: (1) Quia ista duntaxat præsentia corporis & sanguinis, totiusque Christi, commendatur, cujus participes reddimur per spiritualem ad Christum accessum, i. e. per veram vivamque in eum fidem. Ita enim Christus vers. 35. Ego sum panis vitæ: qui ad me venit non esuriet, & qui in me credit, his nunquam sitiet. Et rursus versibus 47. 48. 49. 50. 51. Amen Amen dico vobis qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam. Ego sum panis ille vitæ. Patres vestri ederunt Manna in deserto & mortui sunt. Hic est panis ille qui de cælo descendit, ut qui edit ex eo, non moriatur. Ego sum panis ille vivus qui è Cælo descendi: Si quis ederit ex hoc pane, vivet in æternum. Panis autem quem ego dabo, caro mea est, quam ego dabo pro mundi vita; At per Spiritualem ad Christum accessum fidemque veram ac vivam, non tàm Corporalis corporis & sanguinis Christi quàm Spiritualis potiùs, etiam extra S. Cœnam, reddimur participes.
english: (1) The only presence of body, blood, and whole Christ that is recommended is the one we share by spiritual access — true living faith (John 6:35, 47–51).
By that faith we partake spiritually rather than corporally — even outside the Sacred Supper.

source_text: (2) Quia ista duntaxat cùm præsentia, tùm participatio carnis & sanguinis Christi, commendantur, quas certò & infallibiliter spiritualis cum Christo Unio & Communio ipsaque vita æterna & ad hanc à Christo exsuscitatio è mortuis, insequuntur: Nam sic pergit Salvator vers. 53. 54. 55. 56. Amen Amen dico vobis, nisi ederitis carnem Filii hominis & biberitis ejus Sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Qui edit carnem meam & bibit meum sanguinem, habet vitam æternam, & ego suscitabo ipsum ultimo illo die. Caro enim mea verè est cibus & sanguis meus verè est potus, qui edit meam carnem & bibit meum sanguinem, in me manet & ego in eo. At effectus hi Spirituales, Supernaturales & Cælestes, non nisi Spirituali Christi Præsentiæ & Participationi, indivisim ac necessariò adhærent, non Corporali aut Orali, uti in confesso est, & ex indignorum manducatione sacramentali quidem, etiam orali, ex Lutheranorum hypothesi, at spiritualis vacua, liquidò constat.
english: (2) The presence and participation recommended are those which spiritual union with Christ, eternal life, and the last-day raising infallibly follow (John 6:53–56).
Those heavenly effects cling only to spiritual presence and participation — not corporal or oral; even on the Lutheran view the unworthy’s oral eating is spiritually empty.

source_text: (3) Quia ista solummodò præsentia cum participatione corporis & sanguinis Christi commendatur, quæ etiam cum adscensu corporis Christi in cælum, probè consistere, quin ex adscensu corporis Christi in Cœlum, contra discipulos, manducationi carnis ejus & sanguinis, dum coram adhuc adesset, in terris intercedentes ac obluctati, evinci hisce Christi verbis poterat: Quid si igitur spectaveritis Filium Hominis adscendentem eo, ubi erat priùs? vers. 62. At non Corporalis in terris præsentia ex adscensu corporis Christi in Cœlum, sed Spiritualis tantùm, colligi demonstrarique in promptu erat. Proptereà adscensionis suæ meminit, inquit Athanasius: hina somatikēs ennoias autous aphelkysēi — eos, à corporali intellectu abstraheret & ut deinceps carnem suam cœlestem & spiritualem cibum esse discerent, Tom. I. tract. in illud: Qui dixerit verbum contra Spir. S.
english: (3) The recommended presence must also stand with Christ’s bodily ascent into heaven (John 6:62) — so from the ascent one gathers spiritual presence on earth, not corporal.
Athanasius: He named the ascension to pull them off corporal intellect and teach His flesh as heavenly spiritual food. (Greek transliterated in Pass B.)

source_text: (4) Quia Carnalis seu Corporalis corporis aut carnis Christi Participatio nulli omnino usui esse disertè à Christo perhibetur, quando murmurantibus adhuc Discipulis & sibi durum paulò antè visum verbum nec tum quidem absque indignatione transmittentibus, ipse tandem pertinaciori obmurmurationi finem impositurus & pessulum obditurus vers. 63. respondet: Spiritus est qui vivificat, caro non prodest quicquam. Verba quæ ego loquor vobis, spiritus & vita sunt; Hisce verbis, vel binâ ratione expressa, Carnalem Præsentiam ac Participationem Carnis & Sanguinis sui suppressurus, erectis & in apricum positis solis Spiritualibus: primò quidem, dum carnem suam, non equidem per se spectatam, sed carnaliter manducandam (de qua sola hactenus disputatio, se inter & Judæos partim, partim Christianos discipulos suos, intercesserat) nihil prodesse ait, interpretante sic verba Augustino, Serm. secundô de Verbis Domini & suffragante Paschasio: Sine Spiritu S. inquit sicut nec caro Christi prodest quicquam, ita nec hoc Sacramentum Christi prodesse potest lib. 3. de Corp. & Sangv. Christi, i. e. Corpus Christi non prodest quicquam, non per se, sed per accidens & aliud, quod impedit illius Operationem, ut ipsi Lutherani, Lutherô contra Carlstadium præeunte, non possunt non fateri, quia sine fide Christus & Evangelium non tantum nihil prosunt, sed nocent, sunt odor mortis & judicium Dei accelerant. Unde Brentius in Exegesi Johannis: Verum equidem est, ait, carnem Christi comesam, quomodo Capernaitæ intellexerunt, dentibus laceratam, nihil prodesse, prodest autem plurimùm mysterio fidei & dentibus cordis accepta.
english: (4) Carnal or corporal participation of Christ’s flesh is of no use at all (John 6:63): the Spirit quickens; the flesh profits nothing; His words are spirit and life.

Augustine and Paschasius: without the Spirit neither flesh nor sacrament profits; Lutherans admit Christ without faith harms; Brentius: Capernaite tooth-tearing profits nothing — faith’s heart-teeth do.

source_text: Dehinc verò, dum verba, de carne sua & sanguine participandis, à se prolixius edisserta, non propriè & carnaliter, sed mysticè ac spiritualiter, tum intelligenda, tùm in effectum danda, pronunciat: Verba quæ loquor, Spiritus & vita sunt; Quasi dicat, Cur hâc mea loquendi ratione offendimini? Et vos ignoratis, spiritualiter esse intelligenda, non carnaliter, quæ de carnis meæ locutus sum manducatione? Non enim de corporis alimento, adeoque de carne, corporis mei parte, hôc loco sermo erat, sed de nutritione spirituali, eamque sequente conjunctione vestri, ceu membrorum, mecum capite, vers. 63. de Vita vestra per me, quæ temporalis non est, sed æterna vers. 57. ad quam vos suscitaturus sum ultimâ die: ita Spiritus, i. e. sensus spiritualiter sumtus verbaque rectè intellecta vivificant, Caro verò, verbaque carnaliter & crassè accepta, nil prosunt. Cum ergo verba mea Spiritus sint, deq; spiritualibus agam, cùm de vita non temporali sed æterna, nutritioneque mystica, quâ in unum coalescimus corpus, ego loquar, cur crassum & carnalem mihi affingitis sensum?
english: Second half of (4): understand the flesh-and-blood words mystically and spiritually — Spirit and life — not as bodily food of a body-part, but spiritual nutrition joining members to the Head, eternal life and last-day raising.
Spiritually taken sense quickens; carnal coarse hearing profits nothing — why fasten a thick carnal sense on spiritual speech?
Stop before §.IV (antecedent Institution commentary hands off to the Pauline / Apostolic successor).

source_text: §. IV. Ita habet Commentarius verborum Institutionis S. Cœnæ Antecedaneus, Sententiæ de ea veræ tam originem dans, quàm fundamentum struens, ab ipso Christo confectus, quem excipit Succedaneus Apostolicus, speciatim Paulinus 1. Cor. 10. & 11. capp. Horum Capitum prius quàm plurima pro spirituali corporis & sanguinis Christi præsentia & participatione, nullum verò pro corporali suppeditat argumentum.
english: §.IV: Christ’s antecedent Institution commentary (origin and foundation of the true sentence) is succeeded by the Apostolic / Pauline commentary — specially 1 Cor. 10 and 11.
Chapter 10 supplies many arguments for spiritual presence and participation of body and blood — none for the corporal.

source_text: Primum desumtum à Communione & participatione Christi, eòque corporis & sanguinis Christi (quibus sine Christus ne Christus quidem est) Veteris Testamenti Christianis impertita, de quibus Apostolus versu 1. Non vult nos ignorare, omnes eandem escam spiritualem edisse, omnes item eundem potum spiritualem bibisse, puta non inter se tantum omnes, sed & nobiscum; Nam immediatè sequitur: Bibebant enim ex sequenti spirituali Petra; Petra verò erat Christus; Sed de hoc solo & nosmet Christiani N. T., sanguinem ejus spiritualiter bibimus, sicuti & escam spiritualem, Mannam de cœlo descendentem, i. e. Christum ejusque corpus, nec quicquam aliud, itidem cum Patribus V. Test. participamus, Sacramentis Veterum, quoad Signa quidem, à nostris, diversis, quoad Significata verò iisdem existentibus, dicente Augustino Tract. 26. super Johannem, juxta istud Petrinum: Quin verò, per Gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi, credimus nos Salvatum iri, kath' hon tropon kakeinoi. Act. 15, 11.
english: First argument: OT believers already shared Christ’s communion — the same spiritual food and drink (1 Cor. 10:1–4); the Rock was Christ.
We NT Christians drink His blood spiritually and share the same spiritual food — Christ and His body — with the Fathers; signs differ, significata are the same (Augustine; Acts 15:11).

source_text: Exceptioni seu Dubio: Quâ ratione Veteres Christum eô, quô nos, in sacramentis modô, perceperint, cum Filius Dei eô tempore nondum carnem assumsisset, neque sanguis ab eo effusus exstaret, egregiè occurrit Petrus Martyr, Comment. in hunc locum: Quoad DEUM, inquit, (addo etiam quoad homines fideles & spiritualem eorum manducationem) Mors Christi & Sanguinis ejus effusio & carnis assumtio, semper fuerunt præsentia, rata, placita & accepta. Quare in Apocalypsi dicitur Agnus ab origine mundi occisus: nec non ad Hebræos, Christus heri ac hodiè ac in æternum. Et de Abrahamo pronunciatur in Evangelio, quod Christi diem viderit & lætatus sit. Unde non est firma ea connexio, caro & sanguis Christi nondum per Œconomiam seu dispensationem temporis fuerant assumta, non potuerunt ergo esse Veteribus spiritualis cibus & potus. Nam cùm salus Patrum, quemadmodum nostra, penderet à morte & sanguine Christi, oporteat eos, ut nos, ista fide complecti, alioquin salutem non habuissent. Mors, caro, & sanguis Christi, tametsi non adhuc exstabant in natura, (addo, naturaliter scilicet ac corporaliter, spiritualiter tamen & supernaturaliter non minùs atque nunc, postquam naturaliter localiterque cælum occupat, nec per descensum naturalem Cœnis nostris sacris sese immiscet) attamen ad servandos Patres vim ac efficaciam habere potuerunt. Unde pro ratione sui temporis in suis Sacramentis illa eadem quæ nos consequebantur. Divinam personam, id est, filium Dei præsentem habebant, quem fide complectebantur, & quidem cum hac promissione, vel, ut ita dicam, cum hoc respectu ad humanam naturam, quod eam esset assumturus: Atque hoc discrimen est inter Christum, quòd ipsi accipiebant & quòd modò nos sumimus: Nam quod illi per fidem faciendum præsentiebant, nos jam factum confitemur. Hic idem Martyr duabus præterea speciosis admodum Objectionibus … planissimè & solidissimè satisfacit.
english: Objection: how could ancients receive Christ sacramentally before flesh assumed and blood shed? Petrus Martyr: before God (and for faithful spiritual eating) death, blood-shedding, and flesh-assumption were always present and accepted — Lamb slain from the world’s foundation; Christ yesterday and forever; Abraham saw His day.

Flesh not yet in nature corporally could still save the Fathers spiritually; they held the Son by faith under promise of the nature to be assumed — we confess what they foresaw as already done. Martyr also answers two further specious objections solidly.

source_text: Alterum Argumentum ex decimo Capite prioris Epistolæ ad Corinthios, desumtum, ab ea Communione poculi benedictionis cum sanguine Christi, & ea communione panis fracti cum corpore Christi petitum est, quæ similis existit communioni & in unum corpus coalitiioni eorum, qui ejusdem panis Dominici, vel etiam tou henos artou cum articulo, i. e. ejusdem panis spiritualis, seu Christi Domini ipsius participes fiunt? Ita enim Christus vers. 16. & 17. Poculum benedictionis, cui benedicimus, nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est? panis quem frangimus, nonne communicatio corporis Christi est? Nam unus est panis, unum corpus multi sumus: nam omnes ex eodem pane participamus. At horum Unio in idem corpus communioque, non est corporalis, sed Spiritualis.
english: Second argument (1 Cor. 10:16–17): communion of the cup of blessing with Christ’s blood and of the broken bread with His body is like coalescing into one body as partakers of the one spiritual bread — Christ Himself.
That union into one body is not corporal but Spiritual.

source_text: Subjicitur Tertium Argumentum versu proximo 18. à Communione Israëlitarum sacrificantium & ex sacrificiis pacificis comedentium, cum ipso Deo ejusque Altari; Itemque Quartum vers. 20. & 21. à Communione Gentium, Dæmoniis immolantium & horum mensæ participantium, cum ipsis Dæmoniis, haustum, his Apostoli verbis: Cernite Israelem qui est secundum carnem: Nonne qui edunt victimas, consortes fiunt altaris? Imò verò dico, quæ immolant Gentes Dæmoniis immolant: Nolim autem vos consortes Dæmoniorum esse. Utraque verò Communio, tum Israëlitarum Deo sacrificantium cum Deo ejusque altari, tùm gentium Dæmoniis immolantium mensæque horum communicantium, cum Diabolo & hujus Mensa, non Corporalis exinde, sed Spiritualis, maximè interim realis erat & substantialis.
english: Third (v. 18): Israel’s sacrificers eating peace-offerings are partners of the altar with God — a spiritual, yet most real and substantial, communion.
Fourth (vv. 20–21): Gentile demon-sacrificers share the demons’ table — likewise spiritual, not corporal, yet real; Paul will not have us partners of demons.

source_text: Posterius seu Undecimum ad Corinthios caput Pauli, eatenus potissimum veræ Sententiæ de S. Cœna fundandæ inservit, quòd Paulus in eo, ex ore Christi, Institutionis verba, idque cum emphatica quâdam interpretatione repetit, quâ & panem non simpliciter Corpus Christi, sed corpus pro nobis fractum vers. 24.; Poculum verò, seu vinum in poculo, non simpliciter sanguinem Christi, sed Novum illud pactum per sanguinem suum vers. 25. salutat (hôc pacto Propositiones Sacramentales improprias seu tropicas luculentissimo modo declarans, præsentiam interim ac participationem, tam corporis, quàm carnis Christi spiritualem, neutiquam inficiatus) in sequentibus immediatè versiculis tribus 26. 27. & 28., Sacramentum S. Cœnæ ex duabus rebus, cœlesti & terrestri, non minus, post, quàm ante consecrationis dicta vulgò verba, constare, nec harum alteram in alterius substantiam i. e. panem & vinum in corpus & sanguinem Christi, converti aut transmutari edocturus, panem crebriùs & poculum ingeminat, dicens: Quotiescunque ederitis panem hunc & poculum hoc biberitis &c. Itaque quisquis ederit panem hunc indignè &c. Exploret autem quisque seipsum & edat de pane hoc. &c.
english: 1 Cor. 11 chiefly founds the true Supper sentence: Paul repeats Institution from Christ’s mouth with emphasis — bread as body broken for us (v. 24); cup as the New covenant through His blood (v. 25) — tropical propositions, without denying spiritual presence and participation.
Vv. 26–28: the sacrament is two things, celestial and terrestrial, after consecration as before — bread and wine are not converted into body and blood; he keeps saying this bread / this cup.
Stop before §.V (Pauline true sentence lasting through the Apostolic first age).

source_text: §. V. Expositam hactenus Paulinam de S. Cœna Mentem Sententiamque veram, Christi Verbis Institutionis æquè atque horum Commentario Antecedaneo, Joh. cap. 6. tradito, exactè congruam, totô æræ Christianæ seculô Primô, i. e. Apostolicô, perdurasse, eoque omnium Apostolorum horumque Discipulorum (quos inter Polycarpus, Johannis Discipulus, numeratur) probatam calculo fuisse, haud absurdè intelligi datur.
english: §.V: the Pauline true Supper sentence — matching Institution and the John 6 antecedent commentary — lasted through the whole Apostolic first age.
All the Apostles and their disciples (Polycarp among them, John’s disciple) may fairly be read as approving it.

source_text: Ex Act. 2. 42., ubi Judæi, mediante Petri sermone, ad Christianismum noviter conversi, iidemque primi omnium, proskarterountes, i. e. assiduè atque perpetuò incumbentes sistuntur, non tantum didachē tōn Apostolōn, Doctrinæ, etiam de Cœna, Apostolicæ, sed & tē koinōnia ab Apostolo 1. Cor. 10. à vers. 16. ad 20. inclusivè expositæ.
english: Acts 2:42: Jews newly converted by Peter’s sermon — the first of all — kept attending assiduously (proskarterountes).
Not only to the Apostles’ teaching (didachē), including on the Supper, but also to the koinōnia Paul sets out in 1 Cor. 10:16–20.

source_text: I. e. tàm cum Christo ejusque corpore & sanguine, quàm inter se, Communioni spirituali, huicq; junctæ tē klasei tou artou, i. e. fractioni panis, to sōma hyper hymōn klōmenon præfiguranti, & semper præfiguraturæ, 1. Cor. 11. 24.
english: That koinōnia is spiritual communion with Christ and His body and blood, and among themselves.
Joined to it is the breaking of bread — always prefiguring the body broken for you (1 Cor. 11:24).

source_text: Quorum Christianorum puta primorum hoc pacto Communio seu koinōnia fuit, cum Apostolis fuit, & uti istorum, ita ritè communicantium quorumvis, per omnia secula, cum iisdem, eoque simul koinōnia meta tou patros kai meta tou huiou Iēsou Christou, Communio & cum Patre Cœlesti & cum Filio ejus Theanthrōpō Jesu Christo, semperq; mansura, 1. Joh. 1. 3.; at Spiritualis, quandoquidem Christus, utut venit non tō hydati monon, all' en tō hydati kai tō haimati.
english: So the first Christians’ koinōnia with the Apostles — and of every rightly communicating person through all ages — is at once communion with the heavenly Father and with His Son the God-man Jesus Christ (1 John 1:3), always to remain.
Yet it is Spiritual: Christ came not by water only but by water and blood.

source_text: Tamen id ipsum præstitit hunc in modum, ut to pneuma fuerit to martyroun hoti to pneuma estin hē alētheia, Joh. 5. v. 6. coll. cum Joh. cap. 6. v. 63. h. e. ut Spiritus testatus fuerit, Spiritum esse Veritatem, Spiritum item vivificare, verbaque Christi de participatione Corporis & Sanguinis sui, esse Spiritum & vitam.
english: He did it so that the Spirit should bear witness that the Spirit is the truth (1 John 5:6 with John 6:63).
The Spirit is Truth; the Spirit quickens; Christ’s words on participating His Body and Blood are Spirit and life.

source_text: Ut hôc ipsô, post deductam ab origine, per totius primi Seculi Christiani decursum, veram de S. Cœna Doctrinam, nunc promptô pede ad succedentia Secula liceat nobis pertendere, primorum Patrum testimoniis eandem adstructuris & confirmaturis. Equidem nos hâc operâ levatos per quorundam Protestantium Doctorum egregiam industriam, Pontificias Novitates, circa S. Cœnam demolientium, Joh. Oecolampadii, Philippi Melanchtonis, Martini Chemnitii, Danielis Chamieri, & novissimè Johannis Cosini nec non Joh. Guil. Bajeri, probè novimus; ne tamen Historica hæc Opella nostra hiulca evadat, haud gravabimur ex his ipsis Autoribus, singulorum seculorum saltem puriorum testes pro veritate, vel binos, vel ad summum tres, advocare, in quorum ore & hæc veritas immota perstet, si in antecessum hoc unicum monuerimus, nominatos Veterum Testimoniorum collectores, etsi diversæ Protestantium Sectæ addictos, eadem tamen propemodum ex quinque præsertim Seculis prioribus, hac proculdubio de causa adduxisse, vel non potuisse non adducere, quòd in iis res ipsa solummodò, i. e. duarum rerum, cœlestis & terrestris, Signati & Signi, in legitimo S. Cœnæ usu, præsentia & participatio, citra vel ullum præsentiæ & participationis rei alterius, Signati scil. modum, vel cum hujus solo, duntaxat spirituali modo, ab utraque Protestantium parte concesso, inculcare deprehenduntur.
english: Doctrine now traced from the origin through the whole first Christian age — we may step on to later ages with early Fathers to confirm it.
Protestant collectors (Oecolampadius, Melanchthon, Chemnitz, Chamier, Cosin, Baier) already demolished Pontifical novelties; we still take two or three witnesses per purer age from them.

Both sides cite nearly the same from the first five ages: presence of two things (celestial & terrestrial / Signified & Sign) with only the spiritual mode of the Signified conceded. Stop before §.VI (second century: Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus).

source_text: §. VI. Itaque SECULO Apostolicum proximè excipiente, i. e. Christianæ æræ SECUNDO, dictam de Eucharistia sententiam veram à Christo & Apostolis sibi traditam, apertè satis professi sunt Martyres Christi præstantissimi, IGNATIUS Antiochenus, Seculi hujus initiô; JUSTINUS MARTYR medio, nec non IRENÆUS, sub finem ejusdem celebres, ita verò veritatem Eucharisticam professi, ut primus ad præcipuam Eucharistiæ partem, fide sola tenendam; secundus, ne pars hæc adesse sola crederetur, ad minus principalem, in præcipuam neutiquam transmutandam; Tertius denique, ad utramque, nec non ad utriusq; cùm præsentiam ac participationem, tùm præsentiæ & participationis modum, & suæ, & nostrum omnium, Mentis oculos conversos voluerit.
english: §.VI: in the SECOND Christian age after the Apostolic, the leading martyrs openly professed the true Eucharistic sentence from Christ and the Apostles.

Ignatius (start) turns the mind to the chief part held by faith alone; Justin (middle) to the lesser part not to be turned into the chief; Irenaeus (end) to both — presence, participation, and their mode.

source_text: IGNATII verba leguntur in Epistola ad Smyrenses, quibus affirmat: Eucharistiam esse Carnem Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi, quæ pro peccatis nostris passa est, quam Pater suâ benignitate suscitavit. Quæ verba proptereà fidei sublestæ neutiquam censenda, nec miserè interpolatis Ignatii superstitibus Scriptis adhuc, accensenda, quod illa etiam Seculo Vtô Theodoretus commemorat, Dialogo tertio apathēs seu impatibilis ditô.
english: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans: the Eucharist is the Flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins and which the Father raised.
Not to be written off as weak faith or among interpolated Ignatian writings — Theodoret in the fifth century still cites them in Dialogue 3 (apathēs / Impassible).

source_text: JUSTINUS MARTYR panem Eucharisticum, etiam post consecrationem, eundem permanere, inque alimoniam carnis nostræ (etsi vulgaris amplius non sit, utpote fidelibus communionem corporis Christi tributurus) edocere annisus, in Apol. 2. ad Antoninum Imperatorem prope finem, ita disserit: Postquam Præses gratias egit & acclamavit populus, illi qui à nobis dicuntur Diaconi, seu Ministri, dant cuique præsentium, quod sumant de pane & vino: Et hoc alimentum à nobis vocatur Eucharistia; Non enim ut vulgarem panem, neque ut vulgare poculum hæc sumimus: Sed quemadmodum per verbum Dei, Caro factus Jesus Christus Servator noster, carnem & sanguinem pro salute nostra habuit, sic etiam per verbum precationis & gratiarum actionis, sacratam ab ipso alimoniam, QUÆ MUTATA NUTRIT NOSTRAS CARNES ET SANGUINEM, illius incarnati Jesu carnem & sanguinem esse didicimus. Ad hoc respiciens Cosinus Episcopus Dunelmensis, adductis à se quoque Justini verbis sequens epiphonema annexit: Quare, inquit, & substantia panis etiam post Consecrationem manet & verè corruptibilis cibus est, quod de Christi corpore immortali dici non potest: Neque enim caro Christi carnem nostram alit, nec in eam mutatur, sed cibus iste, qui sacramentaliter Caro Christi dicitur. Caro autem Christi nutrit ad vitam æternam. cit. loc. p. 58.
english: Justin (Apol. 2): after consecration the Eucharistic bread remains the same and feeds our flesh — no longer common, yet the food ‘changed’ that nourishes our flesh and blood we have learned is the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus.

Cosinus of Durham: therefore bread-substance remains after consecration as truly corruptible food — Christ’s immortal body does not nourish or change into our flesh; this food is sacramentally called Christ’s Flesh, which nourishes unto eternal life.

source_text: IRENÆUS tandem uti prolixius ac crebrius, ita & plenius distinctiusve, rem veritatemque Eucharisticam persequitur. Primò quidem, Librô contra Hæreses quarto cap. 34. ex duabus rebus S. Eucharistiam constare disertissimè ratus: Panis, inquit, qui est à terra, percipiens invocationem Dei, jam non communis panis est, sed Eucharistia, duabus rebus constans, terrena & cælestis. Ubi observes velim, divum Martyrem (1) Panem post consecrationem factam, non amplius communem, sed ab omni communi usu sejunctum, interim tamen adhuc panem salutare. (2) Panem hunc ab omni communi usu separatum, non dicere ipsum corpus Christi, quasi in hoc transmutatum, sed verò Eucharistiam, i. e. panem, Eucharistiæ S. destinatum consecratumque.
english: Irenaeus (Adv. Haer. 4.34) more fully: the Sacred Eucharist consists of two things — earthly and heavenly. Bread from earth receiving God’s invocation is no longer common bread but Eucharist.

(1) After consecration it is still bread, only severed from common use. (2) That separated bread is not itself Christ’s body as if transmuted — it is Eucharist: bread destined and consecrated for the sacrament.

source_text: (3) Eucharistiam S., non verò panem, ex duabus rebus censere constare, ne quis cum pane, etiam extra usum Eucharistiæ legitimum, corpus Christi conjungi arbitretur. (4) Duarum rerum alteram, terrenam vocitare, scil. panem è terra natum, alteram verò cælestem, eòque non corpus Christi naturaliter seu corporaliter præsens, quod ipsum corpus res cælestis, non nisi per Hæresin Manichaicam, juxta Spiritûs S. verò mentem, res omnino terrena haberi debet, ex Massa Mariæ sanguinea formata, in utero ejusdem concepta, fota, nutrita, definitô tempore, ex utero materno in mundi lucem egressa, nobis & nostris Infantibus per omnia, etiam ratione præsentiæ localis, unico exceptô peccatô, simillima, Sed verò ob cœlestem unicè ac supernaturalem in Eucharistia præsentiæ modum, cælestis dicta, animarum nostrarum fidelium, eatenus ex cœlo, quin ex Spiritu S. natarum, genuinum pabulum, etiam in corporibus fidelium, saluberrimum usum olim habiturum, i. e. horum beatam ad vitam æternam, procuraturum resurrectionem.
english: (3) The two things belong to the Eucharist, not to the bread alone — lest Christ’s body be joined to bread even outside lawful use. (4) Earthly = bread from earth; heavenly is not Christ’s body naturally/corporally present (that body is an earthly thing from Mary’s mass, like us except sin).
It is called heavenly for the solely supernatural presence-mode in the Eucharist — genuine food of faithful souls from the Spirit, someday serving even their bodies toward blessed resurrection.

source_text: Ita enim iterum Irenæus Lib. 5. contra Hæret. cap. 12. pergit: Quemadmodum granum tritici, decidens in terram & dissolutum, multiplex surgit, & percipiens verbum Dei fit Eucharistia; (quod est corpus & sanguis Christi); Sic & nostra, scil. fidelium, corpora, ex eo nutrita, & reposita in terram ac resoluta, resurgent (scil. cum gaudio) in suo tempore. Quin, ne quis sibi imaginetur, sanctissimum Patrem opinari, corpora nostra corpore Christi nutriri, non verò pane Eucharistico potius ab omni usu communi sejuncto, addit paulò post: Per Creaturam nutrimur, Creaturam autem ipse nobis præstat; Cùm Calicem, qui est creatura, suum sanguinem, & eum panem, qui est creatura, suum Corpus confirmavit. Quando ergo Calix & panis percipiunt verbum Dei, fit Eucharistia sanguinis & corporis Christi (non ipse sanguis & corpus Christi) ex quibus (calice scil. & pane) augetur & consistit carnis nostræ substantia. Quandoquidem non sine magna absurditate impietateque diceretur, ex naturali Christi corpore & sanguine, nostra corpora augeri ac consistere; cùm nihil corpus nostrum naturaliter augere possit, nisi quod per alterationem in carnem nostram & sanguinem convertitur, quod de corpore Christi incorruptibili affirmare blasphemum est.
english: Irenaeus Adv. Haer. 5.12: as wheat falls, dissolves, and rises manifold into Eucharist (body and blood of Christ), so faithful bodies nourished from it shall rise. We are nourished by the Creature He supplies — cup and bread as creature confirmed as His blood and Body.

When cup and bread receive God’s word there is made the Eucharist of His blood and body — not the blood and body themselves — from which our flesh’s substance increases. To say our bodies grow from Christ’s natural incorruptible body would be absurd and blasphemous.
Stop before §.VII (third century: Tertullian).

source_text: §. VII. SECULI TERTII Professor Veritatis Eucharisticæ primus TERTULLIANUS meritô suô inducitur, quippe ipso Seculi initio in flore constitutus, unâque ac eâdem sententiâ tàm Verborum Eucharisticorum Christi: Hoc est corpus meum, improprietatem disertissimè confessus, quam veram nihilominus veri corporis Christi in cœna præsentiam testatus.
english: §.VII opens the THIRD century with Tertullian as first professor of Eucharistic truth — in flower at the age’s start.
In one sentence he both confesses the impropriety of Christ’s words ‘This is my body’ and attests the true presence of Christ’s true body in the supper.

source_text: At inquit, Christus acceptum panem & distributum Discipulis, Corpus suum illum fecit, dicendo: Hoc est corpus meum, i. e. FIGURA CORPORIS MEI; Figura verò non fuisset, nisi VERITATIS FUISSET CORPUS: Res enim vacua, ut est phantasma, figuram capere non potest. Contra Marcionem lib. 4. c. 40.
english: Contra Marcionem 4.40: Christ made the bread taken and given to the disciples His Body by saying ‘This is my body’ — that is, the FIGURE OF MY BODY.
It would not be a figure unless it were a BODY OF TRUTH: an empty phantasm cannot take a figure.

source_text: Quanquam Idem Tertullianus, alibi, nempe Libro de Resurrectione Carnis, etiam præsentiam corporis Christi in Eucharistia ferè corporalem inculcasse legatur, scribens: Caro (nostra) corpore & sanguine Christi vescitur, ut & anima de Deo saginetur: Id quod ceteris Patris hujus, jure alioquin venerandi, erroribus, vel in vulgus eruditorum notis, annumerandum eô fuerit, quia vel ipsi Transsubstantiatores, à nutritione carnis nostræ propriè dicta per corpus Christi, in S. cœna sumtum, omninò abhorrent, ut suprà diximus.
english: Elsewhere (De Resurrectione Carnis) Tertullian seems to push a nearly corporal presence: our flesh is fed with Christ’s body and blood so the soul may be fattened from God.
Count that among his otherwise venerable errors — even Transsubstantiators wholly abhor proper nutrition of our flesh by Christ’s body taken in the supper.

source_text: Rectius Seculi ejusdem Doctor proximus, utut non minus, ob allegoricas Scripturarum Interpretationes justo crebriores, erroribus aliquot exstantioribus scatentes, quàm ob multarum Veritatum sacrarum expositionem verè sublimem, famâ inter Theologos celebratus, ORIGENES puta, non improprietatem tantùm verborum Christi: Hoc est corpus meum, unà cum præsentia corporis Christi reali, in S.
